+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 74.8
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Chapter Two: The Invitation Arthur Neegan had known that power was an unpleasant fact of life, but he had not expected it to provide him with an air-conditioned chair. The transfer vessel was a long steel tube wrapped around an engine and a water tank. It smelled of warm insulation and the synthetic lavender of Antares air recyclers. Through a porthole, Mars was a copper-coloured coin, slowly shrinking. A small display screen on the wall cycled through various system diagnostics in green text: REACTOR OUTPUT, 99.4 PERCENT; CABIN PRESSURE, 0.91 ATMOSPHERES; GRAVITY INVERTER, STABLE; EXTERNAL HATCH, SEALED. He regarded the last entry as a courtesy. Four years earlier, Arthur had acquired a Martian water allocation and a mining lease. Eleven seconds of core analysis had turned both into matters of planetary importance. According to the manifest, he was now “protected personnel.” He had not known the term was so literal. Nineteen hours earlier, six armed men and an unarmed woman had stood between Arthur and his mining drill. The men’s weapons were slung, not hidden. Their grey uniforms bore a red six-pointed star crossed by a gold arrow: the insignia of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. Antares supplied Mars with seed banks, air compressors, legal codes, and most of the private army. It was said to have brought civilization. The air compressors, at least, came with leases. The woman, Director Noll Venn, smiled. “Mr. Neegan, you are invited to a meeting off-world concerning your discovery and the people dependent on it. Attendance is mandatory.” “That is a conscription, not an invitation.” “A courtesy, nonetheless. If we wished to arrest you, you would already be aboard.” “And if I say no?” “Your claim would remain in indefinite escrow. Your neighbours would be questioned. You would remain on Mars until transport could be arranged.” “Which could take a long time.” “We have a great deal of experience in waiting.” Her men never changed position. A rifle muzzle rested beside a potted plant, neither quite accidental nor quite threatening. There were cheaper ways to invite a neighbour to dinner. “Who requested the meeting?” “Various parties. None publicly.” “A conspiracy.” “No. A government.” “Antares, for instance?” “Antares believes your discovery should be contained.” “The Water Commission says the vein belongs to Mars. The Miners’ Union says it belongs to nobody. The Assembly says it belongs to the Assembly. The Terran government says the Assembly cannot be trusted. Antares says it can, provided Antares supplies the guards.” “The Assembly wishes to hear your opinion.” “For the first time, that is interesting.” “They do not usually succeed.” “The Assembly sent you?” “Of course not. They prefer to appear uninvolved.” Arthur had not heard the word. Venn was already moving towards the door. Mars had six million settlers and could not spare a cubic metre of water for luxury. Earth had nine billion people and could not decide which of them deserved the next litre. Between those numbers lay the Azra vein: a corporate dispute in a place where corporations counted planets. “You say attendance is compulsory. I assume that means I must come willingly.” “We prefer that, Mr. Neegan. It is a principle of good administration.” “And if I remain here?” “You would make that decision. It would be honored. The rest of your life would not be.” “And my wife?” “She will accompany you. An unidentified trust has offered accommodation on Ceres.” “I don’t know this trust.” “No. That is what the meeting is for.” “How long will I be gone?” “Long enough to be useful.” Arthur had been promised safe conduct, protection, and transportation. What he had not been promised was a way back. Nineteen days later, he stood on Ceres and missed a horizon. The colony was a wheel turning around its own axle, connected to other wheels and visiting ships by long spokes. Corridors combined the hush of a night garden with the vibration of engines. Signs offered water, oxygen, citizenship, and eight competing employment agencies. A kiosk sold real Martian soil by the kilogram, with a guarantee concerning neither its purity nor its previous owners. In a private office, a woman without insignia sat behind a table of simulated wood. An orchid grew beneath a lamp. Coffee steamed in a cup she had not touched. “Director Venn?” “No. I represent the Mars Continuity Trust. Its capital is on Ceres, its charter is filed on Earth, and its beneficial owners are deliberately obscure.” “Why deliberately?” “Because some of them are military. Others are industrial. The rest are frightened. If you knew their names, you would have fewer friends.” “People are easier to trust when they can be held responsible.” “That is why my employers keep me in front.” She slid a wafer across the table. “Five million credits, a research post, a home on Ceres, and a guaranteed water allocation for the families working your lease. In exchange, we receive your claim, your original core samples, and your signature.” “For how long?” “Forty years.” “Who owns Azra then?” “The trust, in perpetuity.” “A trust is a convenient shelf on which to hide a committee.” “It is also how one avoids appointing another Antares.” “Your employers are remarkably confident.” “They are buying insurance. The name on the document does not matter nearly so much as the signature beneath it.” “And what does my signature accomplish?” “It establishes that these samples are preliminary. A forty-year moratorium follows: no industrial extraction without independent verification and Terran approval.” “And Azra remains where it is.” “Azra remains where it is, while your neighbours receive priority employment. Whoever benefits can wait. The weapons interests cannot.” “Who exactly are these weapons interests?” “Officially? Nobody. Unofficially, several departments of several governments, together with people who sell governments by the metric ton.” “Do you represent them?” “Only their need for a good answer. There are men on Earth who want to put Azra in a bomb, and others who want to put it in a drive. Both begin with the same question: is this sample authentic?” “And I am to answer it.” “You are to certify it. That is all.” “That is never all. That is the beginning of an argument whose conclusion someone has already decided.” “Which is why the stakes are in the signature. The Army wants a weapon, the Combine wants a monopoly, and the Corporations want profit. We want the process to take four decades. You would prefer eight hours of uncertainty.” Arthur had never heard of the Mars Continuity Trust. That was perhaps the most reassuring thing about it. “And if I refuse?” “Then the mining application proceeds tomorrow. There will be no more credits, no more water allocations, and no more meetings. Your neighbours will return to being merely people the corporations can afford to ignore.” “So you are not buying a lease. You are buying a vote.” “Yes.” “Whose?” “Mine, for the moment. Perhaps yours, after.” Outside, the transfer vessel waited against the docking collar, its green diagnostics cycling endlessly. It had carried him from a quiet house on Mars to a room where the future of a world was being negotiated as a private transaction. Arthur looked at the pen, then at the woman. “Suppose I ask for time.” “You have four hours. The offer expires when the ship leaves. After that, the Board will consider someone else.” “Someone less competent?” “Someone more desperate. Desperation is an excellent substitute for engineering judgment.” “And the Board?” “Twenty-one directors, represented by nine lawyers, and a chairwoman who has not spoken in six years. The last director, for example, is a retired ambassador who communicates through a clerk. The second-last is a Martian hydroponics cooperative with no money and no interest in your death. Both are voting. This is why civilization is best managed by nobody in particular.” “Your employers sound remarkably sophisticated.” “They prefer to be called sponsors. Sponsors are paid in gratitude. Governors are paid in other things.” “Then the name does matter.” “It does. But only for bookkeeping.” Arthur Neegan looked toward the porthole. He had wanted to report a mineral discovery, and instead had become a mineral discovery, with a price, a lawyer, and a rifle. The woman tapped the table. “Four hours, Mr. Neegan. The Board does not wait for conscience.” “Neither does history,” Arthur said. “That is why it is late.” He picked up the pen, and discovered, to his surprise, that the hand holding it was steady. The offer was enormous, the safeguards were not, and somewhere beyond the station a transport was still being loaded for Earth. He signed his name. Beneath it, the wafer displayed a second line he had not seen.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent pastiche of Asimov: dialogue-driven, cerebral, with big-picture political intrigue (Azra as a strategic resource, competing Earth/Mars/Antares interests) and small-picture world-building (water allocations, kiosks selling Martian soil). The prose is clean and understated, with some genuinely good lines ("He had wanted to report a mineral discovery, and instead had become a mineral discovery"). The dialogue is crisp and aphoristic in a way that evokes Asimov's style, though it occasionally becomes too clever and stilted — characters speak in polished epigrams rather than natural speech. The chapter structure follows the prompt: armed retinue, invitation, off-world meeting, offer made, hints of larger stakes. The ending cliffhanger (the second line on the wafer) is effective but slightly cheap. The flashback structure (nineteen hours earlier) is handled adequately. Weaknesses: the dialogue occasionally feels like a chess match of quips rather than human conversation; the woman without insignia is under-characterized; some exposition is delivered too directly through dialogue; the emotional register is cool throughout, which fits Asimov but limits emotional engagement. The piece is coherent and never meanders. It is somewhat unsurprising in its beats (mysterious benefactor, ticking-clock offer) but executes them well. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 63.2
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations At twenty-five, I filled silences and made plans. Then I met Elliot, and taking charge became something I had to question. I noticed him in the third week of experimental photography. Silver rings crowded his fingers; black eyeliner followed his eyes with surgical precision. A thrift-shop jacket had storm-gray velvet sleeves, and mesh showed the edge of a tattoo. He dressed like a beautiful argument against ordinary expectations, but he didn’t perform it. In the back row, he asked incisive questions and seemed to remember everything everyone said. His name was Elliot. He was nineteen and sat three rows ahead of me, though he seemed less interested in status than in the work. I learned he used he/him the first week, when someone misread his name and he corrected them so gently I almost missed it. My attraction had a favorite silhouette: broad shoulders, a low voice, a clean masculine edge. Not a rule, only a habit. Elliot blurred those edges, but he wasn’t vague. He was exact. He knew which words he meant and offered them without force. Shy without being submissive, he made every assumption I’d brought into the studio feel unnecessary. When the final-project pairs were posted, I tried not to smile at our names together. The brief required a portrait built from opposing instincts: my appetite for structure and, I guessed, his for accident. I claimed the enlarger and brought coffee. He set out the paper and chemistry with a care that made my fussing look theatrical. He took his black with two sugars, a tiny detail I tucked away. More than that, I noticed how he held the timer: gently, but with complete confidence. “Film first,” he said. “Talk later.” “I like that,” I said, meaning more than the order of operations. Under the safelight, the room turned the color of a pulse. We worked shoulder to shoulder, our shadows faint and intimate. Elliot hummed while the print developed, a soft, wandering tune with no obvious beginning. At first I thought he was nervous. Then I stopped deciding what his sounds meant. “Don’t rush the bath,” I said, too close to his ear. I felt him smile more than saw it. “That’s different from film first.” “I contain multitudes.” “Clearly.” His quiet laugh moved through me. Our hands passed over the tongs, and the air between our wrists seemed charged. “About wanting things, I’m usually more certain,” I told him. He glanced at me. The red light softened his expression, and I wanted to close the distance, take charge, make the wanting simple. Instead, I handed him the timer. “Choose the exposure. I’ll adjust the aperture.” Later, he asked, “Do you think people can recognize themselves in a photograph?” There were clever answers about composition and memory, but his voice stopped me. “Why are you asking?” He turned a print in the fixer, watching his hands emerge. “I’ve been questioning my gender, and how I express it. I still use he/him. But being a boy doesn’t always fit the way I imagined. I like softness when I want it. I like being perceived as a man. Neither cancels the other, but they don’t add up to a shape I recognize. I don’t know what it means yet.” Then: “I wanted someone to know before I figured out what knowing means.” “I can work with not knowing,” I said. “I wasn’t asking for a solution.” “I know. My first instinct is to give you one anyway.” I wanted to tell him it was fine, that I understood, that he didn’t have to be afraid. Instead, I swallowed my first answer and asked, “What do you want from me?” “To listen.” “That I can do.” He looked up. “You like me?” “I really, inconveniently, do.” He smiled cautiously. “That’s helpful. In a confusing sort of way.” “I can be confusing and supportive. Ask me about the second one.” We laughed, and some of the pressure in the room changed shape. I hadn’t promised certainty. I’d offered a place where uncertainty wouldn’t cost him my welcome. Then he leaned into my space, and the certainty I usually demanded broke open. I wanted to pull him closer, answer every question with my mouth. Instead, I asked, “Can I kiss you?” He nodded. The kiss was gentle, brief, and entirely welcome. His softness felt like attention, not surrender. When we drew apart, I kept my hands to myself and let the moment be enough. “Very assertive,” he said. “You asked.” “I contain multitudes.” He smiled. Nothing about him had become an answer. He wasn’t a project to solve, and his uncertainty wasn’t an invitation to take over. I wanted him, but I didn’t get to decide who he was becoming. The print revealed his hands around the enlarger, silver rings dark in the red light. It had his patience and my appetite for structure, an accident we’d spent three hours avoiding. “This is you,” I said. “How can you tell?” “I don’t. But look how you’re holding the camera. Like it agrees with you.” He considered that. I watched him decide not to dismiss it, and that small restraint made my throat ache. He resumed his unfinished tune. I no longer heard it as an invitation to rush in. By semester’s end, I had learned to offer help without making it an order, and to ask questions without demanding answers. My attraction didn’t have to obey the outlines I’d given it. I still responded to broad shoulders and low voices. I also responded to velvet at Elliot’s wrists, rings tapping the enlarger table, intelligence in a pause. None of it erased what I usually wanted. It widened it. He hadn’t made me less decisive. I’d found more ways to be decisive: making plans, defending privacy, holding still when someone else needed to choose. I could be exactly myself and still be surprised. On the last night, he hummed that unfinished melody while our final print rose in the developer. I wanted to tell him I knew how his story would end. I didn’t. He was still he/him, still exploring, still allowed to be certain and unfinished in the same breath. That was the revelation I kept returning to: a darkroom never demanded a finished image. You could develop what was there, fix it, hang it in the light, and choose to make another exposure. When he looked at me, I took his hand. “Still here?” I asked. “Still deciding,” he said. “Good.” I leaned my shoulder against his. The safelight made no promises. It held us in the color of beginning, and I let the next frame belong to both of us.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a confident, controlled narrative that hits nearly every beat requested by the prompt: the darkroom setting, the red-light confessional atmosphere, Dani's assertiveness complicated by Elliot's vulnerability, her confusion about her own attractions, and the tender awkwardness of their exchange. The central metaphor—developing images, unfinished exposures, the darkroom that "never demanded a finished image"—is threaded through the piece with real discipline, giving the story structural unity rather than decorative flourish. Strengths: The dialogue is the standout. It's clipped, oblique, and character-specific—"Film first. Talk later," "I contain multitudes," "Still deciding." The callback of "I contain multitudes" from Dani to Elliot is a lovely touch of intimacy-through-borrowed language. Dani's internal struggle is dramatized rather than merely stated: she repeatedly suppresses her instinct to take charge ("Instead, I handed him the timer," "Instead, I asked, 'Can I kiss you?'"), which shows the tension between control and agency in action. The prose is clean and rhythmic, with occasional striking images ("He dressed like a beautiful argument against ordinary expectations," "the room turned the color of a pulse"). Weaknesses: The piece occasionally tips into aphorism-overload. Lines like "His softness felt like attention, not surrender," "an accident we'd spent three hours avoiding," and the closing paragraphs stack abstractions so densely that the emotional moments sometimes feel narrated rather than lived. The ending's summary reflections ("I had learned to offer help without making it an order") drift toward essayistic telling, and the final paragraphs compress a semester's arc into exposition that would land harder if dramatized. Some phrasing is over-polished to the point of preciousness ("intelligence in a pause"). The kiss scene, while sweet, resolves the tension a touch easily; Elliot's caution evaporates quickly given the setup of his tentativeness. The piece is also somewhat predictable in trajectory—once the premise is established, the story moves along expected lines without subverting or deepening beyond its stated themes. Still, the character work is genuinely nuanced: Elliot is given specificity (his gentle correction of pronouns, the unfinished hum, "I wasn't asking for a solution"), and Dani's self-interrogation feels earned rather than performative. The voice is consistent, the tone controlled, and the emotional complexity real. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 80.0
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma ### I. Trevi Fountain, 8:07 Ben had found a place on the fountain’s lower steps, his back against warm stone and *Renaissance Poets and the Architecture of Memory* balanced on his knees. The guidebook beside him claimed this was where a great artist had found inspiration. The artist, presumably, had faced fewer interruptions. A motorcycle stopped with a squeal of brakes an inch from his knees. *Porca—* He flung himself backwards, scattering guidebooks, half a coffee, and his remaining dignity. The rider kicked down the stand. Her helmet vanished into a battered leather bag, revealing glossy black curls and a square jaw. She looked him over with the unhurried confidence of someone who had never once doubted her right to exist. “Sorry—*mi dispiace!*” “*Dispiace* is ‘I’m sorry,’” she said. “Not ‘I am regretting the entire morning.’” “I stepped on your foot.” “You did. You may add ‘clumsy’ to the Italian.” “I’m sorry.” She laughed. “You really are English, aren’t you?” “Ben.” “Alessandra. I saw your name on your bag.” She offered her hand. He shook it, then knocked his paper cup into the fountain. For a moment they watched it bob away among the silver coins. “Ben,” Alessandra said, “where are you going?” “Eventually? The British School at the Baths of Diocletian.” “*Andiamo?*” “Exactly.” He added *per favore*, a word he had been attaching to questions all morning. Alessandra’s eyes danced. “But first,” she continued, “I’m going to show you the Rome that isn’t in the book.” ### II. An Unscheduled Grand Tour, 10:15 Five minutes later, Ben was crossing Via del Corso with a hand hooked firmly through his elbow. “I don’t know where we’re going.” “That is rather the point.” “Can I have some indication?” “No.” She bought two cornetti from a bakery and handed him one without asking whether he was hungry. He ate it anyway. At a bookshop, she drew him into an argument with the proprietor about an unpublished translation. When the shopkeeper turned away, something small and blue disappeared into her jacket. A tiny Colosseum, Ben realised. One from the tray by the register. He looked at the tray, then at her. She caught his eye and mouthed, *Relax.* In a doorway, a display of lace curtains lifted in the breeze. Ben paused to admire the stitching. Alessandra took his hand, pulled him across the road, and left a man in a Fiat leaning on his horn. “For the intellectually adventurous,” she said. “For people with functioning survival instincts.” “You’ll learn.” “Learn what?” “To enjoy the danger.” Ben was still holding her hand. He did not let go. ### III. Lunch, 12:30 They ate at a crowded trattoria where the proprietor greeted Alessandra in affectionate abuse and refused to let her pay. “He likes me,” she announced. “He says you owe him eleven euros.” “He says many things.” “You owe him eleven euros.” She stole the bread from Ben’s plate and dipped it in the sauce he had guarded all through the meal. Ben, who considered sauce an unreliable narrator of Italian hospitality, watched this happen with exaggerated patience. “You disapprove,” she said. “I’m being diplomatic.” “Your diplomacy needs servicing.” His mouth twitched. “Are you always this—” “Unforgettable? Charming? Inevitable?” “Troublesome.” “Ah.” She leaned closer. “Some people find it refreshing.” Ben looked away. The tips of his ears felt suddenly combustible. Across the table, Alessandra smiled into her wine. ### IV. Two Wheels, 3:15 At the next stop, she handed him a helmet. “I’m perfectly comfortable on the back of a motorcycle,” he said. “No, you are not.” “I’ve been to Rome before.” “Not like this.” She fastened the chin strap for him. Her fingers lingered near his jaw for half a second. Ben’s scholarly arguments abandoned him entirely. She pulled out into traffic, threaded between a taxi and a delivery van, and vanished into an alley barely wide enough for two. Ben’s satchel thumped against his back. The buildings pressed in close. At one turn, her shoulder met his cheek. “Sorry!” he shouted. “Don’t!” she called. “Hold on.” “I am holding on!” “Hold on better!” The Colosseum appeared at the end of the street, its broken arches gilded in afternoon light. Ben forgot the danger. Then she braked, and he remembered. “You look terrified,” she said. “I’m having a wonderful time.” “That will improve shortly. I know where to get espresso.” ### V. Campo de Fiori, 6:10 The market was dissolving into gold as the sun lowered between the stalls. Alessandra slipped away to buy fruit, and Ben found himself beside a silver-haired woman arranging violets by the fistful. “Alessandra!” The woman kissed both her cheeks. “You have brought me an English scholar.” “I haven’t brought you anything,” Alessandra said. “Ben, this is Marta. We have known each other since we were nine.” “Since you were nine,” Ben corrected gently. Marta turned to him, eyes sharp. “She is trouble, English.” “Marta.” “I am being hospitable.” She lowered her voice. “She likes souvenirs. Especially the ones no one offers her. Little thefts, little keepsakes. Then she watches to see who notices.” Ben’s gaze went to the small blue Colosseum gleaming on Alessandra’s lapel. He had noticed. He had said nothing. “Also,” Marta continued, “she collects hearts. With less regard for ownership than that magnet suggests.” “That is not—” “Ask yourself who you will be tomorrow. Ask whether you want to be someone who has already given her permission.” The warning settled between them, delicate and unexpectedly heavy. Ben looked at Alessandra. She watched him, half-smiling, as if she already knew what he would do. ### VI. The Roof of the City, 7:40 “You heard her,” Alessandra said, when they were alone. “I heard a friend being dramatic.” “Marta exaggerates.” “She suggested I’ve already given you permission.” “Have you?” Ben looked out across the terracotta roofs toward the dome of St Peter’s. Below them, Rome hurried home through the violet dusk. “No,” he said. “I thought about it.” Her smile faltered. Just slightly. Ben continued. “I was thinking I might have to.” For once, Alessandra had no answer. She turned away, but he caught her hand. She let him keep it. Above them, the evening bells began. ### VII. A Number, 9:20 They parted beneath a streetlamp near his hotel. Alessandra returned his guidebook, carefully restored, with one deep crease along the spine. “I nearly lost you at the market,” Ben said. “You nearly did.” “You left me with Marta.” “I saved you from a lecture about responsibility.” “I think I liked it.” Her eyes softened, just for an instant. “Ben,” she said. “You have your guidebook back.” “And you have my number.” She wrote it inside the cover. Seven digits, fast and sure, with no country code. “Call me when you’re ready for another day.” “I’m ready now.” “Tomorrow is soon.” “I don’t have anywhere else to be.” “That,” Alessandra said, “is the most dangerous thing you’ve said all day.” She pulled on her gloves. “Ben?” “Yes?” “Where are you going?” He looked at the number in his book. “To bed, I suppose.” “*Andiamo?*” They both laughed. She swung onto the motorcycle, leaving him beneath the lamplight. He watched until she turned the corner and vanished into Rome. Then, for the first time all day, Ben did not feel lost at all.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a polished, confident piece of short-form romance that hits nearly all of the prompt's requirements with economy and wit. The scene structure (seven timestamped vignettes spanning a single day) suits the "series of interconnected short scenes" instruction well, and the word count lands close to the 1000-word target. Strengths: The dialogue is the standout element. It's snappy, character-differentiated, and does heavy lifting — Alessandra's clipped confidence ("That is rather the point") versus Ben's fussy diplomacy ("Your diplomacy needs servicing") creates immediate chemistry. The kleptomania is handled with appropriate subtlety: the small blue Colosseum disappearing into her jacket, Ben noticing and saying nothing, and the payoff of it gleaming on her lapel later — this is exactly the "manifests in subtle, daring acts" instruction, executed well. The recurring "Andiamo?" callback at the end is a satisfying structural rhyme. Ben's quiet rebellion is believable and incremental. The prose is clean, dryly funny, and avoids sentimentality; the humor lands more often than not ("considered sauce an unreliable narrator of Italian hospitality"). Weaknesses: Marta's scene (V) is the weakest — it's a fairly naked exposition device, with a secondary character delivering a direct psychological dossier on Alessandra ("she collects hearts... with less regard for ownership"). This is the piece's most conspicuous tell-don't-show moment, and it slightly deflates the ambiguity the prompt asked for regarding Alessandra's feelings. The ambiguity is also somewhat undercut by Alessandra's "Have you?" and her faltering smile — the enigma resolves a bit too neatly. The near-collision opening is rushed and physically unclear (who nearly hits whom is muddled — Ben says "I stepped on your foot," implying a collision that wasn't quite staged). Some of Ben's transformation from apprehensive to willing participant happens mostly between scenes rather than on the page. The "" placeholder in the prompt is unaddressed, though it appears to be an empty tag. The ending is warm but earned — Ben's "not feeling lost" is a modest, fitting payoff rather than an unearned emotional crescendo. Overall: a skilled, restrained piece with excellent dialogue and structure, slightly hampered by one expository scene and a rushed opening. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 72.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## The Last Outpost: The Double The stranger settles onto the last stool as though their legs have personally offended gravity. Their tentacled dreads fan in seven directions, one draped over a shoulder, two knotted together, the rest trembling faintly toward the hatch. “Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double.” I keep wiping the same spot on the bar counter with a rag. The spot is already clean. It has been clean for ten minutes. “You look,” I say, “as though your ship lost an argument with a small sun.” “Would you serve a double to someone so delicate?” “Not here. I’d serve it to someone tougher, then charge them for the chair.” They place a credit chip on the bar. “Twenty. Keep it.” “That’s very generous.” “I’m risking my upholstery.” One sleeve of their coat is dark with blood, though the stranger keeps their hand tucked into their pocket. Their gaze keeps drifting toward the sealed docking hatch. People arrive at my bar tired, frightened, homesick, and occasionally all three. Tonight, someone has added *desperate* to the list. “Name?” I ask. “Sable.” “Which part?” “What do you mean, which part?” “The first, middle, family, or extremely convincing lie?” They almost smile. “Sable. Just Sable.” “That sounds suspicious.” “I don’t want to cause trouble.” “No? Then why are you whispering?” A pair of off-shift miners claim their usual table. One catches sight of the stranger and nudges his companion, suddenly interested in his drink. I recognize the reaction. Out here, tentacles are common enough. Blood is commoner. Trouble travels with both. I pour two measures of Vega and slide the stranger the larger glass. The whisky is a good amber, with just enough bite to remind you it was distilled by tired people on a rotating farm. “Twenty-two credits.” “Keep the change.” “That’s nearly half the bill.” “I’m celebrating.” “Your face disagrees.” “My face has poor judgment. You should see the rest of me.” I set a water glass beside the whisky. The stranger hesitates, then drinks the water first. I decide that earns them half a point toward not being a murderer. “You didn’t come for the whisky,” I say. “No.” “That’s all right. Most people don’t. They come because the station’s the only place still open, and nobody’s asking what happened yet.” Their fingers tighten around the glass. “I need a favor.” “That costs another twenty.” “I need you to transmit a message. Narrow-beam burst, priority Compact channel. Officially, it doesn’t exist until the stationmaster clears it.” “Unofficially?” “Unofficially, it disappears, and whoever sent me gets a very generous reward for finding me.” Behind me, the tap coughs. I take the glass out, clear the line, and put it back. “What’s in the message?” “Evidence.” “Against whom?” “Harrow Combine.” My hands remember work I’d rather not let them remember. Harrow ran cargo through nine systems, paid well, and considered regulations a decorative suggestion. So did I, once. “What kind of evidence?” “Contracts. Shipping manifests. Orders they don’t want anyone reading.” “They sound boring.” “They aren’t. They explain why three outposts have had pressure failures. Why emergency ships never arrive. Why the nearest inhabited belt has been empty for months.” I set down the bottle. “They’re evacuating people?” “They’re removing anyone who might testify. Then they’ll file a claim for salvage rights. Harrow owns the salvage rights.” The murmur of the bar seems very far away. “This concerns the Outpost?” “If the message doesn’t reach Compact Council before the next merchant ship leaves, this station becomes a convenient accident.” I wipe the clean spot again. The rag is worn soft from years of handling spilled drinks, bad decisions, and stories nobody wanted their families to hear. Usually, I can balance a person’s three complaints, two childhood embarrassments, and one attractive miner. Tonight, the scales feel oddly light. “Can you send it?” Sable asks. “Not through the station board.” “Narrow beam.” “Monitored.” “Only until someone with clearance opens a back channel.” “You’re asking me to do something I stopped doing.” “What exactly did you stop doing?” “Breaking into systems that don’t want to be broken into.” The words hang there, neat as a double. “I knew someone who used to be very good at it.” “Was?” “Didn’t survive the experience.” Sable looks at me for a long moment. Something in their expression shifts—not surprise, exactly, but recognition. “Nets,” they say. “Who’s Nets?” “That’s your name.” “That’s what people call me.” “You used to call yourself Nettle.” I could lie again. Instead, I slide their untouched whisky closer. “Who are you?” “Someone who knows how the Harrow systems work.” “That narrows it down.” “I know how *your* systems work, too.” Now my hands are still. That is not a good sign. At the hatch, the pressure chime sounds. Two figures step through in matching charcoal coats. Neither removes their gloves. Neither looks pleased to see the miners, the ceiling, or me. The larger one produces a flat image panel. On it is a face I don’t know, framed by dark, ragged tentacles. “We’re looking for a courier,” he says. “Last seen arriving on the *Peregrine*. Injured, carrying a black data case.” “Busy place,” I say. “Anyone could be that courier.” “They ordered Vega whisky. Neat.” “Popular drink.” “An unregistered burst was detected near this bar.” “Probably a miner trying to contact his wife.” The second man looks past me. Sable’s glass is empty. Their coat is still buttoned. They have somehow made themselves smaller without moving. The larger man’s gaze settles on the bar. “Who’ve you been talking to?” “Everyone who isn’t you.” “Turn on your terminal.” “Can’t.” “Why not?” “It’s offline.” “It was online six minutes ago.” “I’m touched by your company.” The second man notices the transmitter I’ve been using to clear the tap. His eyes lift to mine. “Step away from the bar.” “Careful. I’ve hidden a weapon under there.” The first man’s hand moves toward his belt. “Not a weapon,” I say. “A very sharp corkscrew.” They don’t believe me. Instead, they activate the panel and turn it toward me. A new image appears beneath the courier’s photograph. Harrow Combine. Recovery Division. A warrant issued six days ago. My name is there. For one bright, unreasonable moment, I consider walking out through the kitchen. Instead, I pick up Sable’s glass. Beneath it, where I’ve been carefully steering it with my rag, lies a black data chip no larger than my thumbnail. I slide it into my palm. “Where did you get that?” the larger man asks. I look at him as if he’s asked me to confess to a crime. Technically, I’m still holding evidence for one. There’s probably a lesson in there. Sable rises slowly. Their tentacles draw close, tight as cables, but they don’t run. “Tell them you don’t know me,” they murmur. “Already considered it.” “Tell them the truth.” “That’s considerably more dangerous.” The hatch cycles shut behind them. One of the recovery men turns it to manual lock. “Nettle,” he says, “you’re coming with us.” I stop wiping the clean spot. “No,” I tell him. “I’m not.” Sable’s hand closes around mine, hiding the chip. Unfortunately for all of us, I know exactly what to do with it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This chapter delivers a competent cozy-sci-fi noir setup with strong dialogue economy and a clear, unresolved conflict. The banter between Nets and Sable is the highlight—wry, clipped, and characterful ("Your face disagrees." / "My face has poor judgment"), and it does real work establishing both characters while keeping the tone light despite the stakes. The first-person present-tense voice is consistent throughout, and the recurring "clean spot on the bar" motif is a nice, understated device that grounds Nets's anxiety without stating it. Strengths: the dialogue-to-narration ratio lands near the requested ~60%; the worldbuilding (Harrow Combine, pressure failures, salvage rights) is delivered through conversation rather than exposition dumps; the ending escalates naturally with the recovery agents' arrival and the warrant reveal, and the conflict is left open as instructed. Weaknesses: the piece leans heavily on a staccato, one-line-per-beat rhythm that becomes mechanical—many exchanges read as interchangeable wisecracks, and the pattern of deadpan retort, deadpan retort, deadpan retort flattens emotional variation. Some lines strain ("as though their legs have personally offended gravity" is a familiar quirk construction; "tentacles... tight as cables" is stock). The Harrow conspiracy exposition arrives in a slightly convenient question-and-answer cadence. Sable's recognition of Nets's old identity is rushed and under-earned—"I know how your systems work, too" gestures at history without texture. The agents are generic heavies. The final beat ("Unfortunately for all of us, I know exactly what to do with it") is a serviceable cliffhanger but a formulaic one. The prose is clean but rarely surprising; imagery is functional rather than vivid. Emotionally, the piece is engaging but not deep—Nets's past is sketched in two or three lines and the stakes, while stated, aren't felt viscerally. Still, this is well above amateur work: coherent, controlled, tonally consistent, and genuinely readable. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 57.0
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Chapter Two: The City Below The strap on my backpack keeps slipping off my shoulder. I have corrected it four times in ninety seconds, which is four more than I corrected it all last week. At this rate, I’m going to stand here until the bag leaves without me and catches a bus back to Tennessee. I hoist it into place and start walking. New Orleans at six in the morning is already damp. The air feels like it has been left in a bathtub overnight, and the streetcar rattles past with a sound like metal teeth. Magnolia trees hang over the road, enormous and green, looking as if they’ve heard better stories than mine. I was almost relieved when the terminal building appeared. Almost. Because getting somewhere means somebody can ask where you came from, how old you are, and why you’re traveling alone. At sixteen, apparently, there are more rules to boarding a bus than there are to boarding a plane. Two days ago, I told my family I’m transgender. I didn’t manufacture a crisis for attention. I manufactured an escape because apparently those are different. A week ago, the school counselor had called my “concerning behavioral patterns” to Mom. That was her word for every uncomfortable silence, every joke that landed wrong, every private drawer I’d quietly locked. I’d spent months rehearsing what I’d say when I told them. I imagined variations of the same scene: a hard conversation, a difficult afternoon, maybe some tears on both sides. In every version, I stayed for the difficult part. Instead, there was a phone call. A packed duffel. My mom standing in the doorway, unable to look at me. *I need some time to think.* I keep turning that sentence over. It can mean a week. It can mean a month. It can mean waiting for some other person to tell me what I am, so they don’t have to feel bad about not knowing. The backpack strap slips again. Damn it. I catch the bag before it hits the ground and head for the women’s restroom. I need to count my money without anybody watching and try to remember what I look like when I’m not actively fleeing. One hundred and twelve dollars. Thirty-eight percent battery. One clean shirt, which I put on because clean laundry is apparently a milestone now. The bathroom mirror is fogged at the edges, but not enough to hide the fact that I look exhausted. I try an expression. Neutral, I decide, is good. Neutral says, *I have a plan.* It doesn’t work. I look like someone who has a plan, but the plan involves crying in a bus station bathroom. I wash my face, refill my water bottle, and go sit on the steps outside. A teenager is already there, wearing jeans and a faded blue T-shirt that says **LOUISIANA IS SPICY** beneath a graphic of a chili pepper. Their bag is propped between their feet, one hand resting on it. “You riding or sightseeing?” they ask. “Neither. Maybe walking.” “Good answer.” They tell me their name is Ari. I tell them mine is Taylor. For a second, neither of us mentions that we’re both under eighteen. The omission sits between us like a third bag. “You got a ride?” Ari asks. “I had one. Then I didn’t.” “So you’re new here.” “Extremely.” The truth arrives embarrassingly fast after that. Ari tells me they left Gulfport that morning. They say they’re eighteen. I don’t know why I doubt it. Maybe the way they say eighteen feels rehearsed. Maybe I’ve spent too long watching people choose their words carefully. A man walks by and calls out, “Need a lift? I got room.” Ari watches him disappear down the block. “Usually, that means somebody else’s ride.” “Excellent. A full car. Truly generous.” “And it’s cheaper than the alternative.” The alternative is $180 for a room, minimum, which neither of us has. We exchange a few more careful sentences, then head back inside. The terminal is full of people going somewhere on purpose. They have tickets in their hands and shoulders that don’t slump. An attendant tells us the downtown hotels require an adult guest. She gives us a flyer for a youth center downtown, but the number rings into an unanswered voicemail. Ari sits back down on the steps. I sit beside them. “So,” I say. “Walking?” “Walking.” By nine, we have crossed the river and entered the French Quarter. I expected a revelation. Instead, we get a cryptid tour, a street musician playing saxophone behind a busking sign, and a woman carrying a tray of beignets balanced on one hand like she’s serving breakfast to the whole street. Aren’t we all. The Quarter smells like coffee, diesel, and something sweet frying in a hot pan. The colors are impossible: turquoise shutters, yellow balconies, purple shadows. A little boy leans out of an upstairs window and throws something at his brother, but only a roll of toilet paper. I like it here. I want to be suspicious of how much I like it. Ari keeps checking the street behind us. “So the cousin,” I say. “The one you thought might help. You never said what happened.” Their hand goes to their back pocket. Not a pocket watch. A phone. “He wasn’t really my cousin,” they say. At the public library, we refill our bottles and sit in a row of plastic chairs. Ari connects to Wi-Fi, then keeps their screen turned slightly away from me. Their sleeve rides up just enough for me to see a fading bruise around their wrist. “He found my phone,” they says. “Got into it. Sent some stuff to my foster mom. I couldn’t go back and explain without everybody deciding I’d caused the whole thing.” “What stuff?” Ari looks toward the doors. Rain has started outside, tapping against the glass. The library is quiet except for the librarian’s cart squeaking between shelves. “Pictures,” they say. “I trusted somebody. That was a bad decision. Then he said if I didn’t send more, he’d show them to her. Not anything I actually did. Just enough to make me scared.” I understand the fear. Not the exact shape of it, but the machinery. Someone finds a soft place. They press until they’re sure you’ll stay still. I should say something profound. Instead, I tell them, “That’s not your fault.” Ari looks at me like the sentence is in a language they’ve forgotten. “I lied about my age,” they tell me. “It doesn’t change anything. I’m still going to get in trouble.” “Probably,” I say. “But not with me.” They almost smile. We eat leftover biscuits from a café because they’re two for a dollar. I pay. Ari argues, then pays for the coffee. It isn’t even a real transaction. It’s a tiny vote about whether we’re still keeping score against each other. Across the street, a man in a white polo is watching us. He smiles when he catches me noticing, then looks away. Maybe nothing. The hair on my arms says otherwise. Around two, he comes into the café and asks if we’re waiting for somebody. I say no. He says he drives for a private service and can take us anywhere, no questions. Ari watches him touch his phone. My stomach drops. “We’re good,” I say. The man nods and leaves. Ari exhales. “That’s the second person today.” “He knows we’re new.” “He knows we’re alone.” Outside, the rain has turned the pavement into a mirror. Traffic crawls past in slow, bright ribbons. The city looks beautiful from here, but beauty isn’t a lock on the door. At three-thirty, we find a woman at the information desk who slides us a card for a youth drop-in center. She says they have meals, showers, and someone who can help us work out transportation. She doesn’t ask for our names. She doesn’t tell us to pray, call our parents, or smile like our lives are fixed. “You don’t need an ID just to come in,” she says. “You do need to be honest about your age, though.” “I’m sixteen,” I say. Ari stares at me. Then they take a breath. “Seventeen.” It’s the first time I feel something loosen in my chest. The woman nods as if this is a perfectly ordinary Thursday. Maybe it is. Maybe everybody here is used to people arriving with a bag between their feet and a story they can’t say yet. By the time we reach the center, the sky has gone orange. The rain stopped, leaving the streets shining. I don’t know where we’ll sleep tonight. I don’t know whether the center is full, whether someone will ask questions we can’t answer, or whether I’ll wake up in a police car and have to explain everything to someone with a badge. But for the first time since I left Tennessee, I’m not walking alone. The strap slips again as we turn the corner. I catch it. For now, that’s enough.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent, controlled chapter that hits the brief: first person, mixed tense, one day in New Orleans, a runaway companion with secrets, wariness about trust, and internal monologue threaded through. The voice is consistent — dry, deflective, wry — and the recurring backpack strap motif works as a small structural device that pays off in the closing lines. Strengths: the prose is economical and often sharp ("Neutral says, I have a plan. It doesn't work."). The dynamic between Taylor and Ari is well-drawn through small transactions — the biscuits, the coffee, "a tiny vote about whether we're still keeping score." Ari's blackmail backstory is handled with restraint, and the predatory men circling the pair create genuine low-grade menace without melodrama. The youth center worker is a nicely understated adult presence. Weaknesses: the piece is somewhat safe and formulaic in its beats — bus station, wary meeting, predator, kind stranger, drop-in center. The resolution arrives a little easily; the "first time something loosens in my chest" moment is earned but the day's dangers resolve without real cost. Some imagery is stock (rain turning pavement into a mirror, sky gone orange). Ari's dialogue occasionally slips grammatically ("He found my phone," they says) — likely intentional but it reads as error. The "concerning behavioral patterns" callback is integrated but the bus/terminal logistics are fuzzy — Taylor arrived by hitchhike, yet the opening dwells on bus station rules that don't quite connect. A few aphorisms ("beauty isn't a lock on the door") gesture at profundity without fully landing. The ending's optimism is modest and mostly earned, though slightly tidier than the situation warrants. Overall: a solid, professional YA chapter with genuine craft in voice and dialogue, held back by conventional plotting and a resolution that softens the stakes. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 64.5
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## My Apocalypse Buddy Home was the upper floor of a laundrette, chosen because the roof barely leaked and the stairs discouraged visitors. Midas had a chair, a sleeping bag, a first-aid kit containing three bandages and a plaster of doubtful age, and Chewy. Chewy was an animo-tronic stuffed koala from the ancient pre-collapse period, when apparently every child required a friend who spoke, and preferably had a removable necktie. One of his ears had been replaced with brown velveteen. A few of his stuffing had escaped through a seam and declined to come back. He sat on the table with the serene expression of a creature who had never once considered laundry. “The situation,” Midas told him, “is food.” Chewy’s batteries had died during the previous winter. His advertising unit had therefore been reduced to occasional statements such as *THERE’S NO TIME LIKE THE PRESENT TO BUY A TOASTER*, delivered without apparent conviction. “I do not want a toaster,” Midas said. “I want a tin of beans, four AA batteries, and a wool blanket.” Chewy brightened visibly. It was largely a trick of the eyes. “I do also want to go to Meridian Retail Park,” Midas added. The retail park lay five miles away, which was a convenient distance: too far to carry supplies, close enough to make sensible people find something else to do. Midas was not a sensible person, but he did have a shopping trolley. It had three working wheels and one that thought differently. They set out shortly after nine. Chewy rode in Midas’s rucksack, wearing his scarf and a small expression of concern. “GOING PLACES?” Chewy announced. “Unfortunately,” said Midas. They found the retail park easily, because half of its enormous sign had fallen into the car park and the surviving letters rearranged themselves into the profoundly unhelpful instruction **DGER PRCE**. Beyond it stood the supercentre, dark except for a few emergency lights and one blue lamp above a door marked **CUSTOMER SERVICES**. “The plan,” Midas said, “is to go in, find the things, and leave.” Chewy produced another slogan. *NEW! IMPROVED! MOSTLY NEW!* “That’s not the plan,” Midas said. The supermarket smelled of dust, old sugar and the particular dampness found beneath stacks of plastic packaging. Midas pushed the trolley towards the electrical goods, with Chewy at his shoulder and a growing conviction that the building was watching him. He found the batteries first. He also found beans, a blanket and a nearly complete fire extinguisher, which he took because carrying it had seemed like the sort of thing a resourceful man might do. Then he tripped over something. It was a pressure mat. Nothing about it said *burglar alarm*, which was probably because it had been intended to reassure customers. The alarm began to sound. It was not a loud noise so much as an enormous number of noises occurring at once, as though every plastic triangle in history had been struck simultaneously and asked to form a committee. Midas considered switching the batteries out of Chewy. This would be sensible, but it required concentration, and concentration was not a talent that survived contact with fire-suppression equipment. The sprinklers went off. Water descended over the electrical goods with the enthusiasm of a ceiling surrendering to gravity. Midas flung himself beneath a shelf marked **DISPOSABLE DISHES**, stuffed the beans and blanket into his rucksack, and stuffed Chewy beneath his coat. The batteries went into his inside pocket. “Perfect,” he said. “All we need is a bear.” “I already am one,” said Chewy. The emergency exit route required passing through the frozen-food aisle, where the floor had become a shallow, brown lake. Midas waded in, lifted the bottom step of the escalator, and found a panel marked **MANUAL OVERRIDE**. There was a crank inside it. This surprised nobody except Midas, who was wet enough to have abandoned the expectation of surprises. He turned the crank. The escalator shuddered, woke with a grinding shriek, and began carrying them upward. This was unfortunate, but at least it was efficient. Midas hurried up the moving steps and emerged onto the roof, followed by Chewy, the rucksack and most of the shopping trolley. The trolley then rolled backwards down the escalator and disappeared, taking with it a box of cereal, two lamps and all hope of an orderly exit. Home lay across the car park. “There,” Midas said. “We can take the plank.” The plank was intended to bridge a gap between the retail park and the former hotel. It had been intended to bridge that gap for some years, however, and had developed a crack of considerable confidence. Midas went first. He reached the hotel fire escape with his ankle intact, his dignity abandoned somewhere above the frozen-food aisle, and the blanket wrapped around the rail. Chewy came next, lowered on a length of washing line Midas had found nearby. The line snapped. The koala fell eight feet and caught a drainpipe. “For a moment,” Chewy said, “I thought I was going places.” The fire-escape gate at the bottom was padlocked. Midas could climb over it, but the landing beyond was full of broken glass, and he had already discovered that the human body has a limited tolerance for novel arrangements involving gravity. They descended to street level by way of a bin store and discovered the shopping trolley waiting below, apparently recovered by a force interested in delivering them home. Midas put the supplies in it and tried to ride down the access ramp while steering with one hand. The fourth wheel stopped. The other three did not. The trolley accelerated. “Ah,” said Midas. It left the ramp, crossed a strip of grass, struck a concrete planter and entered the drainage channel at considerable speed. Midas went over the handlebars. Chewy went over Midas. The trolley went on without them, carrying the remaining shopping into the canal with a triumphant clatter. The water was cold, brown and astonishingly deep. Midas caught the trolley’s broken handle. Chewy caught Midas. The blanket spread across the canal like a badly laundered flag. “Right,” Midas said, teeth chattering. “That’s not the way home.” The canal carried them beneath a bridge, past a drowned garden gnome and into a flooded playing field. Eventually they fetched up against a bank three-quarters of the mile downstream. Midas climbed out with the beans, the batteries and Chewy. The blanket did not survive the experience. Wool, it turned out, was not designed to be dragged through a canal, regardless of what the old advertising had claimed. There was a wheelbarrow in the adjacent hardware depot. It was missing one wheel. Midas found a length of metal pipe and inserted it into the axle, wrapping the loose end in fabric from the blanket. “It is not a good wheelbarrow,” he admitted. “It’s the only one,” said Chewy. Midas loaded the beans, the batteries, the soaking blanket and Chewy into the basket. Then he pushed it home. The replacement wheel was a poor fit and developed a sideways habit. The road was steep. The evening was coming on, and the homeward distance increased in direct proportion to the remaining daylight. They reached the laundrette after dark, having travelled through a tennis court, a bin compound and a patch of nettles that Midas would remember whenever he saw anything resembling a wheelbarrow. He had to finish the journey lying in the basket while pulling it by the handles. “It has been a long day,” Chewy observed. “It has,” Midas agreed. He fitted the new batteries. Something in Chewy’s back clicked, stirred and became briefly enthusiastic. *AT LAST, A PRODUCT WITH NO US!* Midas looked at the dented tin of beans, the ruined blanket, the shopping trolley and the wheelbarrow. “Thank you,” he said. “I think.” He switched Chewy off before the koala could recommend anything else. Then he limped upstairs, wrapped his ankle in the last usable tea towel, and sat beside his friend until morning. It had been a simple mission. It had gone sideways in three directions, which Midas considered fairly restrained.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a competent, at times genuinely funny, Pratchett pastiche that hits the structural brief: deliberation at home base, a supply-run mission that goes sideways repeatedly, and a return home in worse condition than departure. The strongest elements are the deadpan narration ("a shopping trolley... one that thought differently"), the absurdist set pieces (the alarm described as "every plastic triangle in history... asked to form a committee"), and Chewy's malfunctioning ad-slogans as a running gag, which land well and give the koala a distinct comic voice. The "DGER PRCE" sign and "AT LAST, A PRODUCT WITH NO US!" are excellent touches. Weaknesses: the story strains plausibility even by its own loose logic — powered alarms, sprinklers, and a working escalator crank in a post-technological collapse world are never explained or lampshaded, which Pratchett would typically have winked at. The middle section becomes a somewhat mechanical chain of mishaps (plank, drainpipe, padlock, trolley crash, canal) where each obstacle is introduced and resolved in quick succession, reading more like a checklist than an escalating comic rhythm. The "I already am one" koala/bear joke is muddled. Midas is defined almost entirely by narration telling us he's hapless rather than by shown character; his interiority is thin. The ending is tidy and warm but the emotional register stays flat throughout — wry to the point of monotony, with little variation in tone or stakes. Some sentences are choppy in a way that mimics Pratchett's cadence without fully earning it ("This was unfortunate, but at least it was efficient"). Still, the voice is consistent, the humor mostly lands, the prose is clean and unpretentious, and the piece fulfills its brief with confidence. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 55.5
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
### Love in the Limelight: A Borrowed Quiet Rain had turned the high street of a small west Wales town into a dark mirror. Every flashbulb made a small white sun. Rhys Vale, whose face graced half the country’s cinema walls, slipped through the bookshop door as a motorbike engine roared past. “Before you begin,” he said, “I’d like it noted that I’m a guest.” The woman fitting books into place glanced at his wet coat. “You’re dripping on the stock.” “That’s a rather clinical way to offer hospitality.” “It’s the only way I offer it before six.” He removed his sunglasses. She recognised him immediately. He waited for the usual small miracle: widened eyes, a flush, an *Oh, you’re actually here.* She returned a book to its wrong-sized gap. “Can I help you?” she asked. “I’d like something nobody’s photographed, a chair nobody wants, and perhaps tea.” “Tea I can do. Privacy depends on whether you’ve brought photographers into my shop.” “Only three. They’re outside.” “Only?” “I’m trying to be humble.” “You’re dripping on a first edition.” He looked. “I saved your life.” “By making it necessary to mop.” He laughed—genuinely. The charm he usually carried like a well-cut coat slipped sideways. “Most people recognise me and forget the price of fish and chips,” he said. “I recognised you,” she replied. “I also know you didn’t come here for books.” “That’s a depressing assessment of my charm.” “It’s the one I make before six.” He glanced around the cramped shop: rain-streaked windows, handwritten recommendations, a kettle balanced on a hotplate. “You always work here?” “Eleven years. I bought it from my aunt. Why do you want to know?” “Small talk. I like your shop.” “I was enjoying myself. Until you.” “I thought I was improving the atmosphere.” “You were adding damp.” “You always work here?” “Eleven years,” she said. “I bought it from my aunt. Before you arrived, the last person through that door spent twenty minutes arguing about Welsh dictionaries.” “I won.” “Clearly.” He smiled, but it faded when she simply returned to her shelf. He turned towards a table of natural histories. “A field guide to the birds of Cardigan Bay. Do you sell many copies?” “More than people expect.” “Really? Who buys them?” “Birdwatchers, teachers, people who like looking at small wild things without being noticed.” “Ah,” he said, with feeling. “I can offer you the opposite of that.” “Do put the cap back on. In here, you’re merely a wet man with excellent cheekbones.” “I prefer famous.” “I prefer tea. There’s some, if you can tolerate a cup without a saucer.” “I can. Strong, with a splash of milk.” “I’ve already poured it.” “Ah. There it is. The moment someone stops wanting anything from you.” “I want you out before six.” “That’s better.” His fingers hovered over the field guide. “You know birds, then?” Her eyes narrowed slightly. “A little.” “A little?” “I can identify fifty-three species without looking at the colour of their feet.” “Can you?” “No. I made up fifty-three. You looked hopeful.” “My heart’s in the wrong place. Not the right decade.” “That joke was old enough to need retiring.” “I usually retire them before they get embarrassing.” “I can see why.” She returned a book to its shelf, not quite hiding her smile. He noticed. “You like this one,” he said, nodding towards the copy in her hand. “The coast path. My mother and I walk it at first light. You learn which birds have decided that cliffs are the safest housing available.” “First light?” “When everyone else is asleep and the gulls are only moderately aggressive.” “I’ve always loved that hour. As a boy, I spent hours on the cliffs near my grandfather’s farm with his binoculars. I still keep notebooks. Sketches, flight paths, places I’ve been. The birds don’t know who I am.” He glanced at her. “That sounds ridiculous, coming from a man whose face is on a cinema wall.” “No,” Nia said, too quickly. “It sounds like the person you were before everyone wanted you to be.” The silence stretched between them. She became suddenly conscious of the rain tapping the glass, the warmth from the hotplate, the way he had gone uncharacteristically still. He was not performing. That was the dangerous part. “Perhaps that person was less charming,” he said. “He sounds as though he’s worth knowing.” “Does he?” “I’d like to find out.” “Ah.” His smile returned, but it was uncertain now. “I was hoping you’d say that.” “I said nothing.” “You said it three times. Subtitles, perhaps?” “Your Welsh is terrible.” “No, it is. Don’t correct it. Let me have this one.” She looked down at her tea. “Saturday,” he said. “If you’re walking the coast path again, I could—” “You want me to take you birdwatching.” “I want to spend the morning with someone who doesn’t mistake me for the paintings on your shopfront.” “That’s a lot of titles for a walk.” “Two. Possibly three if the weather behaves.” “It will rain.” “Then we’ll get wet. Together. It’s nearly a sales pitch.” “It’s not a—” “Seven?” “Seven is very early.” “I know. That’s why I said it.” “Seven-thirty?” She looked at him, caught between commonsense and the unwelcome fact that she wanted to say yes. “Eight. Bring waterproofs. I’m not responsible for England’s most famous wet coat.” “I’ll bring mine. And binoculars. Do you have a spare pair?” “We can use mine.” “Together?” “If you insist.” “I do.” His phone rang. He silenced it without looking. “Paparazzi?” she asked. “My publicist. She wants to know whether I’ve been photographed looking misunderstood in a bookshop.” “Have you?” “I’ve been photographed hiding in one. There’s a difference.” “Does your publicist know that?” “She’s learning to trust me.” “This isn’t an interview, you know. I won’t give you a good quote.” “I wasn’t asking for a quote.” “No?” “No. I’m asking for your number. And perhaps a second cup of tea, if the offer’s still open.” She picked up the teapot. “It is.” “Then I’ll stay until you change your mind.” “You may have to wait a long time.” “That,” he said, “is the first conversation I’ve had in years I actually believe I’ll be invited to continue.” Nia poured. Outside, the motorbike engine had finally gone. Inside, the rain softened against the windows, and she was glad he couldn’t see her face. She had meant to be unmoved. She had succeeded magnificently at being charmed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The scene fulfills the prompt's core requirements: Wales setting, actor escaping paparazzi, bookstore owner superficially immune but inwardly charmed, rogue with fragile ego whose charm offensive derails into genuine attraction. It's predominantly dialogue-driven with distinct voices. Strengths: The banter is snappy and the bookstore owner's deadpan dryness is genuinely funny ("You're dripping on the stock," "In here, you're merely a wet man with excellent cheekbones"). The actor's neediness shows through small beats—waiting for recognition, silencing his phone, fishing for validation. The reversal where his genuine self emerges through the birdwatching backstory is a decent mechanism for the chemistry shift. The final two sentences cap it well, showing Nia's inward fluster in a wry, show-don't-tell way. Weaknesses: There's a noticeable editing error—a repeated exchange ("You always work here?" / "Eleven years. I bought it from my aunt.") appears twice, which reads like an uncorrected drafting artifact. Midway there's a confusing moment where Rhys describes his own birdwatching hobby and then says "That sounds ridiculous, coming from a man whose face is on a cinema wall"—apparently a speech attribution error where Nia's line was given to him; then Nia's response "No... it sounds like the person you were" doesn't track. Also the "fifty-three species" joke is muddled. The scene occasionally tells rather than shows ("The charm he usually carried like a well-cut coat slipped sideways"—telling his internal state narratively despite a mostly external viewpoint). The birdwatching reveal is a somewhat convenient softening device, and the rapidity of the date arrangement and warm ending, while fitting the genre, feels a touch frictionless—the transformation from sarcasm to "I'd like to find out" is quick and could be seen as lightly unearned. Nia's interiority is thin until the final paragraph. The prose is competent but rarely rises above functional; descriptions are economical but sparse.
