+ Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 53.7
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## The Last Second Ellie was twelve years old, which was old enough to know better than to open a mysterious present and young enough to do it anyway. The box contained a silver smartwatch with a black screen. No brand. No model number. Not even a stupid Wi-Fi password sticker. “Probably a knockoff,” Dad said. “But it works.” He was already heading toward the kitchen when Ellie fastened it around her wrist. The display lit up. **7:43 A.M.** Beneath the time was a single button. **REWIND** She tapped it. The second hand jumped backward. Her father’s chair scraped toward the table. The refrigerator door swung shut. A spoonful of oatmeal arced neatly back into its bowl. Ellie blinked. Her father blinked. “You have to turn it off,” he called after her. She couldn’t. She tried pressing the button again, but nothing happened. The watch was warm against her skin. For a moment, she could have sworn she heard a tiny voice counting backward. Then the screen returned to normal. Ellie forgot about it. That happened sometimes with presents. On the first day of seventh grade, a stack of books crashed into her knees in the hallway. A group of eighth-graders laughed. “Watch where you’re going,” one of them said. Ellie’s palms hit the floor before she realized she was falling. She pressed REWIND. The books flew upward. The boy’s laughter reversed into a cough. Ellie staggered back, catching herself upright half a second before the books landed. This time, the second hand spun smoothly backward. The books dropped into her arms. The boy stared at her. “You just—” The bell rang. Ellie hurried away, polishing the watch with her sleeve. It felt feverish. Probably because she’d run. That was all. At first, rewinding four seconds barely seemed worth mentioning. But soon Ellie was using it constantly. She rewound when a joke was made at her expense. When someone spilled soda on her backpack. When she forgot an answer during a presentation. Once, she even rewound a math test she’d failed. The watch pulsed blue. The teacher began speaking again. This time, Ellie’s paper was covered in correct answers. Her own handwriting. She didn’t remember writing them. The strange thing was that nobody questioned how she knew so much. Older students asked her opinion about parties she didn’t remember attending. Teachers spoke to her as if she were years ahead of the rest of the class. At lunch, a boy she barely knew said, “See you later, Ellie.” She had never met him before. “What do you mean?” she asked. He stared at her like she’d said something sick. “We have a thing,” he whispered. “At the arcade. Don’t forget again.” Ellie had no idea what he meant. By October, her jeans were held together with a belt. Her voice had cracked, deepened, then cracked again. Hair brushed her shoulders. Her face was losing its roundness, sharpening into someone older and much more tired. She needed a new bra. That was when she noticed the countdown. Late one night, she glanced at the watch and froze. **04:17:32** The time was 10:48. The numbers were still moving. **04:17:31** **04:17:30** Ellie tapped the face. REWIND disappeared. The countdown didn’t. She shook the watch. Removed the battery. Pried open the back. Nothing worked. When she looked up, her little brother was standing in the doorway. “You look old,” he said. “Thanks.” “Mom says we’re going to Gran’s for Thanksgiving.” Ellie nodded. Something was wrong with that. She was certain her parents hadn’t mentioned Thanksgiving. But when she went to ask them, they acted as if she was being ridiculous. “We’ve made those plans for months,” Mom said. Ellie went upstairs. She was fifteen, maybe. Or sixteen. She felt ancient. Her knees ached when she climbed the stairs. At school, the younger kids called her Miss Walker. Her old friends had disappeared—not cruelly, but completely. They no longer shared her classes, her table, or her memories. Ellie began to understand. The watch wasn’t rewinding the world. It was rewriting it. And somehow, every stolen moment came from her. The countdown fell faster. **00:59:59** **00:59:58** Sometimes it flickered at the bottom of the watch face. **ONE REPLAY REMAINING** Ellie stopped using the rewind button. The world didn’t stop changing. A storm arrived before the calendar said December. The first drops struck the middle school windows as lightning forked across the sky. Ellie was in the hallway when the lights went out. A crash echoed from the gym. Then another. Students screamed. Emergency alarms shrieked—even though no one had touched them. Ellie pressed her palm against the wall. The whole building shuddered. Through the window, she saw a car lift off the street. The storm outside was barely a drizzle. But rain was pouring from a ruptured water main, flooding the parking lot. The old gym roof, supposedly replaced twelve years ago, crumbled like wet cardboard. Ellie understood with sick clarity. She hadn’t stopped time. She had pulled the future into the present. The countdown on her watch reached zero. For one suspended second, everything was silent. Ellie looked at the REWIND button. Then at the gym, where someone was hammering against the locked doors. She pressed the button. The world screamed backward. Sirens unwound. Floodwater reversed into pipes. Pieces of ceiling flew upward, reassembling themselves. Car doors slammed shut on empty seats. The cry of a trapped child shortened into silence. Ellie’s watch burned into her skin. She tried to let go. It wouldn’t let her. She felt her hand age beneath her fingers. Tendons tightened. Skin thinned. Joints swollen. Her teeth loosened, and something crawled along her spine as if her bones were turning to stone. She was ancient. She was still twelve. The countdown restarted. **00:59:59** Ellie held on until the gym roof was whole again. Until the alarms stopped. Until the water main stopped screaming. Until the world was safe. Then she closed her eyes. When she opened them, she was lying on her bedroom floor. Morning sunlight crossed the carpet. “M Ellie!” Mom called from downstairs. “You’re going to be late!” Ellie sat up. Her hands were small. Her jeans fit. She was twelve again. She stumbled to her desk. The smartwatch sat inside its open box, dark and cold. In her pocket, she found a folded piece of paper. It was written in her handwriting. **DON’T LET IT TAKE ANYTHING ELSE.** Ellie’s mother called again. Ellie looked at the watch. The screen suddenly flickered to life. **23:59:59** **23:59:58** For one hopeful moment, the countdown held. Then REWIND began to glow again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a competent Goosebumps-style horror chapter that hits nearly all of the prompt's beats: a middle schooler discovers a mysterious rewind-capable smartwatch, uses it casually, ages prematurely (puberty acceleration, changing relationships), causes a timeline disaster, and attempts a final reversal with an ambiguous ending. The length target of roughly 1000 words is respected. The strongest element is the prose rhythm. Short, punchy sentences and the recurring bolded countdown (**04:17:32**) create the staccato, page-turning feel of the genre. The reversal imagery is genuinely effective — the oatmeal arcing back into the bowl, laughter "revers[ing] into a cough," floodwater retreating into pipes, ceiling pieces reassembling. These are the moments where the piece earns its keep. There are notable weaknesses. The causal logic of the aging is fuzzy: the watch steals time from Ellie, but the story also implies the timeline is being rewritten (parties she never attended, a boyfriend she never met, Thanksgiving plans). These two mechanisms — personal aging versus world-rewriting — are never reconciled, and the narrator's explanation ("The watch wasn't rewinding the world. It was rewriting it.") is a tell-heavy patch over that gap. The storm sequence is the weakest section: the gym collapse, the car lifting off the street, and the "pulled the future into the present" explanation arrive abruptly and don't follow clearly from anything Ellie did. It reads as a disaster inserted because the prompt required one. The ending reset is somewhat convenient — Ellie wakes up twelve again with a note in her own handwriting — though the final flicker of the countdown and the glowing REWIND button preserve the "maybe?" ambiguity the prompt requested, which is a genuine strength. There's a typo ("M Ellie!"), and the dialogue is functional but thin, mostly expository. Ellie herself is a sketch rather than a character; her interiority is limited to confusion and dread, with little personality beyond genre-standard pluck. Emotionally, the piece works at the level of creepy unease rather than genuine dread or sadness — appropriate for middle-grade horror, but not transcendent of it. The "DON'T LET IT TAKE ANYTHING ELSE" note is a nice touch, implying a loop and prior knowledge. Overall: a solid, genre-faithful execution with strong pacing and imagery, undermined by muddled metaphysics, a rushed and under-motivated disaster sequence, and thin characterization. Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Clara stopped beneath the shooting gallery’s tin stars. Beyond it, Coney Island hung its paper moons above the darkening sea. The crowd pressed past, thick with cigar smoke and hot grease. A carousel organ played three notes, stopped, and began again. She felt the rhythm under her ribs. *His locks.* The phrase had appeared in his letter among instructions: *Come at dusk. Look for the man with dark hair. You will know him by his eyes.* She had not known him then. She did not know him now. Yet here she was, carrying the strangeness beneath her silk like a stone in a shoe. A young man rose across the gallery’s mouth. The word *young* deceived. There was nothing boyish in his black, steady gaze. He removed his hat. A curl fell over his brow, black as the water beneath the pier. “You came,” he said. “You wrote.” “I did.” “Your letter was optimistic.” “Was it?” “And if I don’t know you?” His eyes considered her, unhurried. “Then I shall have to earn the acquaintance.” “And if I remember you?” His smile changed. “You won’t.” “How discourteous.” “Accurate.” A practiced reply, delivered with warmth that made caution seem unfashionable. She distrusted the feeling more than the line. “Your gloves are impractical.” “It’s July.” “That isn’t an argument for surrender.” He lifted her hand. His kiss grazed the linen, brief, courteous, wrong. Heat lingered at her knuckles. “Do I know you?” “I think you do.” “You shouldn’t say such things to a woman who can’t remember her own.” “Which woman, precisely?” “The one standing here.” “Scarcely the woman I remember.” A vendor turned the corner, his drum painted the deep blue of evening. Pink sugar wound around a stick, white as a moon that had never known dirt. The smell caught in Clara’s throat. *A child’s sticky hand. A woman bending close, her face hidden by a yellow hat. A music box giving three notes, then silence. The stranger’s younger face, and her own voice saying, Again.* The image dissolved before she could hold it. “My mother brought me here,” she said. “Twice a year. Always in June.” “She died last winter.” “I’m sorry.” Not one of his words had been cruel. She had begun, without noticing, to listen for cruelty and find only kindness. That was less comforting. “You remember her.” “She wore yellow when she meant for you to remember her.” Clara’s hand tightened inside its glove. “What do you mean?” “I mean you have forgotten something you wished you hadn’t.” “Do you know what happened to me?” “No.” It was the first answer she believed entirely, and the first that frightened her more. Inside, the gallery smelled of oiled metal. Targets hung over painted mountains; rifles rested beneath red globes, their wooden stocks rubbed smooth. “Three shots,” the attendant announced. “Dime.” “Take the sailor doll,” Clara said. The stranger turned. “For me?” “For me. I want to see what your luck looks like when it isn’t impressing me.” “Charming. And here I thought we were being honest.” He raised a rifle. His easy posture vanished. The first shot rang; a tin bird dropped. “Two more,” said the attendant. “Time enough to change your mind about me?” “About the prize?” “About everything.” He missed the moon, then struck a star hidden behind it. A blue-eyed kewpie descended, swinging by one arm. “For the lady,” said the attendant. He handed it to Clara. “You may keep it. I dislike carrying things that can be lost.” “That sounds dangerously close to caring.” “Does it?” “About the doll.” A curl had fallen across his brow. She remembered *locks*: first hair, then fastenings. “Why me?” “Because you came.” “Anyone might, for a curiosity.” “No. They won’t.” He returned the rifle. She had begun, without noticing, to listen for cruelty in his words and find only kindness. That was less comforting. “He is like no one I remember,” she said. “No? You hardly remember anyone.” “That isn’t an answer.” “It is a fact.” “Why the shooting gallery?” “Because you like a spectacle, and because every man needs to prove himself before midnight.” “Did the letter promise you I’d come?” “No.” “Then why did you write?” His smile altered at its edges. “Because I needed you here.” “Need is an ambitious word.” “It is also a dangerous one.” He held the kewpie out of reach when she reached for it. “Ask me something else.” “Why do you keep giving me prizes I don’t want?” “Because you are not obliged to accept them.” A painted sailor hung crooked from the prize shelf, grinning into the electric light. She had come for an answer and was being handed a collection of beautiful irrelevancies. Yet his hand on hers felt unnervingly certain. “Walk with me,” he said. “To where?” “Only as far as the arch.” “No?” He glanced toward the thinning crowd. “You may watch the officers while I steal the kewpie.” “You won’t run?” “I have no reason to.” “I have no reason to trust that.” “A fair beginning.” He offered his arm. After a pause, she laid her gloved hand over it. Beneath the wool, his muscle was taut with an effort she suspected he did not intend to show. “Why are you afraid of me?” he asked. “I am not.” “No?” His gaze touched her mouth. “You keep glancing at the police as if they might rescue you from a particularly tedious stranger.” “I have been thinking of leaving.” “Most people are.” “What should I be thinking?” “That I am not a stranger.” “That is not an answer.” “It is the only one I can give safely.” Beneath the arch, the boardwalk narrowed. On the water, a steamer’s lights moved like a string of yellow beads. His fingers closed around hers, gentle as a decision, firm as a lock. “I saw you before,” he said. “Where?” “At this gallery. Long ago.” “I don’t believe you.” “That is not a complaint.” “Should it be?” “Most people who like me lie better.” “Who said I liked you?” “I did. Badly.” “You are remarkably sure of yourself.” “I learned from a better man.” “Who?” “The man I was before you.” “Perhaps I don’t trust him either.” His hand tightened almost imperceptibly. “No,” he said. “You shouldn’t.” She did not pull away.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a strong noir-romantic atmosphere at Coney Island, 1937, with a mysterious stranger and a heroine (Clara) whose memory gaps hint at a buried past. The prose is spare and controlled, favoring short declarative sentences and clipped dialogue that creates genuine tension. The dialogue-heavy structure meets the ~50% target, and the internal monologue ("His locks," the memory flashes of the yellow hat and music box) is woven in effectively. Strengths: The dialogue is the highlight — terse, oblique, flirtatious-with-teeth exchanges ("Need is an ambitious word." / "It is also a dangerous one.") that echo 30s screwball-noir cadence. The imagery is economical and evocative (paper moons, the kewpie swinging by one arm, "gentle as a decision, firm as a lock"). The recurring motif of "locks" — hair, then fastenings — is a nice structural touch. The ending withholds resolution appropriately, sustaining rather than defusing tension. Weaknesses: The clipped style occasionally becomes mannered and repetitive — several exchanges ("That is not an answer" / "It is a fact") recycle the same rhythm, and the line "She had begun, without noticing, to listen for cruelty and find only kindness" appears nearly verbatim twice, which reads as an editing error rather than intentional refrain. The amnesia/memory-loss element is introduced but underdeveloped; the stranger's knowledge of her mother feels like a plot device dropped in without integration. Some exchanges verge on cryptic to the point of opacity — the reader can't fully parse what's at stake. The scene drifts from shooting gallery to arch without a strong sense of escalation, and the "danger" remains more atmospheric than concrete. The sailor doll / kewpie business is charming but slightly meandering. Overall: a stylish, disciplined scene with real tonal control and strong dialogue craft, held back by repetition, some opacity, and a plot that gestures at mystery without grounding it. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 75.5
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Chapter Two: Before the Moon By the time the coffee came to a boil, Roy Pyle had told us twice about the moon. He was a thin, red-cheeked man with bad boots and a red scarf wound twice around his neck. He had greeted us with the enthusiasm of someone selling kitchen cabinets, talking as he pointed out the woodpile, the game hooks beneath the porch, and the place where we were supposed to park. “The rain’s been late,” he said. “Deer are feeding high because of worms in the clover. Moon’ll be full Thursday night.” He said that last part while looking at me, though I hadn’t asked him anything. Dad glanced up from the stove. “The moon won’t interfere with our hunt.” “I didn’t say it would.” Roy laughed, showing a gap between his front teeth. “I said when you ought to be on the road home.” For all his talking, Roy wanted no company. He ate his breakfast on the tailgate of his truck, a hundred yards from the lodge. When Dad approached, Roy became fascinated by the sky, the tree line, or some difficult adjustment to his rifle. He spoke at us across the yard without seeming to expect an answer. I’d never known a man who could make small talk sound like a warning without actually warning you. That afternoon, I found him splitting kindling beside the woodpile. “You might as well talk,” he said before I could explain myself. “Standing over a man while he works makes him nervous.” “Sorry.” “Don’t be. Your father’s the one who should be sorry.” The axe stopped. “He put his hand on that animal,” Roy continued. “I saw him do it.” “I know.” “Did you?” “He touched its face.” Roy drove the axe into a round of wood with a dull crack. “Hands don’t interest me. I’m interested in what came along to put them there.” The woods clicked around us. A bird called somewhere high in the trees, and nothing answered. “What do you mean?” I asked. Roy split another piece, then another. “That buck asked your father something. Your father hasn’t answered out loud. That isn’t the same as saying no.” “He didn’t seem dangerous.” “Your father would say the same thing if the animal had a rifle.” I almost laughed. Roy didn’t. “He’s going to want to go back,” he said. “If either of you enters those trees after moonrise, don’t follow.” “Even Mike?” Roy looked at me then. “Most of all Mike.” “Mike hasn’t done anything.” “Not yet.” I thought he meant the moon. Roy straightened up. His hands were shaking, though the cold couldn’t explain it. He stuffed them into his jacket pockets. “If something calls you after dark, keep walking.” “What if it’s my father?” “Keep walking.” “What if it’s you?” Roy’s mouth tightened. For an instant, I thought he might tell me to keep walking into the woods and never come back. Instead, he said, “Especially then.” Then he went back to splitting wood, and I went inside to tell Dad we should leave early. He listened without looking up from his rifle. “After breakfast,” he said. “Let’s see how the hunting goes.” I never mentioned the guide’s warning. By dusk, Dad and Mike had seen six caribou. None of them bolted. They stood at the edge of the trails with their heads raised, watching us come, watching us stop. Dad lowered his rifle each time. Mike said one of the does looked tired. Dad agreed that they all did. None of them looked tired. They looked attentive. I told myself Dad was being patient. I told myself Mike was making jokes. I kept telling myself things while the rifles gathered dust, and the caribou watched, and the sky thickened overhead. Then Dad said we were going back to camp. On the path, Mike stopped beside me. “Did you see what it did?” “The buck ran when Dad raised his rifle.” “That’s not what I mean.” “What do you mean?” He looked toward the trees, but before he could answer, Dad called from ahead. Mike followed, and I was left standing there with my hands inside my sleeves, my heart beating like a trapped bird. None of us mentioned the clearing again. That was how I knew something had truly gone wrong. Not because of the caribou or Roy’s warnings, but because Dad and Mike had begun looking at me differently—as if they knew what I had seen and expected me to keep it to myself. Some part of me already did. I woke just after midnight. Nothing stood in the room. Nothing touched me. Nothing breathed against the window. That was the trouble: I expected something to be there. The moon had come out from behind the clouds, whitening the floorboards and the edges of the beds. Dad’s side of the room was empty. Mike’s bed had been thrown back. The front door stood open. I found my boots and went outside. Roy’s truck was gone. His chair sat beside the woodpile, dark with dew. Beyond the outbuildings, I could hear footsteps. They were not coming from the road. I don’t remember deciding to follow them. My feet chose the path through the birches, the same narrow trail Dad and I used to take to the swimming hole. My body knew where it went. My mind stayed several steps behind. The sounds led me to the clearing. Dad and Mike stood on the far side of it, so still that I mistook them for two weathered stumps. Between them waited the buck. It was larger than I remembered. Its antlers rose above the low branches, and its white breath moved slowly in the moonlight. Each time it exhaled, I smelled coffee. Roy stood nearby with his hat in his hands, staring down at the ground. Then the buck lifted its head. Its mouth did not move. “You can come out now,” it said. The voice came from everywhere: from the trees, from the antlers, from the hollow space behind my ribs. It sounded almost like mine. “You don’t have to hide what you saw.” I stayed behind the last birch. Dad had told me not to look at a wounded deer. I had obeyed him in the woods. I had obeyed him when I stayed hidden while he reached toward that buck’s muzzle. The silence afterward had felt like a promise I hadn’t meant to make. But this was different. This was the voice I had used in my own head all day, the quiet voice that said nothing had happened, that Dad was merely strange, that I had imagined everything because imagining was easier than being wrong. “It’s all right,” the buck said. “You can come with us.” Mike turned toward me. His face looked wet, though there were no tears on it. “Little brother,” he said. “You finally see it.” Dad’s gaze found me next. His expression was not empty. It was too full, too fixed, as though he was looking at me through glass. “Come here, JT,” he said. My feet moved before I could stop them. Roy’s voice cut across the clearing. “Don’t answer it.” The buck looked at me, and the woods went silent. I thought of all the things I might have said. I thought of Dad’s hand on its muzzle. I thought of my fear, and my shame, and the relief of having kept both to myself. Some part of me wanted to explain. I wanted to say that I hadn’t meant to leave them out there. I wanted them to tell me I hadn’t seen what I thought I had seen. The buck lowered its head. “We understand,” it said in my father’s voice. I nearly said *Thank you.* That was close enough. The word rose in my throat, and Dad took a step toward me. Mike caught his arm, but gently, the way you might stop someone from walking into a room where something fragile was waiting. The guide shouted my name. I ran. The path was straight. I kept my eyes on the pale strip of it and did not look at the trees. My lungs burned. The rifle stock knocked against my shoulder with every stride, and more than once I heard footsteps matching mine in the brush. When I reached the truck, I opened the driver’s door and climbed inside without looking at the back seat. The key was in the ignition, warm beneath my fingers. I don’t remember putting it there. The engine started on the first try. I shifted into reverse, backed out of the rut, and pointed the truck toward the south road. The headlights swept across the porch, the woodpile, Roy’s empty chair. I should have seen the guide. I should have seen Dad and Mike following. I saw neither. In the mirror, the trees slipped away beneath a pale moon. It hung above them, bright and fixed, as if the truck and the sky were moving at different speeds. “That’s all right, JT,” Dad said from somewhere behind me. “We understand.” I pressed my foot harder against the gas. I didn’t look back. It wasn’t courage. I was afraid that if I did, I would see them waiting for me—and worse, I would believe they forgave me.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The continuation is a strong piece of King-inflected horror. The voice shift to first person present-recollection is slightly different from the past-tense third-limited of chapter one, but it reads as an intentional deepening of JT's unreliable interiority, and the clipped sentences suit the mounting dread. Strengths: The Roy Pyle character works as a classic King "local who knows too much" figure. His dialogue is the best in the piece—"Hands don't interest me. I'm interested in what came along to put them there" and the escalating "keep walking" exchange are genuinely chilling and economically written. The surreal payoff in the clearing is handled with restraint: the buck's voice coming "from everywhere," sounding like JT's own internal voice, cleverly literalizes the theme of self-deception. The "I nearly said Thank you. / That was close enough" turn is an excellent, subtle horror beat—consent as damnation. The ending, with Dad's voice from the back seat, delivers a proper uncanny sting while remaining thematically coherent: the horror is that JT would believe they forgave him. Weaknesses: The shift from ambiguity to overt supernatural confrontation sacrifices some of the requested psychological ambiguity—the talking buck is more explicit than the prompt's "grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism" ideally wants, and the story answers questions chapter one wisely left open. The pacing compresses; the midnight sequence arrives abruptly after a summary-style day ("By dusk, Dad and Mike had seen six caribou"). Some lines verge on over-neat ("I never mentioned the guide's warning"), and the narration occasionally tells us its themes ("That was how I knew something had truly gone wrong"). The moon symbolism is functional but conventional—moon-horror is a well-trodden trope. The word count exceeds 1000, though not egregiously. Mike remains underdeveloped; his "you finally see it" moment would land harder with more prior characterization. Occasionally the prose's terseness becomes a mannerism ("The axe stopped." "Not yet.") rather than a tool. Still, the piece maintains atmosphere, escalates tension toward a genuine payoff, incorporates dialogue naturally, and keeps JT's unreliability active ("I don't remember putting it there"). It is an above-average genre execution with a memorably earned dark ending. + Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 58.4
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Hell Is Other Demons At six-thirty, Lucifer Morningstar made coffee in a kitchen where no one was expecting him. The refrigerator hummed. Beyond the windows, the Lake of Fire burned in a modest strip of orange, because Hell had a noise ordinance. The penthouse had eleven bedrooms. Lucifer used two. The other nine were aired daily for guests, although he hadn’t had a guest in some time and preferred not to examine the discrepancy. Every Thursday, he set his phone to Do Not Disturb. This had nothing to do with Lilith. He checked that this remained true. It was Thursday. Three weeks ago, after another argument about a bridge, she had left through his office window. He had sent her the bill for the window. She had sent him the bill for the bridge. Neither bill had been paid. They were off again. He did not expect her. He simply kept Thursday free, a small administrative error that had recurred for several centuries. At nine, he went to work. Hell was administered from a basalt tower that had once been a mountain and was still disproportionately smug about it. Lucifer’s title was Chief Executive of Eternal Consequences. The position involved mostly forms. His crown sat on top of a filing cabinet. He considered this a matter of job security. His secretary, Mrs. Thrale, was a damned solicitor with immaculate handwriting. She had died during a disputed codicil and retained strong feelings about punctuation. She believed Lucifer’s crown and filing system posed a comparable threat to civilization. The morning brought forty-six appeals, a plumbing dispute involving the River Styx, and a request from Heaven to return all souls “currently on loan.” Heaven had not specified a return date. Hell could not establish that any souls had been borrowed. The request went into the pending pile, which was not known for its punctuality. At eleven, Gary, a former motivational speaker, appealed his sentence of listening to other people’s problems for eternity. “I’d like a transfer,” he said. “Somewhere quieter.” “There is a circle for the solitary,” said Lucifer. “That sounds ideal.” “We do a great deal of solitary.” Gary looked at the forms, then at the window, then at the lake. “How long does the transfer take?” “Forever.” “Send it in.” The appeal was denied. Gary said he understood. He did not understand. The sentence continued, which was the one advantage of eternity: there was always another seminar. At one, there were three knocks, a pause, and a fourth knock. Lucifer knew who it was before he opened the door. He was pleased, then immediately concerned that he was pleased, which was a familiar sequence and one he had never learned to enjoy. Lilith stood in the doorway wearing a charcoal coat and looking like a thundercloud that had been asked to fill out a form. In one hand she carried her scorched leather purse. It clinked as she entered: a plastic saint with one arm missing, a hotel key, a ticket stub whose title had worn away, a teaspoon from a seaside café. Lilith collected small things from the mortal world. When asked, she said they were portable. He had learned not to ask. “You look terrible,” she said. “I haven’t slept.” “That isn’t a diagnosis.” “No. It’s a schedule.” She put the purse on his desk and sat in his chair. He had replaced the chair since her last visit. It made no difference. “I came to return your pen,” she said, and held it out. “You stole that.” “I returned it. You’re confusing two events with a difference in tense.” “It’s my pen.” “It was in my possession.” “For six hundred years.” “I kept it safe.” He looked at the signature on his blotter, which was certainly his, except for a little extra flourish near the final letter. “You used it to sign a property transfer.” “I was making a point.” “With my name?” “Your pen. Your ink. Your inadequately guarded stationery.” The property was their old house in the Fourth Circle. The roof leaked, the garden was poisonous, and the gate he disliked was attached to a door she liked. Neither of them would sell. Their lawyers had made a career from the delay, though not the sort of career they had anticipated. “The deed,” he said. “I need your signature.” “You could have sent a lawyer.” “I could have.” “And?” “And I came here instead.” He found he had nothing to say. He had an empire, several languages, and a very good pen. None of these turned out to be useful. “What if I refuse?” he asked. “Then I keep the pen.” “That seems unjust.” “It’s the principle.” “It’s my pen.” “There you are.” She took it back and put it in her purse. The gesture was unreasonably satisfying. After a moment, he realized she had signed nothing at all. They argued about the gate instead. Then the garden. Then a chair that had survived three centuries of their disagreements and was, according to Lilith, hiding something. At four, he ordered dinner from a mortal bakery because Hell’s sandwich options had failed inspection. “There is cheese in the office,” he said. “Of course there is. This is Hell.” “There is also a sandwich.” “Who made it?” “The chef.” “Then it is not a sandwich. It is an administrative warning.” The food arrived forty minutes later. They ate noodles from paper cartons on his office floor, because the table was for negotiations and neither of them felt like negotiating. “You could come to the penthouse for coffee,” he said. “Why?” “The kettle is new.” “The last one whistled.” “It was the only thing you liked about it.” Her chipped mug was still at the back of the cupboard. He had never thrown it away. It seemed unnecessarily honest now that she had seen it. Lilith considered the invitation, or the kettle, or the eleven empty bedrooms. “All right,” she said. “But I’m not staying the night.” “I have an early meeting.” “Of course you do.” “Eleven o’clock.” “Your meetings used to start later.” “I’m working on my boundaries.” “I see that.” They took the lift up. On the way, she complained about the music. He explained that changing it would require cooperation. She said cooperation was not one of her professional strengths. At seven, she sat in the good chair. He sat in the other one. She did stay the night. It was only coffee, of course. She had a prior engagement, and he had a meeting, and the evening happened for reasons neither of them trusted. They watched a mortal film in which a family attempted to repair a lighthouse. Lilith said the engineering was implausible. Lucifer said the lighting was worse. They argued until one of them fell asleep, which was probably her. He woke at two to find her curled in the chair with one hand around his pen. Her purse rested beside her feet, emitting its faint smell of smoke and cloves. He put a blanket over her and returned to bed without waking her. In the morning, the pen would be on his desk. He made sure his diary was open to Friday.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of understated dark comedy in the Gaiman register — dry, deadpan, bureaucratic Hell punctuated by domestic relationship tension. The opening establishes tone immediately ("coffee in a kitchen where no one was expecting him") and the running gags (unpaid bills for window and bridge, the Do Not Disturb Thursdays, the pen) accumulate meaning with good comic economy. The pen dispute is the highlight: it works as both absurdist bureaucracy and genuine relationship proxy warfare, and "You're confusing two events with a difference in tense" is an excellent line. The Lilith characterization — the clinking purse of mortal trinkets, "portable" — is a nice Gaiman-esque detail that humanizes (demonizes?) her without sentimentality. The Gary the motivational speaker bit is funny though slightly filler-ish; it delays the main relationship plot. The dinner scene and noodle cartons on the floor continue the ironic contrast between cosmic rulership and takeout food. The ending lands well — "He made sure his diary was open to Friday" is a quiet, earned note of hope consistent with the on-again/off-again cycle, without over-resolving anything. Minor weaknesses: some jokes are a touch repetitive in structure (negation-based quips in dialogue occur in near-identical rhythm several times: "That isn't a diagnosis" / "I could have" / "It was in my possession"). The prose occasionally leans on the same deadpan construction so heavily that a few passages feel like they're running the same engine. Character interiority is deliberately thin — effective for irony but limits emotional depth; Lucifer's loneliness is stated through understatement rather than deeply felt. The lighthouse film scene is good but the closing beats arrive quickly. Still, the piece is coherent, controlled, consistently voiced, and genuinely funny — a high-quality execution of the prompt. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
## The Third Knot The day began with the scrape of a bucket against stone. Before dawn, Rome was more smell than sight. Through the dormitory wall came the splash of water, the ring of a barber’s shears, and someone swearing at a lamp that had gone out. Smoke seeped through our roof tiles, bitter with yesterday’s porridge. I lay on my pallet and listened to my ribs whistle, thinking that the silence after the bucket had never been silence at all. I was twenty-six, a murmillo, and a slave. I had not come to the Ludus Magnus for glory. I had come because the streets of Ostia were filling with men whose trades had failed or whose sons had been taken for Dacia, and because a hungry man could be bought for less than a pig. My father had died owing a baker. I was seventeen when the bailiff sold me. The Ludus at least promised regular porridge. I ate that porridge on a stone bench: thick barley, beans, and a heel of bread that scraped my throat. Across the yard, the blacksmith hammered helmet rims. He had no need for decoration. We were not soldiers. The state did not count our victories, and it would not inscribe our names on a monument. But if we pleased the aedile, he might purchase our freedom before the games ended. The wooden sword called the rudis was a poor reward for a life, but it was the only door I could see. Old Nicanor came for roll call, leaning on a stick that had once been a spear. He checked the straps of my helmet, the rim of my shield, and the place where my sword grip had begun to shine. Some of the men he had trained were dead now. He never softened that fact, and neither did he soften the arithmetic: a gladiator could win for years and leave no wife, no children, and no one left to mourn him. We were permitted to hope. That was how the Ludus kept us alive. By the third hour, the sun had reached the yard. I soaked in our bathhouse until the water softened my skin, then scraped away sweat and oil with a bronze tool. The heat brought out an old bruise over my ribs and the smell of every man in the room. On the walk back, the clean wool of my tunic already felt wrong against my skin. In my chest beneath it rested my sister’s last letter. Her words were blurred from much handling: my mother coughed through the winter; my brother’s unit had written that it was too dangerous to send news. No new letter would come today. At midday, we walked to the amphitheatre in formation. The bronze plates beneath my arms felt heavier in the heat. Along the route, the city smelled of hot bread, cabbage, incense, horse dung, and the sharp ammonia of fullers’ vats. Hucksters called their prices in Latin and Greek. Water sellers threaded between the crowds, and a flute player leaned from a balcony, playing as though the day belonged to someone else. On the Forum, officials posted notices about taxes, grain, and the levy for Dacia. People gathered around them, reading names, prices, and obligations in the same breath. Rome praised its soldiers and taxed its poor. It fed the hungry, too, but called the meal generosity. The games made both arrangements seem like peace. We passed men who had come to be seen as well as men who feared missing the free grain. A senator’s name might be announced before a single gladiator’s; his family sat apart from us, whitened by expensive dye. Yet our contracts belonged to the aedile, and if he lost office, they might be sold to another master. We depended on Rome’s favors while despising the hands that dispensed them. I hated the men in the shaded seats. I also hated how easily I watched for their approval. At the service gate, the noise of the street gave way to a hollow roar. The smell changed too: sweat, hot iron, animal waste, and the incense burning beside the statues of the gods. Beyond the gate, the sand shone pale and level. Dark patches marked where the day’s performers had already been used. We were not alone in being afraid, but fear was not permitted to slow us. Before every fight, I tied a red cord around my left wrist. Three knots: one for my mother, one for my brother, one for the life I meant to keep. My mother had tied the first knot before my first public performance. She had said it would bring me home. I knew cord could not turn an audience’s mercy, yet I continued to believe it. Each morning, I pulled it snug enough to feel my pulse, as if the beats belonged to her. Quintus, our lanista, checked our hands and sent us forward. The aedile sat in the white toga of his office, receiving the crowd’s applause as other men receive taxes. Some senators had come to watch; others had sent clients to count the applause. That was power: not the bronze helmet, but the ability to make thousands look the same way. The fear remained: that a mistake would be met not with anger but with hunger. I swallowed, waiting for the hush before my name. No god answered, and I was almost relieved. It meant the next breath, as always, belonged to me. Silence in front of thousands frightened me more than their shouts, because in that silence I was only a man with a borrowed name. My mouth was dry. I thought of my mother’s hands, and the white house I had once promised myself. Then the trumpet sounded, and the herald called my name. The crowd’s welcome struck me like wind against a shield. I touched the three knots one last time. The gate opened. Heat poured out, carrying blood, sand, and incense. I stepped into the light.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a disciplined, well-researched slice-of-life narrative that fulfills nearly all prompt requirements: first person, past tense, non-combat scene, rich sensory detail, interiority, and political/social commentary (grain dole, Dacia levy, aedile politics, slavery economics). The prose is controlled and often striking—"Rome was more smell than sight," "receiving the crowd's applause as other men receive taxes"—with a restrained, weary voice appropriate to the narrator. The three-knots motif is a strong unifying device, and the ending's ambivalence ("I hated the men in the shaded seats. I also hated how easily I watched for their approval") gives genuine emotional complexity. Historical texture (Ludus Magnus, murmillo, rudis, fullers' vats, lanista) is convincing without being showy. Weaknesses: the piece occasionally slips into essayistic abstraction, telling rather than dramatizing ("Rome praised its soldiers and taxed its poor... The games made both arrangements seem like peace"). Some sentences are compressed to the point of opacity ("the silence after the bucket had never been silence at all" is evocative but slightly muddled). There is no dialogue at all, which flattens some scenes; Nicanor and Quintus are sketched rather than voiced. The narrative arc is thin—day begins, day proceeds, gate opens—which suits "slice of life" but means the political commentary is delivered more as reflection than as lived conflict. The sister's letter is introduced and dropped. Still, the piece avoids purple prose, overwrought sentiment, and unearned uplift; the ending is appropriately ambiguous, cutting off before combat as instructed. Word count is roughly on target. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**18 January 1935 — Sgeir Dhonn Light** Mairi, I have been on Sgeir Dhonn three weeks. The rock is smaller than the map makes it. I did not come here for the view. My room is six feet wide. There are ninety-seven steps between my door and the lamp room. At sunset I wind the rotation gear and clean the glass, then write up the weather. Mr Mackinnon is principal keeper; Tam is assistant. The work is simple until a gale makes it necessary at three in the morning. They pay £4 10s a month. I am sending you a pound. Do not send it back. The cookhouse has tinned milk, salt meat and old potatoes. I am not unhappy. I had not understood how much a person talks without saying anything. A letter would help. Your son, Angus --- **8 February 1935 — 27 Coupar Street, Leith** Angus, Your letters smell of salt and wet wool. I mind that more than the postage. Your father died in his sleep in November. I have left his chair by the fire, though not his clock. I wind that on Sundays. I am at the shirt factory four days a week, paid by the dozen. Between the pension and the factory there is food, rent and a little left for coal. Keep your pound. I will not take it while you eat their potatoes. A letter, Angus. Especially if there is bad news. Bad news travels slowly enough without being kept back. Mairi --- **4 March 1935 — Sgeir Dhonn Light** Mairi, Tam has gone ashore with a bad chest, and the Board has not replaced him. I do the stores and water while Mackinnon keeps the light. Our rain cistern is fouled by birds. I boiled the water for an hour, which improved my temper but not the water. Fresh supplies now come in casks. I can lift one four-gallon copper at a time without ruining my back. The sea washes us. It also makes the shirts stiff. A mail boat came yesterday. It brought three words from the postmistress. I have the dates of the post boats now. There is little else to do with them. I have put in for a mainland transfer nearer home. They say there is no suitable vacancy. Your son, Angus --- **19 August 1935 — Sgeir Dhonn Light** Mairi, Something is wrong with my right eye. The horizon is clear, but the print swims. I have tried both pairs of spectacles from Oban and the spare in the stores. I can manage the light. It is the small print I must not let you see. Mackinnon saw me reach for the wrong tool. He has written to the Board. A doctor is to come with the November relief, but I cannot leave the rock until then unless they send a boat. Do not send money for a train ticket. I shall wait, and I shall write every week. Your son, Angus --- **30 September 1935 — 27 Coupar Street, Leith** Angus, My hand has swollen at the wrist. The foreman has put me on counting instead of the press: less wages, more time to think. That is not always a bargain. I have not told the neighbours. If you send more money home, I shall be too proud to say when I need it. Your letters are coming in bunches. The last five arrived together. I can wait for weather, but I cannot make the post boat any kinder. Write in larger letters if your eye is worse. I am not a girl, and I will not faint over a page. Mairi --- **21 October 1935 — Sgeir Dhonn Light** Mairi, Your letters and the parcel came together on Monday. We have flour for a week and coal for three, unless the wind gets into the store. I have written my resignation. Mackinnon has made me promise to wait for the doctor. He is right, and I hate him for being right, which is unfair to him. The eye is worse. I cannot tell whether the screws in the gear are bright or rusty. At sunset I hold the weather book to my nose and put it down before Mackinnon comes. I can still work the light, but not trust what I do. I thought admitting I was frightened was the last thing I could do without help. It appears I was wrong. Your son, Angus --- **25 November 1935 — 27 Coupar Street, Leith** Angus, I have read your letter three times. First I was angry with you. Then with the doctor, who is not here. The third time I did my packing. I am coming on the relief boat on 4 January, weather permitting. The captain has agreed. I have a ticket, a case and a shawl. I shall meet you at the landing, if you can get leave. Do not rehearse anything for the doctor. I want his facts and yours, not a brave version arranged for my benefit. Mairi --- **14 February 1936 — Oban** We came in on the fourth. I was ill two days, and the ship’s steward charged sixpence for the basin. The operation was on the eighth. Your eye is bandaged, and you object to the cooking. The doctor says the left eye is sound. You must not read small print or lift coal. He thinks that will be the difficult instruction. The head keeper is relieved next week. The Board has offered mainland work while your eye is reviewed. I have rented a room near the hospital. The landlady has a cat and does not ask questions. I have used some of your money for eggs and soap. I shall not apologise for either. Mairi --- **28 March 1936 — Oban** Mairi, I can read your letter at arm’s length. I took the glasses off and put them on twice, because the first time I was not certain whether it was true. The right eye is healing. There will always be a blur in it. The doctor says the left, with glasses, is good enough for the work. My place is at Rubha nan Gall, on the mainland. Assistant keeper, with lower wages and a landing stage. It is a smaller tower and not so near home, but there is a handcart beside the stores. Eighteen steps, according to the Board. There is a keeper’s house with two rooms. I have put your name down for the larger one, with the south window. I have not signed for you. The date is 1 June. Your son, Angus --- **12 May 1936 — Oban** Angus, I shall be ready on 1 June. Keep your wages. I have the pension, some mending, and the Leith room for six months if the work here does not suit me. I am not crossing the country to be tidied away in one of your cupboards. Bring the case to the boat. I have packed the blue shawl and your father’s clock. No more shortbread by post. I have found a shop near the hospital. The south window sounds right. Put my chair there and the lamp on my side. You can read to me when your eyes tire. I used to read the tide tables to you, and you never once admitted they were dull. On 1 June, bring the case down to the landing. I shall bring the clock, and you can read me the tide tables while I make the tea. Mairi
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary piece is a quietly accomplished example of the form. The correspondence between Angus, a working-class Scottish lighthouse keeper, and his mother Mairi spans roughly sixteen months and builds a coherent, gradually unfolding plot: isolation, a failing eye, the threat of losing his post, and finally a resolution in which mother and son set up house together at a mainland light. The greatest strength is the characterisation through voice. Angus is terse, practical, and emotionally guarded — his feelings emerge through understatement ("I am not unhappy. I had not understood how much a person talks without saying anything"). Mairi is sharper, wryer, and more commanding, with a dry wit ("I am not a girl, and I will not faint over a page"). The two voices are genuinely distinct, and both are consistent throughout. The period detail (wages of £4 10s, tinned milk, post boats, the Board) is convincing and unforced, grounding the 1930s setting without exposition. The plot mechanics are handled with restraint. The eye condition is introduced obliquely and escalates believably; Mackinnon's intervention and the Board's response feel authentic to the institutional world of the Northern Lighthouse Board. The emotional climax — Mairi's decision to travel to him, and Angus's admission of fear — lands well because the piece has earned it through accumulated small disclosures rather than melodrama. The final letter, with the tide tables and the father's clock, provides a satisfying, warm but unsentimental resolution. Weaknesses exist. A few lines are slightly muddled or over-compressed: "It is the small print I must not let you see" is confusing on first read; the 14 February letter is signed by Mairi but opens with "We came in on the fourth," creating a brief perspective wobble. The middle letters occasionally sacrifice clarity for terseness, and one or two details (the postmistress's "three words") gesture at more than they deliver. The mother's wrist ailment is introduced and then quietly dropped. These are minor, but they keep the piece from full polish. The prose is deliberately plain rather than lyrical, which suits the characters, though it means imagery is sparse — the salt-and-wet-wool letter, the ninety-seven steps, and the fouled cistern are the highlights. Nothing here is clichéd or overwrought; the restraint is the point, and it mostly works. The ending's warmth is earned by the preceding hardship rather than imposed. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 63.0
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Hacker Mindset I notice the salt shaker before I notice my date. The lid sits a quarter-turn loose. The restaurant Wi-Fi probably has a password tucked beneath the till; the host tablet looks old enough to have shipped with a vulnerability and a prayer. Years of white-hat work taught me to catalogue exposed surfaces, weak authentication, possible exploit vectors. Being reformed hasn’t cured the reflex. It only means noticing an opening is no longer permission to walk through it. Unfortunately, my attention often forgets the difference. Across from me, Alex is telling me about the worst hike they ever took. They push up their sleeve, reveal a pale patch of skin, then tug it down again. Old instincts classify that too: concealed detail, uncertainty about exposure, possible defensive perimeter. I want to tell them they’re safe. Instead, I ask whether they prefer something sweet after dinner. Alex looks relieved to talk about dessert. So am I. Then they mention *Magic: The Gathering*, and suddenly I’m not auditing the restaurant. They loved it as a kid, stopped for years, and recently started playing again at a library near work. “Nothing beats being surprised by a weird card,” they say. I understand that in a way I don’t often understand people. Between the bread basket and the salt shaker, my mind starts keeping notes. “Lightning Strike” is the first card they name. I file it under fast, decisive, probably aggressive. Then *Serra Angel*: midrange, efficient, a little flashier than strictly necessary. Alex calls it “a big dumb guy who doesn’t die.” I revise my model to include melodrama. By the second drink, I have a deck list assembled entirely from conversational scraps. Knowing someone’s cards isn’t knowing them, but certainty would be more convenient. Just then, Alex’s phone lights up. They glance at it, swipe through a notification, and unlock it with a quick gesture. My eyes catch the movement: loose, obvious geometry, no secret to anyone paying attention. I know before I know. That kind of confidence usually comes with an unnecessary lecture from someone who wants to feel superior. I am trying not to be that someone. It is not going well. “Sorry,” I say, “your unlock pattern is very guessable.” The sentence leaves before the better version of me can object. That version would have kept the observation to myself, or at least waited until Alex volunteered the phone for inspection. It’s not that I want the password. I don’t want the contents. I want the little win of being right about a weakness. Having spent my life building a self around finding cracks, I know how seductive that win is. Wanting it doesn’t make the interruption kind. Alex’s expression changes. It’s not fury, which would be easier. It’s the small recalibration of someone deciding how much of themselves to show. A person is not a system. A person is not a security assessment. A person is sitting across from me, hoping I see them, while I hand them a reason to wonder whether being seen means being taken apart. I could rescue the moment with a joke. Instead I hear myself say, “That was intrusive. I’m sorry. I notice security patterns as a reflex, but noticing something isn’t a reason to announce it. Especially something private.” No tutorial. No unsolicited advice. I want to add that Alex should change it, too. I want to make the apology useful. I catch myself turning remorse into another optimization problem: how do I make this less costly for me? I breathe. I stop. Alex looks down at the phone, then back at me. “It is pretty bad,” they say. “My younger cousin could unlock it in a second.” I brace for a reprimand. Instead, they slide the phone face-down beside the dessert menu. “You do this a lot?” “Only when I’m trying not to.” It isn’t a charming answer. It’s the truth. They laugh anyway, and the tension becomes something we can both touch without pretending it’s gone. So I stay with the cards. Alex describes a ramp deck: *Birds of Paradise* for mana, *Mulldrifter* for value, a finisher they refuse to name because “it’s stupid.” I add engine, consistency, flexible threats. They correct me: “I like having options, not a perfect plan.” I cross out the word “finisher” in my mind and write “insurance.” For a second, I’m not analyzing them. I’m just hearing them. I realize I don’t know how to do that without an annotation. Then *Dark Ritual* comes up. Sacrifice, cheap mana, a shortcut. “My friends hate it,” Alex says, “but it’s fun.” I add combo, risk, the pleasure of making something happen before the other player can object. The list is a deck I’ve built out of assumptions, and assumptions keep failing their audits. Alex isn’t a strategy. I’m not a profiler. I’m a person trying to be less defensive than my training, with a date trying to be heard. Near the end, I stop calculating whether the date can be salvaged. Salvage is a verb for objects, not for this. I tell Alex I had a good time. I don’t qualify it with evidence. They say they did too, and that next week they’re playing at the library. They invite me to bring a deck. I don’t calculate the best archetype or try to prove I can fix theirs. I say yes. As we leave, I keep my hands in my pockets. Alex’s phone is out of my attention. I still see the weak unlock, the cracks in the Wi-Fi, the salt shaker, the person. The difference is that seeing isn’t taking. A vulnerability is not an invitation. Curiosity is not consent. Tonight, the exploit I don’t execute is the one that would make me less human.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the prompt's core requirements with notable skill: first-person internal monologue dominates, the white-hat hacker's reflexive vulnerability-scanning is established immediately (salt shaker, Wi-Fi, host tablet), the MTG shared fandom lands naturally, and the phone unlock pattern faux pas arrives at the right structural moment with genuine fallout and a believable salvage. The reformed-hacker psychology is handled with real nuance—particularly the self-aware admission that the apology itself risks becoming "another optimization problem," which is the story's best beat and shows the character auditing their own ethics recursively. The MTG material is well-chosen and does double duty: the cards Alex names become a metaphor for the protagonist's habit of profiling people ("Knowing someone's cards isn't knowing them"), and the deck-building-as-people-reading conceit is threaded through without becoming gimmicky. The dialogue is sparse but effective—"Only when I'm trying not to" is a strong, honest line, and Alex's "My younger cousin could unlock it in a second" is a graceful, characterful de-escalation that avoids both easy forgiveness and easy conflict. Weaknesses: the piece occasionally over-explains its own thesis. Lines like "A person is not a system. A person is not a security assessment." and "A vulnerability is not an invitation. Curiosity is not consent." are aphoristic to the point of feeling composed rather than thought—the narrator sounds like a writer summarizing their theme rather than a person mid-date. The ending is somewhat tidy and slightly over-resolved; the final paragraph's litany of "I still see the weak unlock, the cracks in the Wi-Fi, the salt shaker, the person" is elegant but borders on neat closure for what was pitched as an ongoing struggle. The transformation (learning to listen without annotation) is earned but arrives a touch quickly in the final third. Some card annotations ("I add combo, risk, the pleasure of making something happen") are clever but occasionally strain, and the "insurance"/"finisher" revision beat is a little precious. Still, the prose is controlled, the voice consistent, the emotional register complex (shame, restraint, genuine curiosity, the seduction of being right), and the pacing disciplined for ~1000 words. This is well above average execution with only mild over-polish and thematic overtness holding it back. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 59.1
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Overthinking It All I said was “Sounds good.” Three words. Ben smiled, and my nervous system immediately began drafting a report on what that smile might mean. Inside my head, language arrives in full paragraphs, complete with citations and conclusions. Outside, I hand someone a sentence fragment and hope they can assemble the rest. I had spent lunch rehearsing three different ways to say hello, so naturally, by the time Ben spoke, my brain had used up all available words. That is the fundamental problem: my intelligence is most active before I open my mouth, then abandons me at the crucial moment. Today Mrs. Huang announced our science-fair teams, and there was Ben, holding up his role card with a paper bridge folded from the instructions. My pulse did something medically unreasonable. *Partners are not evidence,* I reminded myself. Obviously, random assignment does not imply cosmic significance. I repeated that until I believed it, which was not the same as feeling it. Ben looked over. “I promise I won’t eat the bridge,” he joked. I had prepared a clever reply. What came out was, “Cool.” He said, “Cool,” and returned to folding. Instead, I opened my notebook and immediately started listing variables. Ben was my partner; the others were Jada, Theo, and Maya Chen. I assigned us jobs while drawing tiny pictures in the margins of my lab notes. Jada became a stick figure surrounded by lightning bolts because she identified problems before anyone finished speaking. Theo became a turtle carrying a pencil, because he moved carefully and once seriously suggested a turtle mascot. I became a square head filled with equations. Ben got a triangle cape. I made his cape blue, then deleted it, then made it blue again. Each sketch had speech bubbles, but mine contained complete paragraphs of dialogue. Our question was simple: which folded-paper shape could support the most weight without buckling? My brain found that soothing. Variables, controls, repeated trials—problems with edges I could measure. Ben folded a neat triangle. I watched his fingers sharpen the crease and prepared to say, “Your crease is really efficient.” *Efficient* sounded strange. “Your crease is really good” sounded alarmingly sincere. “Nice crease” sounded like something from a yearbook. Exhausted all three options, I passed him masking tape instead. What finally came out was “This might help.” I managed. Ben nodded. “Probably.” I had rehearsed a conversation and delivered office supplies. Again, stellar social performance. Then came the terrible part: monitoring. Was my smile too eager? Had I answered too quickly? Was I supposed to laugh at that, or would silence have been safer instead? I lifted my ruler, decided my hand looked strange, put it down, and immediately wished I had picked it up again. Every movement generated evidence. Every silence had several possible meanings, all unfavorable. I could analyze a compound sentence, but I could not tell whether my “um” meant I was unsure about the crease or my entire identity. I was maintaining a transcript of someone who was not actually speaking. I was still auditing my facial expressions when Jada pointed at our tallest bridge. “It’s bending,” she said. *Not this one,* my brain supplied. *This crease is distributing the load along two support beams.* A useful observation everyone would respect, delivered in normal human language. I opened my mouth. “It’s… wobbly.” Ben slid a book beneath it and tested it with two fingers. “Yeah,” he agreed. I wrote in the results table: *triangular fold, 412 grams.* Underneath, in smaller letters: *complete sentence spoken; room still intact.* I had rehearsed eloquence and produced one adjective. Nobody looked remotely alarmed by that. Ben noticed the ruler tapping my notebook, not my face, thank goodness, and asked if I wanted to switch jobs. I had a brief internal debate. *Yes* sounded cooperative. *No* sounded stubborn. *Maybe* sounded as if I had invented switching jobs. What about *if*? I rejected that immediately, without trying. “Sure,” I said. “Switching is… okay.” He said, “Okay,” and took the ruler. Relief and embarrassment collided somewhere near my ribs. An ordinary question had taken fourteen answers to answer, but he simply continued measuring. I was already constructing an extremely long thank-you speech, which would have exceeded reasonable limits. The afternoon passed in measurements, pencil shavings, and tiny drawings that gradually developed plotlines. Jada’s lightning bolt rescued a collapsing stack of books. Theo’s turtle measured a bridge while wearing glasses. In the margin, I drew myself holding a ruler almost as large as my body. Ben’s triangle cape dragged across the floor, but he carried our heaviest bridge without complaining. I erased a tiny heart above his head, then replaced it with a star, which seemed equally suspicious and required immediate removal. Theo narrated our results like a wildlife documentary. Apparently, the paper bridge had refused to cooperate again. By the end of the day, our poster was covered with graphs, and Mrs. Huang assigned me to present. Inside my head, my opening was flawless: “Good afternoon. We investigated how folding geometry affects structural strength, and ended with our confident conclusion.” Outside my head: “Um. So. We… tested… paper things.” Ben offered to start. I considered saying, “Yes, please,” and rejected it as helpless. I considered saying, “No, I’ve got it,” and rejected it as defensive. Eventually I said, “I can do the first part.” He nodded. “Okay. I’ll take the graphs.” Even speaking plainly required a committee vote. At rehearsal, I looked at Ben instead of the poster, then corrected myself so abruptly that Theo missed a graph. My voice shook on “load,” which I decided was a betrayal by my vocal cords. Ben waited through my pause. “Again?” he said, as if repetition were a normal part of science. It was, annoyingly. I breathed, stated the result plainly, and finished. In my notebook, I drew all five of us holding one enormous bridge. Ben’s speech bubble said, “Want me to hold that?” Mine said, “Yes, please.” Our drawings finally showed the conversation I wished I’d had.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers the assignment well: an articulate inner voice paired with fragmentary spoken output, constant self-monitoring, rehearsed-then-abandoned conversational options, and the exhausting audit of every word and gesture. The strongest device is the margin-drawing subplot (stick figures, the erased heart replaced by a suspicious star), which externalizes the narrator's feelings without stating them, and the recurring "committee vote" structure for even trivial utterances is both funny and true to social anxiety. The gap between internal fluency and external collapse ("I had rehearsed eloquence and produced one adjective") is the emotional engine and it works. Weaknesses: a few sentences are syntactically muddled or dangle — "He said, 'Cool,' and returned to folding. Instead, I opened my notebook" has no clear referent for "Instead"; "Apparently, the paper bridge had refused to cooperate again" appears from nowhere; "I managed" is clipped to the point of confusion. The Ben material is thin — he's a generic nice boy with little individuation, though that's arguably realistic for a crush seen from afar. The ending resolves slightly too warmly (the notebook drawing where the wished-for conversation finally happens), but it's earned by the drawing motif and doesn't tip into fantasy transformation. Occasional lines strain for cleverness ("my pulse did something medically unreasonable"), and the piece is a touch long on repeated instances of the same beat (rehearse, fail, note it) — the pattern is the point, but the middle sags slightly. Dialogue is intentionally minimal and stilted, which serves the premise; the "weakness" is diegetic. Prose is controlled, wry, and consistent in voice throughout.
