+ First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 78.2
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I told myself I wouldn’t rehearse this. I have already rehearsed the silence. Mara is on her way. Seven minutes, according to the text she sent at 5:53. Seven minutes is not an eternity. Seven minutes is exactly long enough for the room to become familiar, for the light to change, for me to decide she has changed her mind. I am supposed to be happy. I am happy. I am also listening for the wrong number of footsteps in the hallway, constructing an apology I have not been accused of making. I told Mara, *Six is perfect*, and immediately wondered whether perfect meant eager. Whether she read it and thought, *God, not again*. I read it again myself. Three words. No pressure. No plea disguised as punctuation. But I know how I can corrupt three words. *Six is perfect, and I know you’ve been busy, and I don’t mind, and I would never make you feel guilty for that, and if you needed space I understand, and I’m sure you didn’t mean to seem distant, and perhaps I overreacted, but if you didn’t—* There. I have begun without deciding to. I have already played the cancellation. I can see Mara’s face before the imagined words arrive: *Something came up. Tomorrow?* She says it gently. That is worse. I respond, also gentle, because I refuse to give her the satisfaction of hearing me beg. *Of course. I understand.* Inside, I am screaming. Understand what? Understand that I waited all day? Understand that I rehearsed being abandoned between arranging a shirt and choosing a shirt? Understand that every kind sentence is another opportunity to discover the limit of your kindness? If she actually said that, I would say, *You never actually cancel.* And she would answer, *Not this time.* Not this time. The phrase curls comfortably around my fear. A reprieve is not a pardon. Today she comes; tomorrow the cancellation comes. Everyone leaves eventually. Even the ones who love you. Especially the ones who love you, because eventually they run out of reasons to stay. I know this is a script. Knowing has never made it less persuasive. I am sitting on the edge of the bed with one sock on when my phone lights up. *Mara. On my way. Save me the couch.* There. Save me the couch. A command, apparently. She is already taking ownership of the evening, already planning which cushion, already assuming I will be there. I feel relief strike hard enough to make me dizzy. Then I wonder why she had to clarify. *Save me the couch* means she wants to sit beside me. It does not mean she is arranging furniture. It does not mean she needs a place to disappear. I am turning an invitation into an escape route. I know that too. I know it the way I know the room is warm, then shiver anyway. My phone opens our conversation. Three days of short messages. *Working late.* *Can’t tonight.* *Tomorrow?* Nothing cruel. Nothing cold. Mara has been living her life while I have been grading each silence for intent. She said she missed me. In person, several times. But I can no longer distinguish missing me from tolerating me. I need her to say it again, differently, more strongly, until the words become undeniable. Until I can stop translating them. There is a knock. My whole body braces as if for impact. It is only Mara. She stands in the doorway holding a paper bag. *I brought the sesame thing you like. The one you said was probably too sweet.* I laugh. Actually laugh. *You remembered.* *Of course I remembered.* There it is: love, offered plainly. Not a grand declaration. Just a small sweet thing, carried across the city because I once mentioned it. *Thank you,* I say, meaning more syllables than I allow myself. And immediately: She remembered because I mattered enough to remember. Or she is being kind because she knows I need reassurance. Or the sesame thing means nothing. Maybe she bought it for herself. Maybe she plans to watch me eat it and feel smug. Maybe— *You look tired,* she says. *Thanks.* *Not in a “you look exhausted” way. In a “someone has been worrying” way.* I look at her. Her expression is soft. Concern lives there, not contempt. I can feel it. I can almost let it land. Almost. *You look exhausted* was a judgment, rehearsed. *Someone has been worrying* is care, but I wonder what she sees. Do I look transparent? Unstable? Like someone waiting to be handled? I wonder whether she is already tired of me, whether affection has become another task on her list: make dinner, rescue keys, reassure Mara’s anxious mind. I resent her for that. Not for anything she has done. For the possibility that she might someday decline to do it. That is what I do. I prepare my resentment before I have to feel rejected. I get angry first so her leaving cannot catch me unaware. I build a tiny fortress out of preemptive disappointment and call it self-protection. Then I resent her for looking through the joke. I resent her for being kind enough not to punish me. I resent myself for needing so much from someone who has done nothing wrong. *Come in,* I say. *Was I standing in the hallway waiting for permission?* The words are playful, but the question beneath them is immediate. You are joking. You are not asking whether I have imagined you leaving. You are not— *I’m joking,* she says. *Bad timing. Very funny joke.* I know. I know, and I cannot stop listening for the criticism underneath. From the neighbor’s wall comes muffled television dialogue. *I never meant it that way.* *Then why did you say it?* The words are indistinct. Someone in another apartment is having the argument I have already had in every available version. I should turn up the television. I should interrupt my own script. Instead, I listen. *You always do this,* my imagined Mara says. *No,* my imagined defensive me replies. *You’re twisting what I said.* *That’s what you always do when someone mentions their feelings.* *I do not.* *You do.* The argument is flawless. Of course it is. I have refined it over years. I know every pause, every accusation, every reckless justification. I know how to make myself unforgivable in twelve sentences or fewer. The real Mara reaches for my hand. Her fingers are cold from the walk. I notice this small fact, then search her face for disappointment. *I’m glad you’re here,* she says. I feel the words enter me. Not enough. That is my first response. You said it because you have to. You are thinking about work. You wish you had stayed home. You want me to be reassured, but not as much as I need to be. I need her to say it again. I need her to say it when I have not prompted her, misunderstood her, or demanded proof. I need her to keep choosing me after every imagined rejection I have invented. I need the evidence to grow until it overwhelms the voice insisting it is insufficient. That need frightens me. It frightens me because it means I may turn her tenderness into a test she did not agree to take. I recognize the pattern. I recognize that recognition is not the same as freedom. Her thumb moves across my knuckles. *Your hand is freezing.* *And yours are warm.* *So you’re stealing them.* *Apparently.* A laugh escapes me, and for one second I am not rehearsing. I do not trust the second. I begin composing its ending. *Mara rests her head on my shoulder. She says nothing cruel. She does not say enough to remove my doubt. When she eventually sleeps, I will stare at the ceiling and wonder whether she has stopped loving me, or whether I have finally become impossible to love.* Even that fantasy is preparation. Mara lifts the sesame pastry from the bag and holds it toward me. *Eat,* she says. *You’re supposed to be happy you’re still alive.* Still alive. Not *still with me*. Not *still trying*. And for this moment, my hand does not pull away.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a demanding prompt: an almost entirely internal monologue depicting BPD-pattern cognition—rehearsed rejections, preemptive resentment, fleeting self-awareness that fails to interrupt the cycle. The narrator's voice is consistent and controlled, moving between anxious parsing of small data points (text timestamps, "Save me the couch") and elaborate imagined confrontations. The imagined argument ("You always do this") is convincingly rendered as a rehearsed script the narrator admits to having "refined over years," which captures the prompt's requirement of selective self-awareness competing with the compelling nature of the scenarios. Strengths: the dissonance between actual events (sesame pastry, cold hands, "I'm glad you're here") and their immediate reinterpretation is handled with precision and restraint. The prose is economical, rhythmic, and largely avoids melodrama. Lines like "I know it the way I know the room is warm, then shiver anyway" and "A reprieve is not a pardon" are effective without being purple. The preemptive resentment passage ("I get angry first so her leaving cannot catch me unaware") is psychologically astute. The ending resists false resolution—validation is felt, needed, and immediately questioned, with only a small, tentative moment of non-withdrawal. Weaknesses: the piece occasionally over-relies on aphoristic one-liners ("Everyone leaves eventually. Even the ones who love you. Especially the ones who love you"), which can feel polished rather than raw. The Mara dialogue is thin and slightly generic ("Was I standing in the hallway waiting for permission?"), though the prompt's emphasis on internal monologue limits dialogue's role. The neighbor's-wall television argument is a clever device but borders on contrived. Some repetition of the validation-then-doubt cycle risks diminishing returns in the final third. The italicized internal-voice convention is used heavily and occasionally blurs which thoughts are "spoken." The word count falls somewhat short of the 1000-word seed, though not egregiously. The ending is appropriately ambivalent—no incongruent positivity, no unearned transformation. The narrator's limited insight is preserved honestly. "Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Blood Debt The mountain temple had stood empty for forty years. Rain found the ruined altar and slipped through its hairline cracks; the roof admitted silver blades of light, while torch smoke gathered beneath the rafters. Every folding was occupied. Jigen-ryū’s retainers crowded the eastern gallery in dark silk, their clanking scabbards forbidden but their pride plentiful. Opposite them, Piguaquan’s blacksmiths, porters, and bodyguards packed the western benches. Copper strings changed hands between bets: wages, a warehouse deed, the right to carry a school’s name into another province. Men wagered reputations as recklessly as money. At the north end, two paces before the altar, Sōta waited facing south. His school’s black sash bound a lean, aristocratic frame; his rear hand rested beside his hip, fingers poised. At the southern entrance, Ren faced north in a patched gray jacket, wrists wrapped, knees loose, weight forward. Four paces of cracked flagstone separated them, with the stream between: a silver thread trickling from a northeast floor crack and wandering southwest across the arena. Sōta brought Jigen-ryū’s explosive speed and contemptuous precision. Ren brought Piguaquan’s circling steps, whipping arms, and treacherous angles. For four generations, Jigen-ryū had treasured exclusivity; the Piguaquan families it scorned remembered old taxes, old exclusions, old wars. Both masters had expressly forbidden contact. They had answered those prohibitions with private insults, each certain the other would retreat. A temple bell—one note, iron tongue knocked mute—announced the fight. Sōta drove off his rear foot and consumed the distance in three strides. His left fist came straight down the center. Ren stepped a pace east, meeting it with his left forearm; the deflection turned the punch farther south. Sōta planted that foot and fired his right hand. Ren caught it on the opposite forearm, then stepped north inside the reach. His left elbow aimed at Sōta’s ribs. Sōta twisted, presenting only a hard shoulder, and shoved Ren southeast with a flat right palm. Ren yielded, caught the following right kick on his left shin, and slid another pace south. The first exchange carried no blood, but it moved them toward the east gallery: Sōta north of the water, Ren southeast of him. Now Sōta circled east along the bank and set his angle across the stream. He lengthened his stride over the thin water without breaking speed and drove Ren toward the broken flagstones. A straight right forced Ren’s guard up. A left hook followed. Ren’s right forearm intercepted the first; he bent beneath the second as it hooked past his shoulder. Ren pivoted and carried his left arm in a low, accelerating arc. The backhand snapped toward Sōta’s temple. Sōta folded at the hips, letting it pass over his skull, then punched upward from his crouch into Ren’s shoulder. The blow turned Ren but did not stop him. Ren continued the pivot until his chest faced Sōta, then whipped his right hand into the ribs. Sōta blocked low; the force still pushed him a half-pace north, nearer heel scraping wet stone. Ren followed with a short left strike, and a split opened Sōta’s lip. Ren’s blood was still clean. Sōta’s answer was to erase his advantage in distance. He set his left foot beside the stream and advanced in short, stabbing steps, cutting off every route around the southern bank. His left jab drove Ren’s right hand upward. His right fist followed toward the ribs. Ren turned the second blow across his shoulder instead of catching it, conceding two paces west. Sōta’s lips pulled back from his teeth. He lunged after Ren with a palm to the chest. Ren covered, absorbed the shove, and gave ground again. Sōta’s next straight right landed on the edge of Ren’s jaw. Blood ran into the corner of his mouth. This time Ren did not wipe it away. The western gallery’s broken column suddenly stood behind Ren. Sōta saw it and drove harder, trying to end the argument before Ren could turn the ruins into a shield. He sent a left hand toward Ren’s face. Ren slipped south; the fist continued past. Sōta’s right shoulder struck stone with a crack that silenced even the Jigen retainers. He rebounded half a pace east, and Ren was already inside his reach. Sōta straightened with a short elbow. Ren caught it on his forearm, yielded a fraction, then circled toward Sōta’s left. His right arm unwound like a rope and struck the exposed ribs. Sōta caught the blow on an elbow, but his recovery step carried him backward. Ren pressed. He did not chase with straight strides. He used the stream’s threat to narrow Sōta’s choices, advancing northeast then cutting back, making the Jigen fighter turn away from the slick stones. Sōta recognized the tactic. He stopped retreating and burst forward before Ren could complete another circle. Sōta’s right fist came from the hip with all the speed that had made Jigen-ryū famous. Ren caught it on his left forearm. Instead of resisting, he let the punch carry their joined arms eastward while he stepped around Sōta’s right side. The turn became a continuous whip: Ren’s feet crossed, his hips uncoiled, and his right fist struck Sōta’s jaw. Sōta’s heel dragged across grit. He dropped onto one knee, then caught the stone with his left palm. Even there he remained dangerous; his right elbow drove upward. Ren shifted outside its diagonal, slapped it down with a descending forearm, and delivered a short palm strike beneath Sōta’s raised arm. Sōta stayed kneeling. Silence came first from the Jigen gallery. Then a Piguaquan roar rolled through the temple. Ren lowered his bloody fist. Sōta touched two fingers to the stone—the old concession—before drawing himself upright. Now the stream lay behind Sōta; Ren stood nearer the western gallery. Their masters would call the gathering treason. Their followers would call it justice. Looking at the red on his knuckles, Sōta gave no challenge. Their rivalry demanded blood. The blood was paid for his school’s name.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a tightly choreographed duel with strong spatial discipline. The writer tracks positions meticulously—the stream bisecting the arena, the galleries east and west, the broken column, the shifting north-south-east-west relationships between fighters. Every strike has a clear origin, target, and consequence, and the momentum shifts (Sōta's early pressure, Ren's tactical use of terrain, the decisive whip-turn finish) are legible and earned. The prose is lean and declarative, almost hard-boiled, which suits the material and avoids purple excess. Weaknesses: the characters are archetypes rather than people. Sōta is "aristocratic contempt," Ren is "cunning commoner," and neither has interiority beyond the rivalry premise. The animosity is asserted ("private insults," "four generations") rather than dramatized through specific history or memory. Dialogue is entirely absent—not required, but its absence means the crowd and fighters never speak, which flattens the atmosphere; the wagering spectators are described but never heard. The ending is abrupt: Sōta's concession and the "blood debt paid" line lands as a tidy thematic bow, slightly tell-don't-show ("Their rivalry demanded blood"). Some phrasings are odd or overcompressed ("Every folding was occupied," "Copper strings changed hands," "Ren's blood was still clean"), which occasionally reads as mannered rather than elegant. The piece is competent and vivid but emotionally narrow—pride and pain, little else. Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Breaking Formation The scholarship had brought me from a council estate in south London to a dormitory in Seoul. On the first morning, I stood outside Studio Three while rain silvered the windows and neon leaked across the glass. I was homesick for cracked concrete and a bass line thumping through the floor. Inside, the air smelled of lemon disinfectant and expensive sportswear. Everyone wore the same white shirt. I had spent years making my clothes part of my movement. Now my T-shirt was supposed to disappear. Instructor Han already stood at the front-right of the room, a black folding fan in her left hand. Her former students occupied magazines and streaming stages; the stories about her said she identified talent, then cut away every habit that resisted the plan. We stood in three rows of four, facing the mirrors across the front and right walls. I was at the back-left, my tape square just behind my left heel. My right toes pointed forward. Between us, black tape held our spacing exact enough to hurt. On the estate, a beat invited an answer: a shoulder shrug, a heel swivel, a wave rolling out of whichever part of my body had something to say. Here Han opened her fan with a crack and called, “Eight counts. Right leads. Four steps out, four back. Forward, return. Right arm crosses, opens, crosses, opens. Straight lines. No borrowing.” Han moved three paces left into the open space before the first row and showed us the phrase. The fan stayed folded at her left thigh. The feet alternated right, left, right, left: each active foot stepped diagonally forward one shoe-length while the other toe closed beside its heel without taking weight. Her right forearm folded across her ribs on two, then unlocked straight at shoulder height on four. On six the arm crossed again; on eight it opened low and forward. She finished without a ripple. We ran it. I matched her four forward steps, ending with my right leg weighted and my right arm open. Just before the lock, though, I softened my elbow and let a chest pop spill into my shoulder. I was late; the pop belonged between the track’s beats. On five and six I kept walking diagonally forward instead of beginning the return. I traveled six shoe-lengths from my square. On seven, where my right foot should have stepped backward, I stayed on the right ball and lifted my left heel. My left toes swept right, turning my hips a quarter-turn toward the center aisle. The loose rock step had once been my answer to a bass line. Now it aimed my head into a stranger’s lane. At the fan’s clap, I stopped with my left toes hovering and my right arm folded. I lowered the left heel beside my right foot without shifting my weight. “Seven was a change of direction,” Han said. “I gave you a return.” “It was a groove, sunbae.” “It was an error. You have instinct. I cannot teach someone who treats correction as a conversation.” I could still feel the concrete beneath that rock step. On the estate, a misread could become a joke, then an invention. Here every correction arrived politely wrapped in honorifics, which made refusal feel like vandalism. Most of my classmates had trained in professional studios since childhood. I had trained behind a community center, my teacher a straightened speaker cable and my syllabus other dancers’ freestyle. The scholarship called us equals. My knees knew the difference. “Back to your marks,” Han said. We turned front and retraced the diagonal until both feet sat on our tape. I reset right beside left. The track restarted. I stepped right, left, right, left; folded, unlocked, folded, unlocked my arm; then reversed the same feet—right, left, right, left—back to my square. My right leg took the final weight. For once my feet were not the problem. They arrived exactly, again and again. They were also a cage. During the next run, I asked what I was protecting. Not an excuse to disappear. Not a limp wrist because a mark had wounded my pride. I kept every foot placement, every arm angle, every count. As my right arm opened on eight, I let the chest isolation follow a fraction late while my weight stayed over my right leg. A ripple moved through my ribs, private as a whisper, without changing my shape. The track was untouched. My feet stayed on their line. But I had put my accent inside their music. The second time, Han snapped her fan shut. Twelve pairs of feet stopped; I remained in my finishing stance, right leg bearing me, right arm low. “Again,” she said. Then, more quietly: “You were late. But you finished inside the phrase. That is trainable. Your talent got you here. Your attitude hasn’t.” Her eyes stayed on me. “Do not confuse an accident with an idea.” I could not tell whether she meant I had improved or merely found a more interesting flaw. She was offering to remake me. That was the horror: not destruction, but usefulness. I could master every arm angle and commercial groove, become legible—trained, marketable, stripped of the instincts that made me difficult to teach. Success might erase whatever had dragged me onto a stage. I looked at my reflection, shoulders damp, ribs still humming from that stolen delay. I had thought the scholarship was permission to become someone else. Now I understood that the academy might reward me only when I stopped sounding like myself. I would not rebel with sloppy steps. But I would not empty my body for a mirror either. I would learn their formation until every line belonged to me, and keep the pulse underneath. The fan opened. “From the top,” Han said. I kept both feet on my square, weight over my right leg, and faced the mirror. Behind my locked ribs, my heart kept its own time. I gave her the clean reset she wanted—and kept one fraction of the beat for myself.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a tightly controlled studio scene that delivers nearly everything the prompt demands. The physical coherence is genuinely strong: the choreography (four steps out, four back, right arm crossing/opening on counts) is tracked count-by-count, and the narrator's deviations—the late chest pop, the rock step that drifts six shoe-lengths off the tape square, the quarter-turn toward the center aisle—are all spatially legible. The mirror-wall geometry, tape squares, and Han's position at front-right are consistently maintained. The collision of street and commercial vocabularies is handled with specificity (groove vs. formation, "sunbae," honorifics as polite wrapping for refusal). The strongest choice is the resolution: the narrator doesn't rebel with sloppy steps or conform wholesale, but hides a fractional delay inside the demanded precision—"I gave her the clean reset she wanted—and kept one fraction of the beat for myself." This is a nuanced, earned decision point that honors the prompt's threat of losing one's authentic voice without melodrama. Han is also well-drawn: "Do not confuse an accident with an idea" is a sharp, characterful line, and her ambivalence ("trainable... attitude hasn't") avoids the cliché of the sadistic drill instructor. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally over-compresses into abstraction ("Not an excuse to disappear. Not a limp wrist because a mark had wounded my pride" is muddy and requires rereading). Some sentences sacrifice rhythm for precision, becoming list-like ("I stepped right, left, right, left; folded, unlocked, folded, unlocked"). The class-anxiety material is sometimes stated rather than dramatized ("The scholarship called us equals. My knees knew the difference" is effective, but "I was homesick for cracked concrete" tells). The dialogue is functional but brief; Han's lines are good, the narrator's single reply is thin. The setting is sketched thinly—Seoul is mostly neon on glass and lemon disinfectant. The ending is quiet rather than surprising, and the piece stays safely within its single scene, but that restraint is appropriate to the brief. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 57.5
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
### *First Love v. Mora: In the Matter of a Wildflower Meadow* The court is now in session,” announced the bailiff. He was a tall, funereal figure in a wig that seemed to have opinions of its own. His staff struck the floor. The sound was not loud. It was final. “May all parties in *esse* keep their feet out of one another’s dreams.” Nobody present owned their dreams. Least of all the boy sitting in the witness box, neatly folding and unfolding his hands. On one side of the hall, the plaintiff waited in a buttoned white suit and an overly careful necktie. First Love was rosy-cheeked, faintly luminous, and doing his best not to look as though he expected a scolding. On the other sat Mora, an ancient woman in an iron crown, regarding the proceedings with the calm of someone who had eaten the previous witnesses. At the high bench, Dream sat in red and black, pale and motionless. He looked like a verdict nobody had dared deliver. “FURST LUV,” bellowed the bailiff. First Love flinched. “It’s First Love.” “MAW-RA,” bellowed the bailiff again. Mora’s iron eyebrow rose. “And that is *Mora*.” “It is pronounced correctly in the manner of the damned,” said the bailiff. His voice filled the vaulted dark. It also filled the boy’s ears. The boy wished he had brought his pillow. Dream laid one long hand beside the gavel. “Let the record show,” he said, “that this court has spent many centuries considering questions of love, sorrow, identity, and the nature of dreams. It has never been required to settle a dispute over who was choking on what.” “Your Dreamness,” said First Love, “the defendant has stolen a boy’s recurring dream.” “She has *improved* it,” said Mora. First Love produced a small glass sphere from beneath his jacket. Inside it lay a sunny field, full of flowers that had apparently never had responsibilities. “This was our work,” he said. “Max dreams it every week. It is tender, harmless, and carefully made. There is a field. There is a girl. There is a muddled almost-kiss, followed by a pleasant confusion of feeling, which is the point.” “The point is that nobody escapes,” said Mora. First Love snapped his fingers. The sphere brightened. A meadow appeared above the court table, as if the table had been politely asked to make room. Max lay in the wildflowers, wearing the solemn expression of a schoolboy on his first date. A girl in a red dress laughed and climbed onto him. “That isn’t in the draft,” said First Love. “It’s in the *performance*,” said Mora. The girl’s outline rippled. Her face remained pretty, though it became the sort of pretty that made a person understand why they might fail to notice a knife. Then she was chalk-white, sharp-toothed, and vast with appetite. She settled onto Max’s chest with the unhurried confidence of a landlord. Max’s eyes widened. “She’s still confusingly attractive,” Mora observed. “That’s artistry.” The vision-Max tried to scream. Nothing left his lungs. He could not move. Above him, the vision smiled, opened her mouth, and drew the breath from his body like a thread from a spool. “He doesn’t do that in the original,” said First Love. “He doesn’t *notice* in the original,” said Mora. The meadow vanished. The courtroom was silent, except for the bailiff breathing through his nose. “My liege,” he said, “I believe the witness has witnessed something.” “I should think so,” said Dream. First Love stood. “Max’s dream is his. We made it for him, not for her. She entered without invitation, transformed his companion, converted a feeling of affection into a feeding, and made him experience paralysis. Those are trespass, malicious alteration, and theft of breath.” Mora gave a small, unhelpful smile. “Perhaps also artistic vandalism,” said Dream. First Love brightened. “And ruinous interference with a formative romantic experience.” “Objection,” said Mora. “The boy is still smiling.” Both parties turned to Max. He was, indeed, smiling. It was not a healthy smile. “Max,” said Dream. “Are you harmed?” “Yes, Your Dreamness.” “Are you frightened?” “Yes.” “Are you attracted to her?” Max hesitated. Everyone in the hall leaned forward, except the abstractions on the jury, who had apparently seen worse. “Also yes,” he said. “The frightening part was better organised.” “Strike that,” said Dream. “No,” said Mora. “Let him keep it. It supports my artistic reputation.” Dream’s expression did not change. Nevertheless, the candle at his right hand shortened by an inch, as if impatient on his behalf. “And your defence?” he asked. Mora folded her hands. “Girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” she said. “He was breathing. She was hungry. I saw an opportunity. I don’t call it an attack. I call it hospitality with poor boundaries.” First Love put a hand over his mouth. “Your Honour,” he said, “I am the hospitality.” Mora turned towards the witness box. “Furst Luv—” The bailiff leaned towards her. “One does not interrupt the court with one’s *accent*.” “I said that name respectfully.” “You said it like a curse. It is not your language.” “This court knows,” said Dream, “that a dreamer may not be deprived of what passes through his sleeping mind. No one owns a dream merely because they built the scenery.” Mora nodded. “Good. Then First Love has no claim.” “No,” said Dream. “The dreamer has the claim. First Love holds it in trust.” “So she is guilty.” “She is also, at present, the only person here who has eaten nothing, complained of nobody, and frightened no schoolchildren.” “I frightened one.” “You were in the wrong.” Dream looked at his hands. First Love watched him. Mora watched them both. For a moment, the ruler of the Dreaming seemed less interested in law than in possibility. “This court is tempted to exercise discretion,” he said. Mora’s eye narrowed. “How inconvenient.” “The discretion will take the form of a sentence.” She relaxed. “Then I shall be granted a small, dark kingdom.” “No,” said Dream. “One hundred years with First Love.” The hall became very still. “You will assist in the construction of tender, mildly embarrassing dreams,” Dream continued. “No stealing breaths. No frightening young men. No changing anyone into an alarming dinner guest without consent. And when the boy dreams of his meadow again, you will help restore it.” First Love dabbed at his eyes. “It is excessively kind, Your Dreamness.” “It is mostly a nuisance,” said Dream. “There is a difference, though not one I expect Mora to appreciate.” “And my confinement?” she said. “Until the almost-kiss.” Mora stared at him. “There was no almost-kiss. That was the entire tragedy.” “There will be one now,” said Dream. “You will remain in the meadow, helping with the emotional weather, and you will not eat a petal. You will be present for every attempt.” “One hundred years of watching people nearly kiss?” “One hundred years,” said Dream, “is a long time to reflect upon your methods.” He allowed himself the smallest suggestion of amusement. Mora turned to the bailiff. “I want to appeal.” The bailiff struck his staff. “MAW-RA,” he roared. She closed her eyes. “I knew you would say that.” Dream lifted the gavel. “Let the record further show,” he said, “that this court is still better at mercy than she is at breathing.” The sentence was carried out. Max’s meadow returned that night. The flowers stood up straight. The girl laughed, and remained herself, and almost kissed him, and left him beautifully confused. Mora stood at the edge of the field for one hundred years, saying nothing, eating nothing, and learning from First Love how a feeling ought to be made. Meanwhile, the bailiff mispronounced everyone’s name with tremendous confidence. Somewhere in the Dreaming, Dream permitted himself to smile. It was, by the standards of the court, an extremely malicious thing to do.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of understated dark comedy that hits nearly all of the prompt's requirements. The courtroom farce is well executed: the bailiff's mispronunciations, the legalistic framing of dream-theft, and Dream's dry irritation ("this court has spent many centuries considering questions of love... It has never been required to settle a dispute over who was choking on what") land effectively. The prose is spare and controlled, matching the instruction to use descriptives sparingly, and the humor is appropriately deadpan ("hospitality with poor boundaries"). Strengths: Dream's characterization is excellent—his irritation is conveyed through small physical details (the candle shortening) rather than exposition, and his "mischief" in the resolution (sentencing Mora to a century of watching almost-kisses) is both cruel and funny, exactly as requested. The evidence-presentation scene with the glass sphere is a clever courtroom-drama translation of the dream itself. Max's testimony ("The frightening part was better organised") is a highlight. Weaknesses: The middle section gets slightly muddled in the legal logic—Dream's ruling about who holds the claim in trust is a bit confusing and reads as clever-sounding rather than coherent. The bailiff's accent-interruption exchange is funny but slightly overplayed. The ending's "malicious smile" line is a touch too neat, and the epilogue wraps up a little too tidily, though it stays within the piece's established tone. Some minor formatting sloppiness (a stray heading, an unclosed quotation mark at the start). Mora's defense could have been given more room to breathe; her "girl's gotta eat" argument is dispatched fairly quickly. Overall, this is confident, controlled comic writing with a consistent voice and genuinely funny moments, held back slightly by a muddled central legal exchange and a somewhat tidy resolution. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 53.4
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Moon The moon hangs over the village like a wound refusing to clot. Its light stains the church steeple red, turns the fog copper, and gives the silent houses the appearance of drowned things. Wolves call from the forest. Their howls come at uneven intervals. Sometimes two voices answer. Sometimes only one. Sometimes the silence lasts long enough to make a man doubt he has heard anything at all. Alucard steps into the village square and tips his hat. A crimson coat sweeps the mud behind him. Round orange lenses reflect the bloody moon, hiding eyes older than the church surrounding them. In each hand, he carries a handgun with a barrel long enough to shame an executioner’s sword. Silver ammunition gleams in the open cases at his belt. Three vampires crawl before him, their wrists bound with chains. The orders from Hellsing describe them as desperate men: a stablehand, a gravedigger, and a merchant who could no longer afford spices for his blood. Now they snuffle at the stones, begging their master to restore their humanity. “Pathetic,” Alucard says. “A wolf would shame you less.” He fires into the church tower. The report cracks across the square, and a gargoyle crashes through the bell. The remaining villagers seal themselves inside their homes. Somewhere behind a shuttered window, a child begins to cry. The wolves answer. Yennefer appears above the church roof. She wears no crown, yet the village might as well bow. Black hair curls around a face too beautiful to trust. Violet eyes take in the silver, the chains, and the monster holding the guns. She carries a sword at her hip, and the air around her shimmers with power. “The stablehand’s name was Edmund,” she says. “He wanted to be a singer.” Alucard’s smile widens behind his glasses. “Woman, I have neither the time nor the inclination to mourn a man who mistakes transformation for tragedy.” Yennefer raises one hand. The chains snap upward. Silver links whirl through the air and strike Alucard across the chest. He catches two. A third buries itself in his shoulder. He looks at it as though it has offended him personally. Behind him, the three vampires scramble toward the forest. “Alucard,” Yennefer says. “Hellsing’s monster.” He tears the silver from his shoulder. The wound closes before the blood can stain his coat. “Yennefer of Vengerberg.” He rolls his neck, delighted. “The witch who bought her beauty with pain. What an exquisite collision.” Her expression hardens. She hurls the chains back at him. He fires; a portal opens behind his head, swallows the bullets, and casts them down in a rain of shattered stone. He shifts before the last one lands, becoming a black bat that streaks across the square. Yennefer tracks him with one raised finger. A bolt of lightning splits the church roof. The bat’s wing vanishes in a burst of burning fur. Alucard reforms between the burning rafters, regenerating as he drops. Yennefer meets him with her sword. Their blades cross. His handgun reverses, strikes her pommel, and drives her backward through a window. Glass follows her into darkness. “Impressive,” Alucard calls into the house. “Do try not to break the other windows. The carpenter charges by the beam.” Yennefer emerges through the front door, untouched. Wind gathers around her, lifting her hair and making her violet eyes blaze. “You’re too late for them,” she says. “But not for me.” “Do you always greet potential allies with insults and accusations?” She drives the heel of her sword into the cobblestones. A shockwave tears through the square. Alucard’s boots sink beneath the broken stones. He laughs. For an instant, his coat billows around a body losing its human shape. Wings spread. Teeth lengthen. Shadows cling to him like armor. Above the rooftops, the wolves fall silent. Yennefer watches the transformation without retreat. Her nostrils flare, catching lilac and gooseberries beneath the smoke. “Your heart barely moves,” she says. “I expected monsters to rage.” “Rage is heat. I am the cold that remains when the fire is gone.” The accusation irritates her more than his strength. She opens both hands. Silver needles appear between her fingers and descend around him in a tightening constellation. “Clever,” Alucard says. “Would you care to guess where I am?” He becomes mist. The needles pass through smoke. He reforms behind Yennefer and drives a silver round into her shoulder. She staggers but turns, catches his coat, and throws him into the bell tower. Stone explodes. Dust billows. Alucard rises through the ruins with a bullet hole closing beneath his ribs. “Funny,” he says. “I can’t remember the last time anything gave me that much pleasure.” He shifts again. His enormous wings batter the square. Yennefer folds the air around him, crushing bone against bone. He crashes onto the rooftops, tearing through slate and timber. A silver stake punches through his chest from a spell she has yet to finish. Alucard pulls it free with a roar. The regeneration falters. Just for a heartbeat. Yennefer sees it. “You can’t be killed.” “Neither can disappointment,” he says. “Yet both haunt you repeatedly.” Her magic strikes him. Fire, then ice, then force enough to bend iron. The ruined church groans. The blood moon trembles in a halo of broken cloud. Alucard climbs through the destruction wearing a smile. “No more tricks, sorceress,” he says. “Show me the face beneath the beautiful one.” Her lips go pale. He has seen the shape she hides. Perhaps he has sensed the other emptiness too: the future she cannot purchase with power, the loss no spell can undo. For the first time, anger slips through her defenses. Alucard advances. His shadow stretches beneath the rooftops, swallowing the light. Yennefer raises her hands, but the darkness catches at her wrists. For an instant, the power between them tilts toward him. Then she smiles. “No,” she says. “You want to see me afraid. You want me to mistake being understood for being known.” A portal opens beneath his feet. Alucard falls through. He lands in darkness, regenerated and smiling. The space is cold, sourceless, empty of every spell except hers. Yennefer stands across from him. Surrounding them, the wolves howl in a hundred directions at once. Above them, the red light splits. Her portal closes. The blood moon calls. Something enormous crashes through the forest canopy. The wolves emerge with eyes like embers. The first leaps onto Alucard. He catches its jaws, tears it apart, and hurls both halves into the fleeing villagers. Another attacks his shadow. Another climbs the ruined church. Yennefer’s lightning splits the lead beast apart. Her gaze flicks toward the houses. A child screams behind a barred door. A wall of blue light rises around the square, holding back the wolves when their jaws reach the threshold. Alucard fires twice. Two wolves collapse. “I thought those creatures belonged to you,” he says. “No.” “Even monsters have standards.” She binds a wolf in midair with a tightening knot of wind. He shoots through another, close enough for the heat of its blood to touch his sleeve. “They belong to the night,” Yennefer says. “The night belongs to neither of us.” “Then let us disappoint it together.” She strikes him with enough force to stagger him into the fog. He rises, changes, and tears through three wolves at once. They fight back-to-back, neither surrendering ground. When the last wolf falls, silence returns. His coat is torn. Her sleeve is burned. Neither has yielded more than a moment. Alucard replaces his hat. “The bird of Hermes is my name,” he says. “Eating my wings to make me tame. I think, sorceress, you may be the first person in centuries capable of making me interesting.” Yennefer removes the bloodied glove from her hand. “I’m not sweet,” she says, “and I’m not a maiden in distress in need of saving.” “No,” Alucard replies. “You are something far more dangerous.” He walks into the forest. The darkness takes him without swallowing his silhouette. Yennefer watches until even his red coat disappears. Then she turns toward the villagers emerging from their homes. Their gratitude dies on their lips when they see what stands beside her. The wolves begin again. One voice. Another. A third from somewhere beyond the hills. Yennefer lifts her chin. Not surrender. Anticipation.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a moody, atmospheric confrontation between Alucard and Yennefer, and largely honors the prompt's core dynamic: two proud monsters circling each other, neither yielding. The blood moon imagery is sustained effectively, and the setting (medieval village, church, wolves) suits both canons. Alucard's voice—cold, taunting, theatrical—is reasonably well captured, and Yennefer's refusal to be cowed, plus the hint at her hidden vulnerability (her transformed body, her infertility), shows genuine engagement with the character briefs. However, the piece has notable weaknesses. The action sequences are frequently confusing: portals open and close with unclear agency, bullets are swallowed and rained down as stone, and the sudden arrival of the wolf pack feels unearned and convenient, existing mainly to force the two into an alliance. The three chained vampires from the opening are abandoned entirely—Edmund the would-be singer is introduced for pathos and then forgotten, a dangling thread. The fight choreography often reads as a list of escalating effects rather than a legible exchange, and the power dynamic the prompt requested shifts more through set-pieces than through psychological maneuvering. The prose is stylish but sometimes over-compressed to the point of obscurity ("Neither can disappointment... Yet both haunt you repeatedly" is clever but muddled). Some lines are genuinely strong ("Rage is heat. I am the cold that remains when the fire is gone"), while others are awkward ("What an exquisite collision," "capable of making me interesting"). The ending—wolves howling again, Yennefer's "anticipation"—is evocative but slightly unearned; the mutual respect arrives more from narrative decree than from a fully dramatized turning point. The famous quotes are worked in, though Alucard's is slightly garbled into "making me interesting." Emotionally, the piece gestures at depth (Yennefer's anger slipping through, Alucard sensing her emptiness) but doesn't linger long enough to make it land. It's engaging, competent, and atmospheric, but not exceptional. Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Prison Strings The Blackwood Prison occupies a basement that city maps insist is solid earth. Jolyne Cujoh knows its corridors by heart: six flights down, left past the dead laundry, through the ward where the fluorescent lights forget to buzz. She has spent eight months here, framed for murder. She knows which guards hate silence and which floorboards sigh. Tonight, the walls hold their breath. Makima arrives during the midnight count, though no one admits to ordering her. She has auburn hair, ringed yellow eyes, and a smile soft enough to make Jolyne’s shoulders tighten. Two officers escort her, staring straight ahead. Every security camera follows them until she passes. Then its image freezes, its lens clouds, or its recording simply ends. Jolyne has heard the rumor. Watching a camera’s iris physically swivel away from the approaching woman, she stops believing in coincidence. Outside Jolyne’s cell, Makima tilts her head. “What a lovely room. I hate seeing people waste their lives in places like this.” Jolyne folds her arms over the butterfly tattoo on her sleeve. “Yeah. The wallpaper’s got teeth, and the concierge follows orders. Sounds like your kind of hotel.” Makima’s smile never wavers. “I can review your conviction. I can arrange a conversation with your father. All I need is your word to behave.” The guard unlocks Jolyne’s door before she touches it. A fine black strand loops around his wrist and vanishes into Makima’s sleeve. Jolyne’s gaze drops to it. “Word,” she says. “You people really do trade in chains, huh?” Makima produces a cream-colored contract. “Everyone wants something,” she says. “I simply make the price comfortable.” Jolyne doesn’t take it. Eight months in the hole have taught her that nothing offered without a price is a gift; even a sandwich can hide a razor. But curiosity is an old addiction. She hooks a finger beneath the paper and pulls. It slides through the bars, light as ash. “I’ll read it after you leave,” she says. “Usually people leave before I sign anything.” “How refreshing,” Makima replies. “I was afraid this place had already broken you.” After Makima leaves, Jolyne lets Stone Free slip from her wrist. An invisible filament lifts the contract toward the ceiling vent; another copies the guard’s abandoned key ring. Her father is two corridors east. That desire feels like a hook in her spine. Her father waits behind the visitation glass. Cap low, eyes shadowed: exactly as she remembers. When Jolyne raises a hand, he doesn’t raise one. When she says “Dad,” his mouth moves a fraction too late. The speaker hisses in Makima’s soft voice. She loops a thread around the hinge. It tightens. The door opens. Makima waits on the other side. Stone Free unspools from Jolyne’s shoulders in silken lines, each tip heavy with a stone. One lashes around the doorframe; another tangles the officers’ ankles. Jolyne drops, swings upward, and whips a thread at Makima’s wrist. A black chain flashes from the woman’s palm and catches it. Makima’s eyes brighten. “A body made of thread. No wonder I wanted to see you.” “Wrong,” Jolyne says, winding the line around her forearm. “I said no.” The stones hit. Makima’s arm jerks. Jolyne feels the cost through every strand; Makima wears pain like a borrowed coat. The unsigned contract bleeds ink into the floor. The corridor stretches. Cell doors multiply, each stamped with a number Jolyne recognizes. Her father’s voice leaks from the speakers, then her own. “Say you trust me,” Makima purrs, “and this stops. Isn’t that what you want?” Jolyne looks past her. At the ward’s end, Ermes pounds a cell door, a black chain vanishing from her throat into the dark. “That’s not my father.” Jolyne stops fighting Makima’s hold. Her thread slips under Ermes’s door and branches along the walls. Locks click. Grates shiver. “You’re manipulating the building,” Makima observes. “I’m getting these people out of yours. Big difference.” Makima speaks again, softer now. “Your father. Your friends. The life waiting for you on the other side. You want them safe, don’t you?” Jolyne’s threads pull in different directions. Stone Free can unravel her into a living trap, but the trap needs something precious to hold. The prison offers hope on a leash and calls it freedom. Ermes catches the loop Jolyne offers. Other hands reach through neighboring bars and take it. Jolyne isn’t controlling them. They are choosing. Makima stares. For one startled instant, her expression is genuine. The floor drops. Prison walls flex like a living throat. Light drains into a painted sky, bars lengthen, and Jolyne’s threads knot around her ribs. The facility offers her a way out, but every exit belongs to Makima. Every shortcut becomes a command. Jolyne stops demanding that the world arrange itself around her. She doesn’t need rescue. She needs the people beside her to reach the door. She opens every hand, releases every taut line, and falls. The threads follow—not as a weapon now, but as a net. Stone Free lashes from her back in a fountain of cord and wire. The false corridor tears like wet paper. Real red emergency lights flare along the walls. A blast door grinds open, and cold rain rushes in. Jolyne lands hard, rolls, and comes up beside Ermes. One by one, the others follow. In the shrinking cellblock, Makima remains untouched. Stones slide from her sleeves. The ink stops spreading. She watches the escape with the warm, absorbed patience of someone who has just discovered a particularly interesting animal. Jolyne pauses beneath the ruined gate. Rain plasters loose hair to her face, but her smile holds no trace of the cell. Behind her, every security camera turns to face the escaping prisoners. Makima steps into the storm. The nearest lens clouds at once. “Jolyne,” she says. “We will speak again.” “Don’t flatter yourself,” Jolyne says. “Next time, bring a better mask.” Makima laughs, almost pleased. “You can count on it.” The camera clears. It shows the road, the rain, and Jolyne walking away. This time, nobody switches it off.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent, atmospheric crossover with strong control of tone and some genuinely inventive imagery (cameras swiveling away from Makima, the contract bleeding ink, the false father behind visitation glass). Jolyne's voice is well captured—skeptical, foul-adjacent without overdoing it, loyal to Ermes and the other prisoners. Makima's menace is conveyed effectively through environmental details rather than exposition, which is a strength. However, the piece has notable weaknesses. The plot compresses too much: the middle section (the prison turning into a living throat, the escape) moves in abrupt leaps that sacrifice clarity for lyricism. Several moments are under-motivated—Jolyne's sudden decision to "release every taut line and fall" is more asserted than dramatized, and Makima's retreat feels like the author ending the scene rather than the characters resolving it. The climax is muddled: what exactly defeats Makima's manipulation is vague, and Makima's "startled instant" of genuine expression is a promising beat that is dropped rather than developed. The ending's "This time, nobody switches it off" is a tidy button, but the escape itself feels too easy and unearned given Makima's established omnipotence. The prose is polished but occasionally over-compressed to the point of obscurity ("The prison offers hope on a leash and calls it freedom" is thematic but reads as authorial intrusion). Dialogue is decent but not exceptional—Makima's lines are appropriately soft, Jolyne's quips land sometimes ("bring a better mask"), but exchanges are brief and lack the crackle of the source material. Word count is roughly on target. Third-person present tense is maintained consistently. Character nuance is moderate: Jolyne gets an internal arc (suspicion → temptation → refusal → solidarity), Makima remains mostly opaque, which is faithful but limits depth. The theme of control vs. chosen solidarity is present and reasonably well integrated. Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. Model Output:
# SCP-7319: The Notes of My Future Self **Object Class:** Euclid I was a junior researcher at Site-██ when I found the first note. I had spent that shift reviewing SCP-████, an entity that implanted alternative memories in subjects who merely heard its description. That detail later made every coincidence feel like an attack. > *Don't let them open Sublevel 4. The breach starts at 0400.* The note lay in the center of my desk, although I had watched the desk for six hours. I recognized my handwriting immediately. I did not recognize having written it. The overhead camera glitched at 23:41:12, exactly when the paper appeared. When the image returned seven seconds later, I was sitting in the same position, and the note was there. > *V—* > > *Please. I don't have time to explain.* I reported the incident, and the Foundation assigned Dr. Rusk to investigate. She did not dismiss me. That was worse. A containment team cleared my office while I waited elsewhere, removed the pen, and searched the walls. Nothing was found. They replaced the desk, sealed its drawers, and placed an independent camera inside a Faraday cage. I watched through the monitor from the corridor. > *You're already being tested. So am I.* At 02:17, the camera lost six seconds. I was alone inside. When the picture returned, a new note had appeared: HELP ME. The handwriting was mine, but the pen pressure suggested an older, arthritic hand. Fingerprints matched me, although the prints from my left hand were smooth, as though they had no friction ridges. The paper was ordinary office stock. Its ink was not. Dr. Rusk arranged two competing investigations. One team treated the notes as evidence of a localized temporal anomaly. The other treated SCP-████ as a psychological weapon capable of reproducing its victims' memories and expectations. We tested the paper in chronology laboratories, compared every word with correspondence I had written years ago, and interviewed personnel who had no access to my files. The handwriting gradually became less like mine. I recognized vocabulary I had never used and memories I could not authenticate, but some details were exact, including an argument I had had with my sister. > *The argument happened yesterday. You called her Ana. Her name is Elise. I was the one driving.* The first team searched for the paper's manufacture. The second searched my mind. Cognitive shielding made several technicians ill, so Dr. Rusk replaced it with mechanical observation, sedation, and two-person verification. I underwent a psychiatric evaluation, MRI, and polygraph. I insisted no one else had entered the room, although the corridor cameras showed a second figure leaving just before the note appeared. Dr. Rusk assured me that the footage was corrupted. I stopped arguing. Her certainty was more persuasive than my uncertainty. > *THANK YOU FOR BEING REASONABLE. THEY'RE NOT.* By 03:30, new notes appeared every few minutes. Each occurrence froze every camera in the facility for the same six seconds. Unpowered monitors showed the same interference; synchronized clocks continued without interruption. They warned against trusting Dr. Rusk, claimed the Foundation was hiding the entity's victims, and said the contained object was not dangerous. That contradicted everything in my security briefing. I visited its cell under escort. It was an empty room. The occupant's file listed my name, with a photograph of me in the future. > *At 0400, the breach happens. Close the corridor. Do not open the door behind you.* We moved the entity into an empty blast cell and placed myself under sedation. At 03:54, a note appeared on the desk beside me. I was unconscious, and two observers watched continuously. They saw blank paper, then static, then a written page. They also saw my hand move. When I woke, the note said I had slept for six years. The cameras showed nine minutes had passed. I could not decide whether the observers were lying, the recordings had been altered, or my mind had supplied a memory of a future I was never meant to experience. > *YOU DIDN'T WAKE UP. I DID. PLEASE DON'T LET ME BECOME YOU.* At 04:00, every door in Sublevel 4 released simultaneously. The blast cell remained sealed, but the corridor beyond it opened onto a darkness that the cameras rendered as pure black. I heard Dr. Rusk calling from it. She was still in the debrief room, confirmed by personnel I had known for years. I nearly ran toward the voice. Then I remembered the first note and ordered the corridor bulkhead closed. The darkness struck the other side. For eleven seconds, something made the same movements as I did, one moment ahead. > *THAT WASN'T THE BREACH. THANK YOU. THE FIRST TIME WAS BETTER.* The Foundation restored containment, and the record classified the event as a prediction. I could not accept that description. We had not prevented the breach; we had answered it. I requested a transfer and spent weeks reviewing the camera interference. Each missing interval contained images of my desk, although the footage had been recording a corridor. In the last frame, my future handwriting read, DO NOT BELIEVE THIS. > *There is no Site-██. There is no Foundation. There is no one reading this.* I distrusted instruments almost as much as my senses. If the cameras showed a note, I asked whether the entity had altered them. If they denied one, I wondered whether I had invented it. I kept records with colleagues, but their memories differed from mine. Small disagreements widened into arguments about other people, places, and events. I could no longer say which version of my past deserved belief. I filed this report. The Foundation could classify the notes as temporal correspondence, SCP-████ as the author, or my perception as the entity's influence. I preferred to be a victim rather than a message. The alternative meant the danger continued, and I could not know whether the next warning would describe a breach or my own disappearance. > *It was always dangerous. You were the warning. —V*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, disciplined piece of SCP-format fiction that hits nearly all the prompt's requirements. The first-person past-tense researcher perspective is maintained throughout, the interspersed notes escalate convincingly from terse warning to desperate incoherence ("YOU DIDN'T WAKE UP. I DID."), and the Foundation's dual-track investigation (temporal anomaly vs. psychological manipulation by SCP-████) is rendered with convincing bureaucratic texture: Faraday cages, chronology labs, polygraphs, two-person verification. The prose is lean and clinical in a way that suits both the format and the narrator's deteriorating trust in their own perception. Strengths: The escalation is well-paced across the night's timeline (23:41 to 04:00), and the details are genuinely unsettling and specific — the left-hand fingerprints without friction ridges, the six-second camera freezes appearing on unpowered monitors, the entity's file listing the researcher's own name with a future photograph. The central ambiguity is preserved rather than resolved, which is exactly right for the prompt: the Foundation classifies it as a "prediction," the researcher rejects that framing, and the final note ("You were the warning. —V") lands as a chilling inversion. The researcher's epistemic collapse — unable to trust instruments or senses, colleagues' memories diverging — is shown through concrete incidents rather than stated. Weaknesses: The compression required by the 1000-word target makes the middle feel slightly rushed; the "argument with my sister / Ana vs. Elise" thread is introduced and dropped without payoff, feeling like a planted detail that never earns its keep. The ending's meta-note ("There is no Site-██. There is no Foundation. There is no one reading this.") flirts with cliché reality-break material, though the final line partially redeems it. Some contradictions (the corridor camera showing a second figure, then Rusk saying the footage is corrupted) are effective ambiguity, but a few pile up so quickly they risk reading as the author throwing in every trick rather than a controlled design. The researcher's voice is somewhat flatly affectless even for a Foundation researcher — appropriate to the genre, but it limits emotional range. Dialogue is nearly absent (appropriate to the format), so that criterion is largely moot. The piece is coherent, atmospheric, and engaging, but stops short of masterpiece because its ambiguities occasionally feel arbitrary rather than meaningfully layered.
