+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 60.0
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Anything But Boring Forty minutes ago, I was on a city bus with one plastic shopping bag and a phone at twelve percent. Now I’m standing beside the Mississippi River, trying to remember how to breathe. A saxophone starts somewhere behind me. Low and mournful, it slips between the streetcars and tourist chatter like it knows a secret. I turn. A man in sunglasses is playing outside a jewelry store, fingers moving over the keys like he’s apologizing for something that happened years ago. That seems dangerous. You play too long, and people might mistake sorrow for an invitation. I turn back toward the river. The water is brown and mysterious, moving with the confidence of somebody who has never once been grounded. Seven dollars in my pocket. One clean shirt. Two pairs of underwear in a Ziploc bag. Not much of a plan. I came out to my family two days ago, and now I live here. Don’t sound impressed. It was an accident, mostly. The escape plan took thirty minutes. The courage took sixteen years. Mom’s face had gone strange and careful, like I was a house with an unexpected new room. Dad kept saying he needed time to process. The school counsellor had already told Mom my “concerning behavioural patterns” were escalating, which would have been humiliating if I hadn’t been too busy being terrified to care. *This is real*, I kept thinking. *Don’t make it a drama. It’s real.* I bought three beignets from a woman with a folding table. She gave me an extra one because I looked stupid enough to need it. I ate beside the river, watching gulls fight over something I couldn’t identify. Sugar stuck to my fingers. My binder dug into my ribs, and the tape along its edge had started to peel. That was when the saxophonist started playing. No wonder Mom thinks I’m dramatic. Now I’m getting a soundtrack. By noon, I was hiding in a library bathroom, staring at myself between the stalls. I look ordinary. That’s the problem. People see ordinary and assume they know the whole story. They don’t. At the sinks, I peel off the binder tape, smooth it down, and apply a fresh strip from my pocket. My hands only shake a little. I look up. There’s no mirror. Of course there isn’t. For a second I can’t breathe. Then I push through the doors into the cool, quiet main room. It’s beautiful. High ceilings. Tall windows. Computers humming along one wall. A girl in glittery shoes is doing her homework. An old man is asleep over a newspaper. Nobody asks whether I’m all right. It’s the kind of place that takes a person exactly as seriously as they can manage. I find an unused computer and search for jobs. Housecleaning. Food service. Warehouse work. One listing asks for a résumé, a reference, and “extreme enthusiasm.” My reference is dead. My enthusiasm is moderate. So I fill in the application anyway. *Availability: tomorrow.* The cursor blinks, impatient with me. Across the river, I spot a HELP WANTED sign in a bicycle shop. The owner is a broad-shouldered man in a green apron, dragging a bike through the front door. “Can you fix brakes?” he asks. “I know how.” “You know how, or you’ve watched a video telling you how you know how?” “Both.” He snorts. “Come back tomorrow morning. I’ll hold the interview.” I blink. “I don’t have experience.” “Neither does half this city. Show up, and I’ll show you the rest.” It feels less like a job offer and more like somebody leaving a light on. By early afternoon, I’m in a laundromat, watching my one pair of jeans turn in soapy water. A red-haired girl sits on the far bench. Nineteen, maybe twenty. Paint-stained black T-shirt, one sneake lace missing, a duffel bag held between her ankles like it might escape. Her eyes flick toward the machines every few seconds. I should mind my business. “I have detergent,” she says. I turn. “Sorry?” “You keep looking at the machine like it insulted your mother. I have detergent.” “Most people don’t carry emergency laundry supplies.” “Most people aren’t running out of clean clothes.” She says it lightly. Too lightly. “I’m Taylor,” I offer, because apparently meeting people in laundromats is my new life. “Birdie.” “Like the bird?” “Like the animal that steals things and doesn’t apologize.” A grin, quick and sharp. “What are you running from?” “Depends. You?” “Yesterday.” “What happened yesterday?” “I don’t have anywhere to sleep.” The machines thump and hiss between us. I think about every version of the answer I gave on the road: *cousin’s place, sure. Good family. Probably a room with a door.* “I’m working on it,” I say. “Cool.” She nods. “I’m working on not being homeless, but we’re both very committed to the process.” There’s a bench between us, but I move over anyway. Birdie watches me for a moment. Then she shifts her bag closer. “You don’t have to tell me your whole tragic backstory,” she says. “I’m excellent at ignoring people.” “Clearly,” I say. “You gave me your detergent.” “Was that a mistake?” “Probably.” She laughs, and something in her shoulders loosens. We stay until our clothes are dry. Later, walking beneath the iron balconies, I tell her about the job. About the library. The saxophone. The bathroom without a mirror. She listens without interrupting, which makes me want to keep talking. “So,” she says at last. “What’s your plan? Besides becoming a professional laundry observer?” “Go back to the library. Find somewhere cheap to sleep. Wash my socks.” “Very detailed.” “I’m a leader.” Birdie is quiet. Then she says, “I have a cousin here.” It comes too quickly. “Who is she?” “Her name’s June.” “Does June have a couch?” “Maybe.” “Does June know you’re coming?” “She knows I might.” I glance at her. “That sounds like a no.” Birdie shrugs. “Cousins are complicated.” The honesty of that almost makes me laugh. We pass a streetcar, and somebody bumps my shoulder from behind. “Excuse me, ma’am,” a tourist says. I feel the word land somewhere soft and unprotected. He notices my expression. “Oh—sorry. I meant—” “It’s fine.” But it isn’t fine. It snags under my ribs and stays there. I keep walking. *My name is Taylor. I’m not somebody’s misunderstanding.* Birdie gives me space, but I can feel her looking at me. A street musician launches into a fast, bright tune on a trumpet, cutting between the traffic and the pigeons. For half a block, it’s as if the city has decided to be kind. At the next corner, she says, “We should find a motel before dark.” “I have almost no money.” “Same.” “I can probably afford half a room.” “I can probably afford the other half.” I look at her. “Can you?” Her smile flickers. It’s the smallest thing. I almost miss it. But I don’t. At a café near the market, we split a plate of noodles and bread. The air-conditioning makes Birdie shiver. She pulls a folded envelope from inside her jacket and lays it on the table between us. “I lied,” she says. My fork stops halfway to my mouth. “I don’t have a cousin named June. I don’t have anywhere to go. I’ve been staying in cheap motels, then crashing on friends’ couches, then sleeping in my car when nobody had room.” She touches the envelope. “I stole this money.” “How much?” “Three hundred and twenty dollars.” “From who?” “A man named Roy.” “Roy who?” Birdie looks toward the windows. “Roy with the silver truck.” A silver pickup is parked across the street. My stomach drops. “He said we were going to Mobile,” Birdie says. “He said his friend had work for us. I got scared. I took the money and left him unconscious in a motel parking lot.” “Did you hurt him?” “No. I don’t know what I am. I know I couldn’t stay.” I stare at the envelope. For a terrible second, I imagine walking away. I don’t. “I’m not going to tell you it doesn’t matter,” I say. “But I don’t think you stole it before he scared you.” Birdie’s eyes go glassy. “You don’t know that.” “No. But I know what it looks like when somebody decides they don’t have a choice.” She looks down at the noodles. “I wanted to get here without asking anyone for anything,” she says. “That’s the worst part. I keep saying I’m brave, but I’m really just terrified.” “Same.” “You’re allowed to be terrified.” I laugh, a wet, ugly little sound. “I’d better be.” The silver truck starts moving. Birdie grabs my wrist. “Don’t go outside.” I look at her. At her fear. At the money she took. At all the things she left between one second and the next. “I don’t know you,” I say. “I know.” “I don’t trust you yet.” Her face falls, but she nods. “That’s fair,” she says. The trumpet player starts up again somewhere down the block. This time, I don’t turn around.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of YA first-person narration. Taylor's voice is consistent, wry, and wounded in a believable teen register — the self-deprecating asides ("Now I'm getting a soundtrack," "My enthusiasm is moderate") land well and give the narration personality without tipping into quippiness. The prose is economical and often elegant: "The water is brown and mysterious, moving with the confidence of somebody who has never once been grounded" and "like I was a house with an unexpected new room" are genuinely good images. The short-line, fragmentary structure mimics anxious internal monologue effectively, and the mixed tense is handled without confusion. The New Orleans texture is present but somewhat generic — saxophone, beignets, streetcars, iron balconies are the postcard version of the city, though the library scene (no mirror, "takes a person exactly as seriously as they can manage") is a lovely, specific beat. The binder tape detail is excellent characterization through physicality. Birdie is the strongest element: her deflection-heavy dialogue ("I'm excellent at ignoring people"), the too-light delivery of "I don't have anywhere to sleep," and the stolen-money reveal give her real dimension. The reveal itself is slightly rushed — the envelope appears and the confession arrives in a tidy paragraph — and Roy's silver truck appearing across the street is a convenient thriller beat that feels a touch plotted. Taylor's response to it ("I don't trust you yet") is refreshingly unsentimental and true to the prompt's instruction about not knowing who to trust. Minor flaws: the timeline wobbles (the bike shop interview "across the river" from a library is geographically fuzzy; the day's chronology compresses oddly), a typo ("sneake lace"), and the "ma'am" misgendering moment, while emotionally apt, is a familiar beat in trans coming-out fiction. The ending is appropriately unresolved — no forced positivity, no rescue — which suits the prompt. The emotional complexity is real: fear, dark humor, guarded generosity, and the refusal to either romanticize or condemn Birdie. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 75.2
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy “First,” said Chewy, “you will not fall into anything. Second, you will not chase anything. Third, you will not speak to anything that speaks back.” “That leaves very little for the day.” “It leaves a useful amount.” Chewy consulted his list, which he had written for Midas with a pencil sharpened using a kitchen knife. “You will acquire a water-filter cartridge, a tin of seed potatoes, and a replacement spring for my neck. Then you will return before dark.” “And if I encounter the water from the flooded quarry?” “Don’t drink it. Don’t look at it. Don’t think its name.” Midas considered this. “That seems excessively restrictive.” “We live in a concrete pumping station, half our roof is a tarpaulin, and I am nineteen inches tall. I have already exceeded your reasonable expectations.” The pumping station had been chosen for its solid walls and its pump, which still raised water if persuaded. The filter attached to it possessed a ceramic sleeve with a crack fine enough to be optimistic and wide enough to be fatal. Their remaining drinking water was therefore best described as a deadline. Chewy himself was an animo-tronic stuffed koala from a time when retail establishments sold friendship by the metre. His plush had faded from grey to the colour of an old dishcloth. His eyes moved independently, which made him an excellent scout and a poor witness. Springs held his ears away from his head. A voice box in his chest still spoke with the enthusiasm of a hotel receptionist greeting a foreign guest, though each utterance reduced the battery’s output a little further. He remembered almost nothing of before. Midas considered this a mercy for both of them. “The spring’s for me?” Midas asked. “I’m told I’m becoming hunched.” “You’re stuffed.” “The distinction has not been as useful as you imagine.” They set out shortly after dawn, pushing a shopping trolley badly repaired with wire and determination. Midas had drawn a map from the ruins of a tourist information centre. It showed the retail park seven kilometres away, a storm drain, and a blank space labelled IMPORTANT TERRAIN. Their route took them beneath a collapsed flyover, where fresh paint marked the concrete. WHERE THE SILVER RIVER BREAKS, THROUGH THE HILL THAT LOST ITS CROWN, LIES A MOUTH IN THE STONE. KNOCK WITH YOUR HUNGER. “Deeply moving,” said Chewy. “It’s meant to be a location.” “It has never been clearly told the difference.” Midas studied the hill. The hill resembled a collapsed cooling tower, which resembled, if one were feeling charitable, a jawless crown. “The silver river must be the railway. The railway goes straight past it.” “And your important terrain?” “Possibly the whole area.” They diverted from their route to investigate the broken hill, thereby giving fresh inconvenience to a landscape that had been quite content without them. Midas found a concrete drainage tunnel beneath the railway embankment. It was blocked by fallen blocks, but he was prepared to squeeze through. His shoulders, like his plans, had never been robust. It took him forty minutes to reach the other side and discover that the tunnel deposited them in the basement of a garden centre. Not their garden centre. Their garden centre was four kilometres further on, beneath a roof decorated with faded plastic flowers. This one had closed for reasons involving damp. Midas searched the offices for cartridges. Chewy searched the shelves, returning periodically with a leaf trapped in one ear and useful intelligence in the other. After ten minutes, they had found four tins of seed potatoes, a box of cracked plant pots, and a boot. “I believe this belongs to you,” said Chewy. “It’s larger than mine.” “Then perhaps it belongs to the previous owner of the garden centre.” They had spent two hours by the time they admitted their error. The graffiti, Midas realised, had described a quarry on the far side of the hill. A cut in the rock. A wound in the stone. His talent for finding the worst kinds of trouble had, characteristically, prevented him from finding the best kind: the kind directly in front of him. “It isn’t my fault,” he said. “I should certainly hope not,” said Chewy. “It would depress us both.” They found the quarry by falling into it. Midas landed in soft chalk, damaged his ankle, and overturned the trolley. The potatoes scattered across the slope. A hungry flock of crows arrived to assist, apparently interpreting both Midas and the potatoes as part of the natural order. Their escape involved pursuit, a mouthful of rainwater, and a ladder that had been fixed to the wrong wall. It was not, however, a ladder capable of bearing Midas’s full confidence. By the time they reached the quarry face, evening had begun tapping its fingers on the sky. There, among the loose stone, a slab of rock bore a deep diagonal scar. Beneath it stood a steel door, painted the same green as the hill. Midas knocked. Nothing happened. “I think the hunger was supposed to knock,” Chewy said. “That would be a remarkable amount of hunger.” Midas knocked again. Somewhere inside, a mechanism ground awake. A strip of light appeared beneath the door. “We have made an error,” said Chewy. The door opened six inches, revealing blankets, shelves, tins, and a voice. “Who’s there?” “Readers,” said Midas. There was a pause. “That’s not a listed category.” A hand reached through and took the potatoes. The refuge had been stocked by people accustomed to anticipating the end. Seeds occupied shelves labelled with the continents they had once needed to conquer. Emergency supplies waited in labelled boxes. Water stood in covered tanks beneath the floor, clean enough to make Midas homesick for rain. They exchanged their worthless boot for a working filter cartridge. Midas left a note explaining where they had found the door. Then Chewy laughed, which he did by drawing air through a small speaker in his chest. “To think,” he said, “we nearly missed this because you wanted a tin of potatoes.” “I did find the potatoes.” “You found a boot first. It was larger than your foot. I remain concerned about your standards.” They left before full dark, but darkness had already begun making administrative arrangements for the landscape. The trolley’s front wheel fell into a ditch. Midas removed it, put it back, and promptly fell into the ditch himself. They abandoned the trolley, wound the spring in Chewy’s neck, and used him to pull what remained of their supplies. “You could at least walk,” Midas said. “I have no legs.” “You have trousers.” “They are decorative.” By the time they reached the railway, the spring was failing. Midas carried the potatoes in a rusted wheelbarrow borrowed from the refuge. The barrow rolled downhill without him, picked up speed, and deposited him in a puddle. “It’s going the wrong way,” he observed. “So are you,” said Chewy. On foot, they might have reached home by midnight. Instead they took a woodland path, became trapped in a hedge, followed a fence until it ended in a reservoir, and finally stumbled home at dawn in a wheelbarrow belonging to somebody else. Chewy’s right ear was gone. One eye had developed a pronounced squint. Midas had lost a boot, gained a limp, and ruined the shoulder of his coat against a thorn hedge. He fitted the new filter while sitting on the floor. The pump coughed, sucked, and produced water. “Worth it?” Chewy asked. Midas looked at the crippled koala, the stolen potatoes, and the puddle shining through the roof. “Worth it,” he said. Chewy wound himself upright. “Tomorrow, then.” “Tomorrow we’ll be prepared.” “That,” said Chewy, “is what people say shortly before being unprepared again.” Outside, the empty world continued without them, which was the finest thing about it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong pastiche of Pratchett-style comic fantasy: dry, wry narration, deadpan dialogue, and a world rendered through understatement. The opening rules ("you will not fall into anything") set up the comedy of inevitability well, and the story pays off each rule by breaking it. Chewy's characterization as a fading animatronic koala with failing springs and a hotel-receptionist voice is genuinely inventive, and the dialogue between him and Midas carries most of the story's charm — "I have no legs." / "You have trousers." / "They are decorative" is a highlight. Strengths: consistent ironic voice, economical worldbuilding (retail friendship by the metre, water as "a deadline"), a satisfying structure of mission-gone-sideways, and a closing line with real Pratchett-esque melancholy ("the empty world continued without them, which was the finest thing about it"). The graffiti prophecy and the door that answers hunger are nice genre touches. Weaknesses: the middle sags slightly — the garden centre detour and the refuge encounter resolve a bit too easily, and the refuge dweller appears and vanishes without consequence, feeling like a dropped thread. Some jokes overwork their mechanism ("evening had begun tapping its fingers on the sky" is fine; "darkness making administrative arrangements" repeats the trick). The plot logic occasionally wobbles — the trolley is abandoned, then supplies appear in a wheelbarrow with only a sentence of bridge. Midas's "knack for trouble" is more told than shown in places, though the quarry fall does literalize it well. The ending's "Worth it" exchange is warm but slightly pat. Still, the prose is controlled, the humor lands more often than not, and the tone never breaks. It reads as competent, occasionally excellent comic writing with minor structural looseness. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 69.5
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Love in the Limelight ### The Quiet Shelf The bell above the door jangled as Rhys Henley stumbled backwards into the bookshop, shut the door with his shoulder, and leaned against it. Rain ran from his cap. Across the market square, a camera lens peered above a delivery van. “Please,” Rhys said, “if anyone asks, I’m here under duress.” Nia looked up from wrapping a paperback in brown paper. “By the weather?” “By the weather. It’s very persuasive.” He pushed back his cap, revealing a face she knew from a dozen magazine covers. “Keep the cap on,” Nia said. “You’re dripping on the Welsh crime section.” “I’ll move.” “Please do.” “That’s the welcome I get from a woman who had absolutely no idea who I was?” “I knew at four seconds. You took seven to admit it.” “I was making an entrance.” “It was a wet entrance.” “I don’t usually do wet.” “Clearly.” Something flickered at the corner of her mouth. She hid it by examining a receipt book. “I know who you are,” she said. “You’re on the poster outside.” “Rhys Henley.” “Rhys,” said Nia, tapping her name badge, “bookseller, owner, and source of local information. Tea?” “Tea? That’s your solution to celebrity?” “My solution to wet wool. Strong or polite?” “Strong. Milk, no sugar.” “Typical.” “I’m from Cardiff.” “That explains the vowels.” “The rest is insurance.” “The vowels are from Surrey.” “Is that criticism?” “It’s an observation.” “So is your accent.” “Can you read the weather with that?” “No. But I can tell you it’ll rain until four.” He glanced towards the window. “How do you know?” “Because I live here.” “Ah. Experience. The unimpressive kind.” “The useful kind.” Outside, the delivery van moved. The camera lens dipped with it, then reappeared beside a motorcycle. “Can I borrow your back room?” “No.” “A cupboard?” “There’s no room in Wales for cupboards. It’s all mountains and poor decisions.” “I thought you were Welsh.” “I said no.” “Which no—the cupboard, or my accent?” “To borrowing anything without buying something.” “Two pounds.” “That’s my price for a private cup of tea.” “Private how?” “You’re still wearing sunglasses.” He removed them with theatrical care. “Better?” “Absolutely not. I can see you’re famous now.” “Have you got a fan club?” “Not in this shop.” “Would you join one?” “No.” “Good. Mine has appalling seating.” He laughed. She looked at him for half a second too long. “I don’t collect celebrities,” she said. “No?” “Only paperbacks. And only when they’re good.” “That does narrow the market.” “It narrows it beautifully.” “So you’re not impressed.” “I’m neither impressed nor unimpressed. They are not the only two options available.” “Ah. The impossible middle ground.” “It’s not impossible. It’s just less exciting than you’re hoping for.” He settled into the chair nearest her desk. “You’re a difficult woman.” “Thank you.” “No, I mean genuinely difficult. Is that Welsh, or do you practise it elsewhere?” “Here. The rain improves it.” His smile faltered almost imperceptibly. She noticed. “What?” he asked. “Nothing.” “That was definitely something.” “It was you pretending to be offended so I’d reassure you.” “That’s not why I—” “I know.” The words were quiet, but they stopped him. He turned a paperback upright, then righted it again. On the table lay a collection of Dylan Thomas, open to a poem about a night in a town that no longer existed. “You know Thomas,” Rhys said. “I own him. There’s a difference.” “Of course. Ownership. Very convincing.” “Have you read him?” “Not properly. Everyone says he’s important, so I smile and wait for them to stop talking.” “So you did your homework.” “I did my listening.” Her voice softened. “The music in the Welsh is different. I never knew that until I was seventeen.” “What does it change?” “It doesn’t change the meaning. It changes the weight of it.” She became absorbed in the page. Rhys watched her rather than the book. “I don’t understand you,” he said. “Good.” “That’s usually where I begin to charm people.” “Perhaps that’s the problem.” He opened his mouth, visibly reassembled the joke, and abandoned it. Outside, a shutter clicked. The motorcycle engine idled. “I don’t usually talk to strangers about books,” Nia said. “I don’t usually flee them by sitting in wet wool beside a Welsh weatherwoman.” “Is that what I am?” “At the moment, yes. You can appeal.” “To whom?” “The management. She seems reasonable.” Nia’s mouth twitched. She bent over the receipt book again, making no progress with its neat columns. “I was beginning to think you didn’t like me,” he said. “I don’t know you.” “That’s worse.” “Is it?” “It’s much worse.” She looked up. “Then we’d better find out.” His smile arrived without permission. For once, he didn’t shape it for a camera. Nia seemed more unsettled by that than by anything he had said. “Tell me something true,” she said. “That sounds dangerous.” “Why?” “In my profession, truth is usually something to edit out.” “Not here.” He stared into his tea. “My mother stopped recognising me last year,” he said. “She held my hand and asked whether I’d really done all those films. I said yes. It was easier than explaining that the man who used to make her tea was somewhere underneath the names.” The rain filled the silence between them. “She still calls me Danny,” he said. “I can be Danny for the length of one cup of tea. No lighting technician. No opening-night speech. No deciding which version of myself deserves to come out.” His thumb worried the mug handle. Nia did not tell him how sorry she was. She did not offer a solution. Instead, she said quietly, “My father used to say the Welsh keep secrets because they run out of room to carry them.” “Your father sounds dangerous.” “He runs a bookshop.” “So does his daughter.” “He retired.” “Temporarily?” “When I stop making his tea.” He smiled. “And here I thought you made it for me.” “I made it because you’re wet. Don’t confuse basic hospitality with affection.” “Too late. I’m choosing to be flattered.” “I can see that.” Across the square, the camera turned towards the bakery. For a moment, neither of them watched it. “What do people see when they look at you?” Nia asked. “Depends who’s looking. A face they recognise. A photograph they can sell. Occasionally, a man who forgot his lines before the second act.” “So very many versions.” “Only one of them’s real.” “That sounds lonely.” His charming smile returned, but it was thinner now. “It sounds like a professional triumph.” “No. It sounds like a lie you’ve repeated until the seams show.” He laughed quietly. Nia felt it somewhere inconvenient. “Do you always interrogate customers?” “Only famous ones who interrupt my stocktake.” “I could leave.” “You could.” “Would you mind?” “Probably. But I won’t stop you.” He stood, then caught himself before reaching for his cap. “That,” Nia said, “was a surprisingly good impression.” “An impression of leaving?” “An impression of someone who doesn’t know whether he’s wanted.” Her gaze held his. He swallowed. “Do you want me to go?” she asked. “No.” “Honest answers now. I’ll remember that.” “There’s a price?” “Two pounds. One for the tea. One for the conversation.” “I can afford it.” “Can you? I’m beginning to think your ego has swallowed your wallet.” “Never. It simply has excellent priority.” She glanced at the clock. “You should go before those photographers find another angle.” “In a minute.” “We’ve been in a minute for an hour.” “Time behaves differently under duress.” “Try living in Llanrwst.” “I might. Provided the bookseller keeps making tea.” Nia wrapped the last corner of the brown paper with unnecessary precision. “That depends on whether you come back without a disguise.” “A disguise implies I’m hiding.” “You’re still wearing wet sunglasses.” “I forgot.” “Clearly.” He retrieved his cap, leaving her no sign that he might return. At the door, he paused with his hand on the bell. “Nia.” She looked up. “Your accent isn’t an insult.” Her eyes met his, briefly undefended. “No,” she said. “It isn’t.” He smiled—unguarded, private, entirely for her—and slipped back into the rain. The camera immediately began to click. Nia watched through the window as Rhys Henley raised one hand in farewell, then crossed the market square with his head down and his ridiculous cap pulled low. She waited until he disappeared before allowing herself to smile. Then she looked down at the receipt book. The page was still blank. “Right,” she murmured. “Stocktake.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This scene executes the brief with notable skill. The dialogue-forward structure is honored throughout, with the vast majority of the scene carried by exchanges between Rhys and Nia. Their voices are distinct: Rhys deploys rapid, deflecting wit and charm offensives; Nia answers in clipped, dry rebuffs that carry an undercurrent of reluctant fascination. The dynamic requested — his charm failing, which paradoxically provokes genuine attraction — is dramatized rather than stated: his smile falters, he "visibly reassembled the joke, and abandoned it," and his final smile is "unguarded, private, entirely for her." Nia's flustered interior is shown through small physical tells (looking "half a second too long," wrapping with "unnecessary precision," the blank receipt page), which is effective show-don't-tell work. The Welsh setting is present but thin — Llanrwst, Dylan Thomas, rain, "mountains and poor decisions" — adequate but not deeply textured. The Dylan Thomas beat is a nice pivot into sincerity, and Rhys's confession about his mother ("She still calls me Danny") is the emotional center, earning the scene's shift from banter to vulnerability. It's a genuinely affecting moment that deepens the "fragile ego" requirement rather than merely asserting it. Weaknesses: the banter occasionally becomes too clever and self-referential, reading as writerly sparring rather than character speech — some exchanges ("Which no—the cupboard, or my accent?") circle cleverness for its own sake. A few lines are confusing or misattributed: "Do you want me to go?" she asked — context suggests this should be Rhys's line, an attribution error that momentarily breaks the scene. "He retrieved his cap, leaving her no sign that he might return" is awkwardly constructed. The middle section occasionally meanders through one-liners without forward motion. The ending is well-earned and tonally consistent — the blank page and "Stocktake" land as a satisfying, understated close rather than forced positivity. The prose is clean, economical, and controlled; no purple passages. The emotional complexity is real, if slightly schematic in places. Overall this is a strong, professional piece with minor craft blemishes. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The stair descended through wet stone, past pipes sweating rust into pools of lamp oil. Brass fittings shone along the handrail, and iron wards had been nailed to the walls at every seventh step. The magic in them was faint but unmistakable, like a word whispered behind Aya’s teeth. Katra went first, one hand near the pistol beneath her cloak. Simeon followed, shoulders squared inside a coat too respectable for the company it usually kept. “No sentries,” Katra murmured. “No footsteps above,” Simeon said. “The street is deserted.” Then the door at their feet clicked. A key turned on the far side. Aya’s instincts reached towards the immateria, towards that cold hollow space behind the world where her mother’s gift had waited for her since childhood. Something answered there. Something noticed. The door swung inward. Two lamps illuminated a chamber ribbed with black stone arches. A woman stood beyond the threshold, a long-barrelled pistol in one hand and a sabre in the other. Both weapons appeared loaded. Two more guards waited behind her, one carrying a shotgun wrapped in oilcloth, the other a pistol with a hammer polished to a dull shine. Between the woman’s feet lay a key of black iron. “Guildmaster Vey,” Katra breathed. The woman’s mouth curved beneath a severe fringe of dark hair. “Ivetta Vey. Master of the Morska Conspiracy, keeper of its secrets, and, as of this morning, a remarkably poor prisoner.” Simeon’s gaze dropped to the pistol, then the sabre, then the neatly parted skirts. “The arrangements for your detention have changed.” “They have.” Vey stepped aside without lowering her weapon. Behind her, something enormous curved through the chamber, its pale metal catching the lamplight. “I disliked the cell. The bed was damp, the wine was vinegar, and the constable snored.” “You bribed him,” Aya said. “I disliked the wine most of all.” A distant foghorn sounded beyond the guild walls. Once. Katra drew her pistol. Vey’s guards did not rush forward. They simply set their feet and watched Katra’s hand, the barrel, the delicate matter of its hammer. The shot would have to travel through master and servant before it reached anything worth killing. “Lower that,” Vey said pleasantly, “or leave it where it is and spend the evening admiring it.” Katra’s thumb rested against the safety. “Katra,” Aya said quietly. The pistol lowered. In the silence, the second foghorn note arrived, mournful and prolonged. Simeon’s fingers tightened around his walking stick. He was considering a retreat, a wager, an argument with an armed woman. Aya knew the expression. He was calculating the precise wording of his surrender. “Simeon,” Vey said, “you may keep the stick.” “I believe, Guildmaster, that we are the party being disarmed.” “I have no interest in your walking stick. I have an interest in the door behind you.” The iron door struck the wall and closed with a boom that set the lamps shivering. A black smear appeared in the mortar around its lock. Katra spun. Her pistol came up again. This time, no one warned her. A guard caught the barrel, another struck the underside of her wrist, and the pistol dropped onto the stone. They removed her second weapon, a narrow knife sewn into her sleeve, and a weighted length of chain from beneath her collar. Simeon surrendered two knives with the dignity of a man handing over his hat. No one had struck him. That was worse. “Now the masks,” Vey ordered. Aya touched the edge of hers. Silk, leather, and a faint breath of camphor: the ingredients of a hundred respectable deceptions. Behind it she was merely a guild clerk with excellent handwriting. Unmasked, she belonged to a drawing room. She belonged to the marriage market. She belonged to the women who watched from carriage windows while cities decided the fate of people like her mother. Her pulse began to hammer. Vey seized the mask away and held it beneath the lamp. The light found Aya’s face. A small silence followed. The guard holding Katra looked away first. “The Lady Aya,” Vey said softly. “Of the—the Lady Aya. How delightful.” Aya heard the article in it. *The* Lady Aya. The daughter, the curiosity, the girl in the illustrated scandal sheets. By noon, her name would be in every countinghouse and police station in Morska. “Your mother had good bones,” Vey added. “Yours are prettier.” “Take off your gloves,” Aya replied. Her voice sounded strange without the mask, too thin, too much her father’s. “They’re conspicuously clean.” Vey laughed. The third foghorn sounded, rolling through the fog beyond the walls. Its fading note trembled in the iron pipes before dying away. “That was the harbour packet,” Vey said. “It carries the magistrate’s clerk, two witnesses, and a very inadequate quantity of ink. They were meant to find me in a cell and record an extraordinary escape. Instead, they will find this room.” She gestured at the three of them. “Your masks will be in their possession by supper. Katra’s fingerprints are already on our ledgers. Master Simeon can explain how he selected the guard rotations for this morning. And you, my lady, will tell us where your mother hid her papers.” There it was. The consequence Aya had spent half the night refusing to imagine, now entered the room wearing a policeman’s coat and carrying a pen. Katra laughed shakily. “If you wanted the papers, why advertise your disappearance?” “Because Aya is clever. Clever people become careless when they believe themselves alone.” Vey turned the black key between two fingers. “I let the guild believe I had been taken. I let them appoint a successor. I made certain *you* would come for the relic.” Behind Vey, the Scythan artifact rose from its cradle: a curved blade of bone-coloured metal, toothed along its inner edge, mounted upon a handle engraved with figures that seemed to have no hands. The shadows around it lay in the wrong direction. Aya felt the immateria stir inside her own skull. “Then you wanted the artifact,” she said. “I wanted to see who came for it.” “And us? What was the plan?” Vey smiled. “Execution, originally.” Katra’s silence became ragged. Simeon studied the floor. *No*, Aya thought. *Not like this. Katra dangling from a yardarm. Simeon found in the harbour with a sail across his mouth. The constables clapping behind their gloves.* She let none of it touch her face. “Execution is wasteful,” she said. “I am worth more breathing.” Vey’s pistol dipped by a careful inch. “Are you?” “My mother’s papers list the names behind half your magistrates. They record which nobles purchased the ward-stones, which merchants paid for the harbour patrol, and which officers of the city guard divide their wages with this guild. I know the ciphers. I know the combinations. Your locksmith can duplicate brass. He cannot duplicate the voice required to open certain doors.” “The upper vaults,” Vey said. “The upper vaults, the old reliquary, and the chamber beneath the tax office. All keyed by her notation.” “You could open them?” “My blood opens them. My memory decides which locks open.” Katra looked sharply at her. Simeon understood. He stepped forward. “If Lady Aya is to be treated as a hostage, I must also be secured. Katra is no scholar, but she knows the river entrances used by the salt ships.” “Katra knows where to hide stolen coffee,” Vey replied. “She knows which coffee ship will be missed,” Katra snapped, “and how long the harbour watch takes to discover it.” Aya’s mind raced beneath its outward calm. The ledgers, the ciphers, the blood-keyed doors: these were real things, not promises conjured from air. Yet Vey had prepared for every risk except the possibility of a valuable prisoner becoming a valuable speaker. “You have the ledgers,” Aya said. “I have most of them.” “Most is not all. My mother distrusted paper. There are names my father never learned, passages written in the margins of books I sold for you. If I disappear, they disappear with me.” “No,” Vey said, “they do not. They will be copied from your skull by men who are less delicate than I am.” The two guards shifted. One touched the sigil at his belt—brass, oil, a little tube of compressed powder. Aya glanced at it. “Do you know what that is?” Vey asked. “No.” “Good. Neither do they.” Simeon closed his eyes briefly. “You may keep us,” Aya said, “but you will not take us outside these walls before the transaction is completed. The harbour clerk sees the viscount’s daughter among criminals, and every guard learns the name before your men have left the chamber. You would have a scandal instead of a secret.” Vey considered this. “Your first sensible offer.” “My second concerns my companions. Katra and Simeon leave freely, bearing a message that I remain alive and cooperative. Otherwise, the magistrate learns that the Guildmaster arrested a frightened girl and delivered the other two to harm.” “She’s not frightened,” Katra said. “Be quiet,” Aya and Simeon said together. Vey’s eyes narrowed. “You bargain like your mother.” “I learned from a skilled teacher.” A long silence stretched between them. The artifact hissed softly, though the lamps burned steadily. Then Vey lowered her pistol and turned towards the inner chamber. “Bind them,” she said. “Give the lady a chair. Bring the ledgers.” Aya’s knees nearly buckled. She had bought them time. Only time. The bargain was not safety, and Vey had not surrendered an inch of her authority. Somewhere beyond the fog, a magistrate’s clerk was sharpening his pen. But the noose had not closed yet. “Where do you want me to begin?” Aya asked. Vey glanced back, dark eyes bright with amusement and something colder. “With the first name,” she said, “that you never wanted to speak.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response is a strong execution of the prompt. It hits every requested beat: the trio enters the underhold, encounters the un-incarcerated Guildmaster Vey with weapons and bodyguards, is captured without a fight scene, Aya is unmasked, and she negotiates her value as a hostage while grappling internally with exposure of her aristocratic identity. The Victorian/gothic texture is well maintained — brass fittings, iron wards, foghorns, oilcloth-wrapped shotguns, the harbor packet carrying a magistrate's clerk. The worldbuilding detail that men trust "brass, oil, and a little tube of compressed powder" while fearing what they cannot name is a nice touch. The dialogue is the piece's chief strength. Vey's voice is crisp, wry, and menacing ("I disliked the wine most of all"; "Execution, originally."), and Aya's bargaining has genuine tactical intelligence — she offers concrete leverage (ciphers, blood-keyed vaults, marginalia) rather than vague pleading. Katra and Simeon get distinct small moments ("She knows which coffee ship will be missed"). The negotiation feels like a real chess match rather than a plot-convenience. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally leans on fragmentary dramatic lines ("Once." / "No one had struck him. / That was worse.") that verge on mannered, and the repeated foghorn motif, while atmospheric, is used three times and slightly overworked. A few moments have unclear agency (the iron door closing on its own is presumably meant as a ward or trap, but reads as a mechanical confusion). "Fingerprints on our ledgers" is a slightly anachronistic-feeling flourish. The artifact is described evocatively but remains mostly set dressing. The internal monologue is present but somewhat sparse; the prompt asked for a heavy dialogue component, which is delivered, though Aya's inner grappling with consequences could be deeper — it surfaces mostly in brief italicized flashes. The ending is a well-judged cliffhanger that avoids false resolution: Aya buys time, not safety, and the text is honest about that. Overall this is polished, controlled genre writing with authentic voices, coherent stakes, and only minor stylistic excesses. Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The jukebox in the corner spits static between chords, then starts the same scratchy rock track again. It has looped since Spike Spiegel walked into the Anchor Bay Grill twenty minutes ago. He nurses a whiskey he cannot afford, smokes his third cigarette, and studies a photograph of a man who supposedly cannot hide. The man is Harlan Voss: former fixer, current arms dealer, and the answer to two separate contracts. One pays enough for Spike to eat. The other pays enough to disappear. His artificial eye makes the photograph shallow and unreliable. The real trouble arrives through the door. Revy shoulders her way inside like the room owes her an apology. Black crop top, denim cutoffs, a lit cigarette, and a blue dragon curling over her right arm. Two holsters sit at her hips. She orders bourbon, sees Spike’s envelope, and stops. Spike lifts his glass. “Well. This is awkward.” “It gets worse.” She drops the second contract beside the first. Different stationery. Different signatures. The same photograph. “Voss,” she says. “You?” “For the next six hours, I have to pretend I’m not faster than you.” Her mouth twists. “You’re not.” He knows the name from his past. Voss handled debts for men whose fingerprints belonged on other men’s guns. Worse, both clients answer to an intelligence broker willing to fund anyone, provided the hunter does not survive the invoice. Spike hides it. Revy drinks too quickly for someone pretending to trust him. “So,” she says, “which one of us gets him?” “First.” “Wrong. First means we both try anyway.” Their cigarettes smoke between them like a fuse. Spike draws slowly on his, hiding his smile. “We should compare notes.” “After you tell me why your clients keep changing.” “Ask nicely.” “I don’t.” The comparison lasts an hour. Voss’s last signal came from a motel called the Blue Hour, two blocks east. He trusts no one, changes rooms hourly, and keeps armed muscle nearby. Spike supplies a floor plan he claims to remember. Revy supplies the room number. Both distrust the coincidence. As the bottle empties, her gaze catches on his eye. “That’s messed up.” “Depth’s a suggestion.” “So’s trust.” “You sound like someone who’s looked for it.” Her expression hardens, but something flickers beneath it: interest, or pain. “Don’t,” she says. “Unless you’re offering.” Spike’s cigarette stalls halfway to his mouth. “Depends on the terms.” “Nothing.” He returns to Voss. She hides disappointment behind bourbon. The attraction feels safer with a contract between them, though neither admits the danger. Revy pulls her chair close, her knees brushing his. Spike lets her. “You always work alone?” she asks. “I work alone.” “Liar.” “You first.” “I lie when I talk.” “Try me.” She leans close, cigarette smoke between their mouths. “You’re scared I’ll take the money and sell you.” “I’m scared you’ll stay.” His voice gives him away. Her hand rests on his thigh. Glass breaks before either of them answers. A man jerks upright, then falls.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece opens with a strong, atmospheric bar scene and captures both characters' surface traits reasonably well: Spike's fatalism and dry wit, Revy's aggression and chain-smoking. The banter has moments of genuine snap ("Depth's a suggestion." / "So's trust."), and the noir tone is consistent with both source materials. However, the piece has significant structural failures. The prompt requires drinking, gunplay, unresolved sexual tension culminating in a motel room standoff, and roughly 1000 words. The response is well short of the length, and the story cuts off abruptly mid-scene ("Glass breaks before either of them answers. A man jerks upright, then falls.") — no motel room, no standoff, no actual gunplay, no resolution of any kind. It reads like a truncated first act rather than a complete story. The dialogue, while occasionally sharp, is frequently too cryptic and staccato to land. Exchanges like "I lie when I talk." / "Try me." feel like imitation noir patter rather than character-driven conversation. Some lines are confusing or nonsensical in context ("For the next six hours, I have to pretend I'm not faster than you" — why six hours?). The exposition about Voss and the intelligence broker is compressed to the point of incoherence; the plot mechanics are hard to follow. Character nuance is thin. Revy's vulnerability is hinted at but stated rather than dramatized ("something flickers beneath it: interest, or pain" — telling, not showing). Spike's fatalism is present but generic. The mutual attraction escalates quickly through shorthand rather than earned buildup, making the tension feel asserted rather than felt. Prose is serviceable and occasionally evocative ("Their cigarettes smoke between them like a fuse"), but the heavy reliance on short declarative sentences and fragmented dialogue becomes monotonous. The ending's abruptness means there is no payoff, no emotional or narrative resolution, and no "well-earned" anything — the piece simply stops. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Útiseta I was fifteen when my father’s job transferred us from Stockholm to a village north of Umeå. We arrived in June, my parents speaking carefully, as if the red farmhouse might object to their Stockholm accent. I missed the traffic outside my bedroom window. By the second week, I missed it less. Astrid was the only person who made the silence seem deliberate. I thought Astrid was showing off. She had found me beneath the school steps at lunch, with a broken sandwich in my lap, and asked whether I wanted to do something people only did once a year. Then she mentioned a mound in the meadow behind the old dairy. “Not a church thing,” she said. “Older.” “Your grandmother taught you this?” I asked. “Midsummer things my grandmother taught me,” Astrid said. “Not the mound, specifically. The mound is older. You never say its name when you’re standing on it, and you don’t call it a game.” I thought she was being solemn for my benefit. She called the practice *útiseta*: sitting out after midnight to receive knowledge from beyond. I pictured using it to uncover who had stolen my gym shorts. On the night of the school dance, we slipped out after the last song. Astrid carried a cloth bag: two stubby candles, saucers, a needle, a skein of gray wool thread, and a sprig of rowan. She had also brought a square of white cloth, which she said had belonged to her grandmother. “Trim the wicks,” she said. “No metal touches the mound. Set the saucers three paces apart, then draw the thread between them. Three knots, all turning the same way.” “What if we’re wrong?” “Then we admit it was wrong. We don’t guess.” She made magic sound like operating a radio. The path climbed past the dairy, where fine grass covered the old foundations. Astrid stopped at a wire fence. “Beyond here, we walk single file. Don’t step on the little stones.” “There aren’t any stones.” “That,” she said, “is what people say before they step on them.” The meadow dipped and rose. The mound was a smooth swell in the grass, broad as two parked cars, with birches along one side. It was an ancient burial place, older than the dairy, the fences, probably the village itself. At school we had been told not to disturb such ground. No one had said not to sit on it. On the crown, Astrid spread the cloth. She poured milk into each saucer and set a candle upright in it, then placed the rowan at the eastern corner. I watched as if she were defusing a bomb. “We don’t command anything,” she told me. “The women borrowed knowledge; they didn’t own it. And we don’t use this for gossip.” I stared at her. “What else would we use it for?” She adjusted the candle. “That’s the sort of question that gets us sent home.” I had decided what I wanted. Emil had stolen my radio during maths class. I wanted the ritual to make him apologize and tell me if he was writing notes to Johanna. Astrid said such wishes spoiled the gift, so I kept them behind my teeth. We sat facing west, heels touching and knees apart, the wool loop around our hands. Astrid set her watch alarm for five past midnight. Its red display vanished when she slipped it into her satchel. “Wait for the bell,” she said. “If anyone speaks, don’t answer. If anyone uses your name, don’t look back. Whatever you hear before midnight, we leave without discussing it.” I pulled my sleeves over my hands. “You sound calm.” “I’m freezing.” “That isn’t what I meant.” She smiled, but not at me. The sky was pale blue at midnight, never quite becoming night. Midges circled the candle flames. A curlew called from the ridge, and a farm dog farther off barked twice and stopped. I heard the grass hiss whenever the wind came through it. Then the wind dropped, but the grass kept moving. I was trying to work out whether we had made a mistake with the saucers when the church bell sounded. One stroke. Exactly one, though midnight was long after the last service and there was none due until morning. The note arrived through the still air, too clear for the distance. I counted as it faded: one. Not a peal. A summons. Astrid went rigid. “Don’t move,” she whispered, although neither of us had. I was waiting for the second stroke when the candle beside my knee went out. No gust. The flame shortened to a blue bead and vanished. I felt movement behind us: not footsteps, but a disturbance of air. Something brushed my neck. My skin crawled, but I was more afraid of being laughed at. I would have run if Astrid mocked me. She didn’t. She stared into the dark and began counting under her breath. Five, six, seven. “It heard the bell,” she said. “We have to wait.” “For what?” “Stop asking.” I opened my mouth. Beneath the counting I heard a dry, patient scrape, as if a finger were being drawn along thread. The mound did not move. I told myself it was a mole, a branch, water finding a tunnel, anything innocent. I thought I heard an answer taking shape, a syllable disguised as wind, but perhaps I supplied the silence myself. Then Astrid’s watch shrilled at five past. The sound broke the spell, or ended the pretence. I snatched it from the satchel and stood so quickly that the milk saucer tipped over. White ran through the grass, across the knotted thread and cloth. Neither of us noticed that the other candle had burned down to its metal pin. We did not look back. We ran. We never called it a game again. Astrid said her grandmother would have spat. I know now the danger lay not in ghosts, but in treating their silence as ours to fill.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of folk horror that hits nearly all the prompt's requirements. The setting (rural northern Sweden, mid-90s implied via watch alarms and gym shorts, though the decade is lightly sketched), the teenage dynamic between Linnea and Astrid, the ritual preparations with specific traditional elements (rowan, milk saucers, knotted wool thread, single-file walking, not naming the mound), and the mounting ambiguity are all present. The first-person past-tense recollection frame is transparent, with only light touches of present-day perspective ("I know now..."). Strengths: Astrid is well-drawn—matter-of-fact, slightly bossy, mixing teenage practicality with genuine inherited knowledge ("She made magic sound like operating a radio"). The dialogue is naturalistic and does a lot of work establishing character and rules. The ambiguity is well maintained: the single bell stroke, the candle dying, the grass moving without wind, the "dry, patient scrape"—all could be psychological. Linnea's fear of being laughed at as a competing motive is a nice touch of teenage realism. The prose is clean and controlled, with several excellent lines ("She smiled, but not at me"; "A summons"; the final line about filling silence). Weaknesses: The word count is somewhat under 1000 (roughly 850-900), a mild adherence issue. The stolen radio/gym shorts motivations feel slightly underdeveloped and a bit interchangeable. The ending's closing reflection ("the danger lay not in ghosts, but in treating their silence as ours to fill") is a touch aphoristic—slightly telling rather than showing, though it lands well enough. The mid-90s period detail is thin; the piece could be almost any decade after electrification. Some minor logic wobbles: the watch alarm "broke the spell" conveniently, and the "burned down to its metal pin" contradicts the earlier "no metal touches the mound" rule in a way that may be intentional but isn't clearly flagged. Overall, the piece is coherent, atmospheric, restrained, and avoids purple prose and overwrought sentiment. It's genuinely engaging folk horror with earned darkness. ## Therapeutic Boundaries I hated that my rehabilitation room had a body on the wall. It loomed above the head of the treatment table, a life-size anatomical diagram showing the anterior and posterior musculature. Painted muscles overlapped one another in reds and browns, surrounding exposed bones. The broad quadriceps looked powerful enough to sprint. The Achilles looked like a clean, dependable cable. Mine had become unreliable wiring. I stared at the diagram while the physiotherapist finished fastening my left knee brace. “I hate this,” I said. Mara paused. “The brace or the room?” “Recovery.” She let the strap lie loose in her hands. Beneath the wall diagram, her face was almost unnervingly familiar: the same dark eyes I had once watched down the final straight, the same mouth I had seen tightening when she pulled ahead of me. I had known her before I knew her name on the clinic door. Mara had been my training partner, my rival, the woman who made an eight o’clock session feel like the start of a race. Then she had left competitive athletics for physical therapy. She had completed her degree, specialized in sports rehabilitation, and built a successful practice while my career had collapsed into a single ruined joint. I hated her competence almost as much as her beauty. “Your surgeon called the sessions mandatory,” she said. “So today we work. No bargaining.” “I’m not trying to run again.” “That isn’t what this is for.” “Then what is it for?” She rested her fingers against my knee. “Being able to use it.” Easy for her to say. Recovery kept implying there was someone I ought to recover into. I no longer wanted the old body’s speed, its promises. I wanted the certainty that had once accompanied it. I sat back on the table. Mara stood on my injured side, where she could handle the knee without reaching across me. I leaned into the headrest and extended my left leg, thigh resting flat, heel near the end of the table. “Shorts up,” she said. “I need access to the knee.” I obeyed without looking at her. The fabric moved above my thigh. Her fingers found the quadriceps tendon immediately above my kneecap. “Now press the back of your knee gently into the table. Heels down.” I tightened the front of my thigh. The muscle responded sluggishly, a tremor running through it before the tendon firmed beneath her fingertips. “Better,” she said. “Don’t lift the heel. Just activate it.” I could feel her attention more than her touch. That was the problem. Professional contact should have felt impersonal; hers felt like being recognized somewhere the injury had not reached. I looked up. She was watching my thigh, but her gaze lingered against mine half a second too long. Then she moved my leg. One hand supported my heel; the other cradled the soft tissue of my thigh just above the knee. She lifted the leg clear, keeping the thigh pointing toward the end of the table, and guided the heel toward me. As the heel traveled back, my knee bent. My hip remained against the surface. The motion began comfortably. Then resistance gathered inside the joint—not a blockage, exactly, but a hot, insistent objection. My calf tightened. I caught my breath. Mara stopped. “Stay there,” she said. “Don’t retreat. Don’t force it either.” “I thought you were supposed to make it hurt.” “I’m supposed to keep you inside the range your surgeon approved. Tell me what you feel.” “Stretching.” “And?” “Also pain.” “Good distinction. The pain shouldn’t be sharp.” My calf spasmed once, the ankle flexing involuntarily. The movement tugged the lower leg forward a fraction. Mara followed it without wrenching the knee, then held everything still. “I have you,” she said. Her palm remained beneath my heel. Warmth passed through the skin. The contact was necessary, bounded, entirely professional. I found myself studying the curve of her wrist instead of the wall diagram. When the calf settled, she eased the leg down rather than dropping it. The knee opened gradually, the heel returning until both knee and thigh rested on the table. With the leg straight, she placed her hands around the kneecap. One supported the upper edge; the other supported the lower edge, without pressing the kneecap sideways. “This will feel like pressure,” she said. “Not force.” She glided the patella a few millimeters toward my foot, then released it. The motion was small enough to look insignificant, but I felt a deep scrape of sensitivity beneath the skin. My thigh jerked. Mara withdrew her hands immediately. “Too much?” “No.” It was. “Again.” “You don’t have to prove anything.” “I know.” That almost made me smile. Instead, I looked at the painted kneecap above us, absurdly smooth between the painted tendons. She resumed within a gentler range. The patella moved under her fingers while my leg stayed extended. I imagined her hand traveling higher, felt the thought cross my body before my mind could stop it. Her gaze lifted to mine. It dropped briefly—toward my mouth—and returned. For a moment, neither of us said anything. Then she removed her hands. “Face down,” she said. “We’ll finish with the front of the thigh.” I rolled onto my stomach and rested my forehead in the table’s face cradle. My left thigh stayed aligned with the table. Mara stood beside it, one hand at my lower thigh and the other beneath my heel. She bent my knee, bringing the sole of my foot toward the ceiling. The shin rose until it was approximately vertical; the ankle remained relaxed rather than forced. At that right angle, she began taking the knee farther into flexion, drawing the heel upward. The quadriceps tightened, then burned. The sensation ran from above the kneecap toward the front of my hip. It was different from the deep ache of knee flexion: broader, more exposed. My breath shortened. “Where is that?” she asked. “Front of the thigh.” “Is the knee stable?” “Yes.” “Good.” She increased the bend by the smallest amount. My heel rose higher; my hip stayed heavy against the table. She did not twist my pelvis or lift my thigh to manufacture extra range. The stretch belonged to the knee and the front of the thigh, not to my lower back. At the edge, my body tried to cheat. My toes curled. My stomach clenched. She stopped. “Release your toes,” she said. “You’re not running from this position.” “I don’t want to run at all.” Her hand stilled around my ankle. “I know,” she said quietly. “But you don’t have to punish the part of you that might want to.” The words landed harder than the stretch. I hated that she could still speak to me beneath the language of training. I hated that her voice made even my resentment sound childish. She lowered my leg slowly until the knee rested on the table. Her hand remained there for one unnecessary second. “We’re finished,” she said. “And no, that wasn’t an invitation.” I felt heat cross my face. “I didn’t think it was.” “You looked at me as if it might be.” “So did you.” She stepped back, restoring the distance her uniform required. Her slight smile vanished before it could become a breach. “No,” she admitted. “I did.” I had spent years resenting what I had lost. I had not expected to discover that she was also trying to hold something in place—not my knee, not my former self, but the line between clinician and former teammate, friend and woman I had once wanted even when wanting her had seemed another form of competition. The wall-mounted body watched us, flawless and symmetrical, muscles connected by every tendon and bone I could no longer take for granted. I was not grateful. Gratitude would have been too generous to recovery. But I no longer demanded that every session punish me. I lifted my leg when she indicated it was time, and followed her instructions without pretending they were fair.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a controlled, physically coherent therapy scene with genuine tension between the narrator's resentment and Mara's professionalism. The anatomical precision is a real strength: knee flexion, patellar glides, quad stretches in prone—each movement is spatially consistent and believable. The dialogue is spare and effective, particularly the closing exchange ("So did you." / "No. I did.") which lands the mutual attraction without melodrama. The wall diagram as a framing device works nicely, bookending the piece with the body he's lost. Weaknesses: the prose is occasionally flat or repetitive ("I hated... I hated..."), and the emotional register stays narrow—the narrator's resentment is stated more than deepened. The transformation at the end (no longer demanding punishment) is lightly earned but somewhat abrupt. Some lines strain ("her gaze lingered against mine") and the tension, while present, is more restrained than the prompt's request for "flaring" tension. Still, it's disciplined, coherent, and avoids purple excess.
