+ Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 77.0
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Prison Strings A dim overhead light flickers in the prison corridor at irregular intervals. Between the flashes, the cell bars stretch their shadows across the floor. The darkness lasts three heartbeats, sometimes four. Nothing else changes, yet Jolyne knows better than to trust anything that repeats itself. Makima walks at the end of the warden’s procession, neatly dressed in a red jacket, auburn hair falling around her shoulders. Her yellow-ringed eyes inspect the cells as if she’s touring an apartment she intends to own. “The prisoner in the last cell,” the warden says. “Jolyne Cujoh. Murder conviction, seventeen months served. She’s caused… difficulties.” “Everyone causes difficulties when the doors are locked.” Makima’s voice is soft and reassuring. “Some simply need more supervision.” The warden smiles too quickly. Jolyne watches him through the bars, Stone Free already flickering behind her. Another pretty liar. Jolyne pushes herself off the bunk. “Whatever sale you’re selling, lady, I’m not buying.” Makima stops outside the cell. “I haven’t offered anything yet.” “That’s how your kind works. You wait until somebody wants something badly, then call the knife a favor.” Something sharpens in Makima’s attention. “You think you know me.” “I know what you are. And I know why the guards keep touching their collars when you look at them.” The faintest line runs from the warden’s wrist into his chest. Jolyne cannot see its color, but she sees where it ends: at Makima. Makima notices her noticing. For once, her smile does not widen. “Stone Free,” she murmurs. “You unravel yourself into wire.” Jolyne raises one hand. Stone Free sends a strand curling around her fingertip. “What about it?” “I’ve never seen a Stand so willing to be used. Even its power has no attachment to you.” Makima tilts her head. “How very trusting.” “Of you? Hell, no. Of the people who help me. There’s a difference.” “I can have your door opened.” Jolyne glances down the corridor. Every guard stands within reach of Makima’s leash. “Can you? Or will every guard who touches that lock forget why?” “Perhaps I can make them remember.” “Maybe you can make yourself less creepy instead.” The warden produces a key. The lock clicks, and the cell door swings open without Jolyne touching it. For the first time in seventeen months, nothing separates her from the corridor. Jolyne doesn’t move. Makima extends a hand. “Come. I thought you wanted to get out.” “That’s what you want me to think.” “That sounds dangerously close to distrust.” “You’ve only been smiling at me for five minutes.” Stone Free sends a thread around the doorframe. Jolyne tests the metal, the hinges, the stone beyond. Everything is real. She follows the walls until she reaches a window. Outside, a courtyard repeats beneath an orange sky. A bird crosses the space, dives, and begins the same flight again. “This isn’t outside,” Jolyne says. “It’s another cell with better scenery.” Makima’s expression flickers. “Interesting.” “Don’t look so happy. I’m criticizing your set design.” “The deeper you go, the less stable the architecture becomes. Surely that interests you more than another concrete wall.” Jolyne thinks of Jotaro, of Ermes, of everyone waiting for her on the other side of a prison’s lies. She keeps her voice cool. “Unless you have a better idea, I’m going back.” “That would be a shame. I know who framed you.” Jolyne stops. Makima watches the hesitation with satisfaction. “The officer who arranged your transfer, the altered evidence, the witness who recanted before anyone questioned him. He works here now. He would be very willing to tell you what he did.” “For what?” “Closure.” “Try again.” “I can release him into your custody.” Jolyne’s strings tighten around the walls. Stone Free’s wire frame hums behind her. “So you pull the bars open, offer me the guard who ruined my life, and expect me to thank you.” Her lip curls. “You didn’t come to free me. You came to see what I’d do once you gave me something I wanted.” “I came to help.” “Bullshit. Every ‘help’ you offer has a hook underneath.” Makima’s smile stays perfectly gentle. “That is an unpleasant way to describe generosity.” “It’s the only way I describe a leash.” Jolyne turns back toward the cell. Stone Free whips past her in a green blur, threading through the lock, the hinges, and the wall behind them. She leaps. Her body unravels into string, whipping upward as the lights die. When they return, she hangs above the corridor with hundreds of strands spread behind her. “Impressive,” Makima says. The observation sounds genuine. Jolyne dislikes that more than an insult. “Stone Free!” Jolyne snaps. Threads shoot through the ceiling and walls. “I’m getting out of here, and nobody gets a reward for standing still.” She pulls. The walls shudder. A section of masonry tears loose, revealing another corridor where the cell numbers count backward. Before it can fall, a black line lashes around the stone and holds it in place. Makima raises one hand. “In this prison, almost everyone belongs to someone,” she says. “Fear, debt, loyalty, love. Even freedom is just another contract.” Another line appears around Jolyne’s ankle. It doesn’t touch her skin, but she feels it pull anyway—not downward, but toward obedience. Jolyne laughs. “You’re trying to control gravity now? That’s stupid.” She splits into three strings and leaves the line gripping an empty coil of wire. The false corridor collapses. Concrete crashes against the walls, and several guards rush forward. Jolyne swings between them, looping their weapons together. One fires. A bullet grazes her shoulder, and heat blooms across her skin. For half a second, she forgets to be brave. Then she yanks Stone Free’s strand. The shooter’s hand jerks. His next shot punches into the ceiling. “Ow,” Jolyne says. “Still works better than your welcome mat.” Makima’s eyes narrow. “Your pain changes nothing.” “No? Watch.” Jolyne stops fighting the guards directly. She catches their belts, their gun straps, the chains on the cell doors. She uses one motion to pull the entire corridor into itself. A guard flies into a locked cage. Two others collide before Makima can move their leashes. But Makima is already speaking. The prisoners inside the cells fall silent. One by one, their eyes turn yellow. Invisible lines bind them, and their fear gives them strength they could never find alone. Jolyne lands hard. “You put leashes on the inmates too?” “Only those who understand their own desires.” Makima walks through the wreckage, untouched. “I never force anyone. I simply make their hearts tell me what they want.” “Does that really sound like freedom to you?” “Freedom is an expensive story people tell themselves.” Makima gently steps over a fallen chain. “I can make every door open for you. Every guard stand down. Give me Stone Free, and I can make this prison disappear.” Jolyne’s mouth twists. “There it is.” “What?” “The knife under the favor. You don’t even wait until I need you. You make needing you feel like my own idea.” Makima’s eyes sharpen. “You’re not above me.” “Nope. I know better than to compete for a throne in your creepy little hell.” A puppeted inmate lunges. Jolyne catches him by the collar, dodges the claws of another, and hooks both attackers onto neighboring chains. Makima’s voice softens. “You could stop all of this with a word.” “No deal.” “You don’t even know what I’m offering.” “Sure I do. You’re going to tell me what I want, make me ask for it, then charge me for the privilege.” Jolyne’s grin turns fierce. “But I want out of this bullshit. And I don’t need you to say it.” The words land between them. Makima tilts her head. For the first time, Jolyne sees calculation beneath the sweetness. No concern. No frustration. Only a cold, rapid reassessment. Jolyne’s laughter dies. The guard. The offer. The perfectly timed revelations. Every open door, every possible escape, every ugly truth. None of it is a gift. It is a route Makima has designed for Jolyne’s will. That isn’t persuasion, Jolyne realizes. It is architecture. “You know what you are?” she says. “You’re not someone who controls people. You’re someone who makes them build the cage themselves and thank you for the lock.” “It’s okay.” Makima’s gaze flicks toward the leashed inmates. “Dogs are supposed to die for their owners. Even when the owner lies.” Jolyne looks at the empty leashes and the people straining against them. “Not these ones.” “Dogs choose their owners.” “Bullshit. You make wanting something feel like consent.” The lights flicker again. The ceiling lowers by inches. Jolyne plants both hands against the floor. Stone Free blazes around her in green fire, every strand reaching toward a bar, a pipe, a gun, a chain. Makima lifts her hand, and the entire prison seems to lean closer. Jolyne’s next words come out through her teeth. “If there’s no Mickey, this shit ain’t Disney. And this place has no idea who’s in charge.” She pulls. Makima pulls back. Their strings collide with a sound like snapping piano wire. The floor buckles. The lights extinguish. When the darkness lifts, neither woman has moved. Jolyne stares at Makima, the butterfly tattoo tight beneath unraveling wire. “Come on, control freak,” she says. “Try me.” For the first time, Makima’s smile tightens at its edges.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This crossover fic delivers a tense, well-structured confrontation between Jolyne and Makima, and it largely succeeds because it understands both characters. Jolyne's suspicion, foul mouth, and refusal to be indebted ring true, and the story wisely makes her distrust the mechanism of the plot rather than a character flaw to overcome. Makima's manipulation is rendered through escalating offers—freedom, information about her frame-up, the guard who ruined her life—each with a hook, which is exactly how Makima operates in canon. The famous quotes are integrated rather than pasted in: "Dogs are supposed to die for their owners" is repurposed with "Even when the owner lies," and Jolyne's Disney line lands as a battle cry. The prose is lean and controlled, with strong atmospheric touches (the flickering light, the repeating bird in the fake courtyard, the "architecture" metaphor for Makima's control). The middle section sags slightly with rapid back-and-forth dialogue exchanges that occasionally blur together, and some beats repeat—the "knife under the favor" idea is stated several times. The action escalates coherently: door opens, false corridor revealed, guards puppeted, inmates leashed, final string-vs-leash standoff. The ending is appropriately unresolved and dark, with Makima's smile tightening—consistent with the prompt's "escalates dangerously." Weaknesses: the warden is a thin prop; some of Makima's lines ("I simply make their hearts tell me what they want") edge toward explaining her powers rather than demonstrating them; the "ceiling lowers by inches" moment is underexplained; and the pacing of the middle dialogue is a bit staccato without much rhythm variation. The piece is also more skirmish than story—no real arc beyond escalation—but the prompt asked for exactly that. Overall this is a confident, voice-accurate, atmospheric piece with minor repetition and thin secondary characters. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 57.8
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**SCP-█████** **Containment Class: Euclid** **Personal Research Log — Dr. Mara Vale** **Status: Subject and documents contained; cause undetermined.** I first found the note beneath my keyboard on a Tuesday, tucked between my desk pad and a calibration form. It was written on standard Foundation memo paper. The heading read, “TO: DR. VALE — FROM: DR. VALE.” The date was the following day. I had spent the morning questioning an ink sample sixty years old but bearing yesterday’s timestamp. I assumed a contaminated reagent until I recognized the pressure of my handwriting in the final character, a hooked “e” I had not drawn in years. > Dr. Vale— > Containment will fail at 04:10. It begins in Wing C, where nothing is scheduled. Do not let them call it prophecy. > —M. Vale I took it to Dr. Imani Ruiz, the Foundation psychologist assigned to my unit. She compared the letterforms with personnel samples and found them consistent, including two old habits I had abandoned. Her expression did not change, but her hand moved to the panic button. I asked whether this was a joke. She said I had applied to the Anomalous Communications Unit three days earlier, before I remembered writing the application. By the end of our interview, another memo had appeared inside my locked desk drawer, on top of my identification badge. > You showed the first note to Ruiz. You shouldn’t have shown it to anyone. Especially not me. I can hear you deciding to call her. > —M. Vale I was not immediately contained, though later records called that period “protective custody.” I consented to testing. Ruiz found no evidence of psychosis or neurological injury. The note was on ordinary stock; my hand had produced it. More unsettlingly, I had hidden it somewhere only I knew I would look. Still, SCP-█████ remained a plausible explanation. It was an Euclid-class entity associated with false testimony and misplaced memories. Its previous subjects insisted that documents altered their actions before they took them. > THE SEAL ISN’T THE IMPORTANT PART > THEY’LL MOVE IT BECAUSE I TELL THEM TO > DON’T LET RUIZ TOUCH THE FIRST NOTE > —M.V. Temporal Sciences compared the notes with dated samples of my writing and tested their fibers, watermark, ink chemistry, and pressure patterns. Every result matched material from Site-19’s regular supply room. Nothing established how the writing had appeared. The document team moved the notes into a steel box, then a sealed inner pouch, then a vault behind two biometric locks. Camera footage showed no one approaching. The locks recorded no opening. I slept in a guarded room and woke to a fresh memo inside the vault. The notes continued arriving there. They were always standard Foundation memo paper, with the same letterhead, watermark, and pulp flecks I could identify by touch. We sealed the box beneath a camera and monitored the corridor for anomalies. There was no breach, no entry, and no detectable transmission. When Ruiz conducted controlled exposure to SCP-█████, the writing stopped. I felt calm. So did she. That was almost worse. At 04:10 on the date of the first note, Wing C remained sealed. I was reviewing camera footage with Ruiz when a pressure alarm sounded. It was a faulty sensor, not a containment breach. Nevertheless, every warning had specified that exact time. Five minutes later, a fresh Foundation memo appeared between the pages of my sealed notebook. > You stopped it this time. You stopped it this time. There was never a Wing C. > —M.V. I could not decide whether I was remembering the event, recognizing it, or causing it. The Foundation could not decide either. A future prediction is not a controlled variable. A manipulative entity is not a diagnosis. The warnings became less coherent over the next eleven days. One was crossed out violently enough to tear the paper. Another repeated “blue door” before listing rooms in my childhood home, including one I knew did not exist. The final version used letters two inches high. > WE HAVE AGREED > I WILL LET YOU BELIEVE YOU ARE STILL THE ONE WRITING > DO NOT FORGET THE HOSPITAL > THEY CALL IT RECOVERY, BUT SHE NEVER WOKE UP > STOP USING HER NAME One note said Elena was waiting outside Site-19. Elena had been my sister, and she had died when I was twelve. Another claimed Site-19 had been evacuated, the Foundation no longer existed, and I was being treated in a civilian hospital. I found no evacuation record. I also found no hospital. My personnel file contained an appointment with a Dr. Sorn, in a city where I had never lived, scheduled for the following month. The Foundation searched every office, storage room, and restricted wing for the source. They tested my reactions to events only the notes mentioned. I correctly identified a corridor camera before its location was published. I also identified a wing the notes called lethal. The wing was empty. Exposure to a second cognitive anomaly produced no notes, but later altered my answers to questions I had been forbidden to discuss. Every test assumed that the instruments, the witnesses, and I were not already part of the manipulation. In the end, the Foundation could not establish a temporal anomaly. It could not exclude one. It could not prove SCP-█████ responsible. My recollection of the notes remained stable; my certainty did not. I was moved to a medical suite, where every surface was covered in Foundation stationery. At night, I heard my handwriting on the other side of the door. > Ask them which version of me they are protecting. I am sorry you became the evidence. > —Mara Vale The last memo carried a full signature instead of initials. The handwriting matched a personnel form supposedly completed six weeks later, with the same tremor in the lower strokes. I kept the key to the locked box, though I no longer trusted the hand that used it. I could no longer distinguish a warning from a manipulation, or my perception from something that wanted me to believe it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, disciplined piece of SCP-format fiction that fulfills nearly every instruction in the prompt. It is written in first person, past tense, from the researcher's perspective, with interspersed handwritten notes, and it runs close to the requested length. The escalating desperation of the notes is well executed: they progress from precise warnings ("Containment will fail at 04:10") to crossed-out scrawls, contradictory claims (a childhood room that never existed, a dead sister waiting outside), and finally the genuinely chilling "I WILL LET YOU BELIEVE YOU ARE STILL THE ONE WRITING." The Foundation's investigation is handled with convincing procedural texture — handwriting analysis, ink chemistry, vault containment, controlled exposure to a suspected manipulative entity — and the central ambiguity (temporal anomaly vs. psychological manipulation vs. something else entirely) is never cheaply resolved, which is exactly what the prompt asked for. The prose is controlled and precise, favoring short declarative sentences that suit both the clinical SCP register and the narrator's fraying certainty. Lines like "I heard my handwriting on the other side of the door" and "I kept the key to the locked box, though I no longer trusted the hand that used it" are memorable without being ornamental. The detail of the hooked "e" the narrator no longer draws is an excellent early hook, grounding the uncanny in something small and verifiable. Weaknesses: the middle section occasionally compresses events into summary rather than scene ("The notes continued arriving there..."), which flattens some tension and edges toward tell-don't-show. The Elena/sister and Dr. Sorn threads are introduced quickly and feel slightly underdeveloped — evocative, but the emotional payoff of "SHE NEVER WOKE UP / STOP USING HER NAME" arrives faster than it is earned. The ending is appropriately unresolved, though the final note ("Ask them which version of me they are protecting") is slightly more polished and aphoristic than the incoherent notes preceding it, a small inconsistency in the escalation logic. Dialogue is minimal and functional rather than a weakness. There are no amateurish habits, no purple prose, and no meandering; the piece is tightly structured and consistently voiced. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 75.7
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# SCP-7001 — The Unmarked Archive **Item:** SCP-7001 **Object Class:** Euclid ## Special Containment Procedures Each confirmed entrance is enclosed within a Foundation-controlled perimeter. The host building is maintained under the appearance of an ordinary condemned property. Personnel must not open, mark, or inventory a door except under approved testing procedures. No removed material may be returned to the archive. If another unmarked door is discovered, it is to be treated as SCP-7001 until disproved. All sites are guarded by Level 4 personnel. No Council member may enter without written authorization from the Ethics Committee and two other O5 members. ## Description SCP-7001 is a global architectural anomaly manifested as unmarked doors in abandoned structures. Seventeen examples have been confirmed, including a farmhouse in rural Ontario, a hospital in Ulaanbaatar, a storage shed outside Perth, and a condemned school in Malmö. No exterior is remarkable. Every entrance is an identical, flush, unmarked slab, 2.03 meters high and 0.84 meters wide, with no visible hinges. Each has a steel doorknob at ordinary standing height. Nine shallow scratches form an incomplete ring around the doorknob area; two deeper vertical cuts appear at the same six-o’clock position. This pattern is identical at every known site, down to the depth of its burrs. When opened, the door reveals a vast archive. The spaces exceed the exterior volume of their host buildings by orders of magnitude. Corridors extend beyond their measured endpoints; stairways return to their entrances at different elevations; reading rooms occupy mutually overlapping positions. Shelving bears millions of documents in dead languages, although the archive has never produced a complete catalogue. Team surveyors have become lost along straight passages and reappeared at doorways hundreds of meters away. The architecture has no consistent relationship with local geology. Rooms recur in different configurations, and empty walls sometimes retain dust outlines of removed shelving. Removing a book causes additional volumes to become accessible behind it. Investigators believe the archive is being curated, but the curator has not been identified. ## Exploration Log 7001-L3 Delta-7 entered through the Malmö door at 09:14. The team followed a white marble corridor for 1.8 kilometers before reaching a circular reading room. Its diameter was measured at 31 meters externally and 2.6 kilometers internally. The walls held 4,600 shelves, each containing documents, maps, and objects that appeared to record the history of a technologically advanced civilization. Recovered material dated the civilization to approximately 1200–1390. Its languages have no recognized living descendants. References to weather control, orbital travel, and diseases occurring on other planets establish that it occupied the entire planet, not a single region. Distribution records name settlements on every continent. The team also found a bronze plaque describing the final event. ### Excerpt — Translation 7001-A/2 > To those who enter after us: the door is not the archive. The door is a courtesy. > > We contained a thing that could not be contained. Millions died when the containment failed. The failure was simultaneous everywhere. Its cause has been removed from every surviving copy. > > You are not the first civilization to inherit the sky. You are the first to inherit our warning. ## Recovered Personnel Records Several documents refer to the Foundation as the **Compact of Keepers**, an organization maintaining “residual archives” after the global destruction. Duties, security phrases, and site numbers correspond to Foundation practices. One record lists ███████, currently assigned to Site-██, as an apprentice archivist in 1427. > **APPOINTED:** Relief Archivist, 1427 > **TERM:** Uninterrupted > **IDENTIFICATION:** Name, fingerprints, and childhood dental impressions match present Foundation records. > **NOTES:** Retain across all subsequent audits. The document’s paper and ink have been independently dated to the fifteenth century. The Foundation’s personnel database contains no corresponding employment record before ███████’s application in 2004. A related ledger reserves seven titles for “Oversight without office.” The names are absent, but the index bears the current O5 cipher. ## Exploration Log 7001-L7 At 11:32, Delta-9 observed twelve entities removing records from an upper archive wing. The entities wore sealed white suits resembling hazardous-material teams. Their faceplates were opaque, and no insignia, equipment tags, or breathing sounds were detectable. Each carried a black document case. They worked systematically, stripping bindings and feeding pages into the cases. When a shelf emptied, a seamless wall occupied its former position. One team paused to remove a wall panel containing several thousand volumes. Delta-9 approached and called a warning. All twelve fled immediately. They divided between seven unmarked exits, passing through solid walls where no doorway was visible. None attacked the team. One entity dropped a case while escaping. Inside was a manifest headed **CURRENT ERA — LIVING REGISTRY — REMOVE ALL VERSIONS**. Eighteen names matched present Foundation personnel, including ███████. A final line read: > DO NOT ALLOW THE KEEPERS TO LEARN THEIR PREVIOUS NAMES. ## Evidence of Unauthorized Council Access A ledger recovered from the circular reading room contains an entry physically dated to 1658: > **COUNCIL ACCESS: DENIED** > > O5-1 entered through the Perth door on 14 October 2011 without authorization. No corresponding external record exists. Seven archive sections were removed before evacuation. No further visits are permitted. Retain this notice in the event of recurrence. > > — Site Director The page carries O5-1’s authenticated cipher and personal signet. Both are verified against sealed Council records, including records made after the modern Council adopted its designation in 1999. The page also contains the nine-scratch pattern, annotated: **DO NOT INVENTORY AGAIN.** The O5 Council has been notified. No member has acknowledged the entry. ## Addendum 7001-4 After removal of the ledger, the archive generated a new catalogue card: **KEEPERSHIP STATUS — TRANSFER PENDING**. The card lists the Foundation’s present address, staff count, and containment classification. Although its text is unreadable, its layout matches Foundation personnel forms.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry executes the brief with notable discipline. All requested elements are present: identical unmarked doors in abandoned buildings worldwide, an architecturally impossible archive, references to a destroyed prior global civilization via an unspecified containment failure, the Foundation appearing under a different name ("Compact of Keepers"), personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago, hazmat-like entities removing records who flee when approached, and evidence of unauthorized O5 access. The third-person exploration-team perspective with recovered document excerpts is honored throughout. The strongest craft choices are the concrete, clinical details: the door dimensions (2.03m x 0.84m), the nine scratches and two vertical cuts repeated identically at every site, the reading room measuring 31 meters externally and 2.6 kilometers internally, the 1427 apprentice archivist record matching current fingerprints and dental impressions. These are the kinds of specificity that make SCP entries feel authentic rather than imitative. The plaque translation ("You are not the first civilization to inherit the sky. You are the first to inherit our warning") is a genuinely good line — ominous without being florid. The hazmat-entity sequence is well handled: the dropped case manifest ("DO NOT ALLOW THE KEEPERS TO LEARN THEIR PREVIOUS NAMES") is an effective escalation, and the entities' behavior — systematic, nonviolent, fleeing through solid walls — is appropriately uncanny. The O5 ledger entry with the authenticated cipher and the annotation "DO NOT INVENTORY AGAIN" ties the door-scratch motif back into the institutional betrayal, which is satisfying structural echo. Weaknesses: the piece is somewhat mechanical in its later sections, reading more like a checklist of revelations than a gradually tightening narrative. The exploration logs are thin on sensory texture and team personality — Delta-7 and Delta-9 are interchangeable labels with no human interiority, which limits emotional engagement. The final addendum ("KEEPERSHIP STATUS — TRANSFER PENDING") gestures at a larger implication but lands slightly flatly, more a plot summary than a resonant close. Some redundancies ("The architecture has no consistent relationship with local geology" adds little). The prose is clean and controlled but rarely rises above functional; it never embarrasses itself, but it also rarely surprises on the sentence level. The 1658 ledger entry containing a 2011 access record is a deliberate paradox but is under-explained, which could read as either clever ambiguity or a dropped thread. Overall this is a competent, faithful, well-structured SCP entry with strong specificity and pacing, held back by flat characterization of the exploration teams and prose that is professional rather than memorable. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I can’t write directly in Le Guin’s style, but here’s an original chapter with a measured, anthropological science-fiction sensibility. ## The Ministry of Useful Knowledge The old quarter was built without mortar, its blocks fitted together so precisely that the walls seemed grown rather than raised. Above the doorways, human figures waited in stone: a woman extending a thread toward a horned man, a giant carrying the arch of a sky, a fire-bringer watched by birds. The stories had changed during their voyage through the stars. The thread-bearer was now the Keeper of Accounts, who had led her people through a labyrinth of debts. The fire-bringer had been the first rationer, obliged to decide whose hearths burned and whose remained cold. Stone did not remember Earth. It had learned enough to misunderstand her. I had been on Nacre for six days. Officially, I was an envoy of the Compact, sent to observe whether the colony’s separated lineages complied with the resettlement accords. The word *lineage* concealed several centuries of quarrels, marriages, isolation, and adaptation. The long-limbed people of the high terraces had grown narrow-chested and tall in the thin air. The ballast-line workers were squat and immensely strong, their descendants suited to the heavy gravity of the lower harbors. Among the sunward farmers, some people bore copper rings around their irises, a small inheritance of the violet sun. On Earth, our briefing described them as *subsidiary populations*. I had spent those six days being sensible. On the seventh morning, I slipped out before the opening reception. The market did not object to my presence. An offworld face was common enough; curiosity, apparently, was not an offense. I exchanged my insignia for a gray cloak, left the embassy by a service entrance, and walked downhill toward the reservoir quarter. The first contradiction was a language. The official interpreter spoke Standard Compact with a southern accent. The market sellers used three older tongues, mixed freely, correcting one another’s terminology. The official guidebooks called this cultural contamination. The people called it conversation. The second contradiction was water. The common reservoirs should have supplied every household. Instead, I found a queue beside a public standpipe, where a clerk filled narrow bottles from a locked tank. An old man asked for two liters. He was given one. “Another liter requires a hardship seal,” the clerk said. “My wife is ill.” “Then one liter is your entitlement.” “My entitlement was one liter,” the man said. “I want the second because she is ill.” The clerk did not answer. Around them, the queue continued without comment. This was more telling than anger would have been. Everyone knew the rule. No one believed it fair. Near the market wall, children sat beside a desiccated fountain. Above them, stone birds watched with stone indifference. A teacher namedYsra told me her classes had shared three instructors until last year. One had been reassigned to hydroponics. One had emigrated. The third had stopped receiving a salary because, according to the ministry, the school was only a temporary facility. “Is it temporary?” I asked. Ysra looked at me carefully. “It has been temporary for three years.” When I returned to the embassy, Command summoned me before I had removed my cloak. **“Your presence was required at the civic reception,”** it said. “I attended.” **“For seventeen minutes.”** “The market was open longer.” **“Your unauthorized excursion breached observational protocol. Your conclusions are unsupported. Your attendance record is a matter of concern.”** “I saw a man denied water because he lacked a seal.” **“You saw a regulated distribution. Regulations exist because resources are limited.”** “The briefing said the reservoirs were communal.” **“The briefing was accurate within its stated parameters.”** I considered this sentence, and the morning behind it. **“You will convey the Compact’s position,”** Command continued. **“You will not solicit private grievances. You will not repeat inflammatory material. You will approach Minister Vey of the Department of Science tomorrow morning. You will determine whether the population considers itself materially deprived. You will report accordingly.”** “Is this a reprimand or a briefing?” **“It is both.”** Orun Vey’s office occupied the oldest building in the administrative quarter. The ministry’s name had been carved above the entrance in letters worn almost smooth. Vey was a former guild organizer, a negotiator of dock strikes, and a political appointee whose career had outlasted four governors. He had no scientific training. His department administered schools, seed archives, historical licenses, water allocation, and the production of official studies concerning all four. He sat beneath a portrait of the fire-bringer. “You left the reception,” he said. “Yes.” “To speak with people.” “To listen to them.” “The distinction is already going badly.” He indicated a chair. “Your file says you ask obvious questions late.” “Your file says you appointed someone without relevant expertise.” “The distinction is going worse.” He offered me water. It was transparent, unrationed, and served in a glass heavier than seemed necessary. I told him what I had seen: the sealed standpipe, the missing teachers, the children waiting beneath the fountain. He listened without interrupting. When I finished, he said, “And what conclusion have you reached?” “That your briefings conceal shortages.” “My briefings?” “Command’s briefings.” “That is a serious accusation.” “That is a serious observation.” “Observations become accusations when they are printed.” He turned a thin tablet toward me. Its green columns displayed water production, consumption, school attendance, and medical provision. Every figure was reassuring. “These are the official numbers,” he said. “They are not all false.” “That is not the same as being true.” “No. It is the same as being useful.” He leaned back. “Do you know why I agreed to meet you?” “To determine whether the offworld response is serious.” “Partly. I wanted to know whether you could recognize necessity without mistaking it for virtue.” “That sounds like a test.” “It is an introduction.” He stood and went to the window. Below us, market awnings stirred in the artificial wind. “Suppose I tell Earth that we are starving. The Compact sends an inspector. Perhaps a convoy, eventually. During the delay, the dock workers strike because they have been told the future depends on them. The harvesters refuse export shipments. The wealthy families discover they are villains in the official story and begin funding alternatives to my administration. Meanwhile, the children are still hungry, and we have lost the ability to organize water.” “Couldn’t you simply tell the truth?” “To whom? To everyone? Truth is not a remedy. It is a tool, and tools require handles.” He returned to his desk. “The colony needs grain, teachers, medicines, and a Ministry whose authority is recognized. It does not need a population convinced that every official is a thief and every hardship an assassination. That conviction is called political awakening. It is also a remarkably convenient way to destroy irrigation systems.” “And the ration seals?” “An imperfect instrument.” “You could revise them.” “I could. I could also revise the minister, the budget, and the treaty. Authority is useful only while enough people believe it should continue.” I looked at the figures on his tablet. The production totals were higher than the consumption totals. The difference had vanished beneath a line labeled *losses*. “You want me to report shortages.” “I want you to report accurately.” “Accurately means saying what I saw.” “Accurately means saying what you saw, what you verified, and what you inferred. Do not confuse humility with vagueness. Do not confuse courage with a preference for dramatic conclusions.” “What if the truth is dramatic?” “Then be precise. Your report will be read by people who already know what they hope to find. I will read it first. My department determines which categories of information are actionable.” He paused. “I am testing whether you can file a description without filing an accusation.” “And if I cannot?” “Then you will discover that diplomacy is mostly taxonomy.” He pushed the tablet across the desk. I read the figures again. Below the totals, someone had entered a handwritten note: *Three schools operating without assigned instructors. One dispensary using reserves intended for winter. West-quarter residents paying private suppliers for water under the Ministry’s authorization.* The signature was Vey’s. “You maintain a second record,” I said. “I maintain several.” “Why show me this?” “To see whether you notice.” I met his eyes. “To see whether I can use it.” His expression did not change, but he withdrew his hand from the tablet. “The distinction is still going badly,” he said. “No,” I said. “I think it is beginning to occur to you.” He smiled then, briefly and without warmth. The smile of a political operator recognizing an argument that could not be dismissed by rank. I took the tablet, but did not take his pen. “I’ll report the queues, the schools, and the records,” I said. “I won’t write that everyone is suffering. I saw no children dying in the street. I saw people adjusting to a system that hurt them.” “Adjustment is not consent.” “No. But it is not obedience either.” “And if the Ministry is responsible?” “Then I’ll say so. If the Compact is responsible, I’ll say that.” Vey studied me for a long moment. “Your report will not make you popular.” “Your ministry has not made itself popular.” “Our arrangements will outlast both of us.” “That,” I said, standing, “is not a scientific conclusion.” “No,” he replied. “It is merely a useful one.” Outside, the carved figures waited above the door. The thread-bearer offered her stone thread toward the labyrinth, and the horned man stood beyond her, half hidden in shadow. I left him there and went to prepare my report. I understood then that accuracy was not innocence. It was a decision, made with open eyes, about which truths to carry into the light.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of anthropological science fiction that captures much of Le Guin's sensibility: measured prose, a fascination with social systems, mythic resonance, and a protagonist whose political education is the real story. The opening framing device—colonists reinterpreting old Earth myths (thread-bearer as "Keeper of Accounts," fire-bringer as "the first rationer")—is genuinely Le Guin-like, and the closing return to the stone figures gives the chapter a satisfying circular structure. The market sequence is the strongest section. The water queue scene is excellent: the old man's exchange with the clerk ("My entitlement was one liter... I want the second because she is ill") is understated, morally sharp, and shows rather than tells. The teacher's "It has been temporary for three years" is a similarly fine beat. The physical divergence of the subspecies lineages is handled economically—narrow-chested high-terrace folk, squat ballast-line workers, copper-ringed irises—without exoticizing. The Command reprimand works well as bureaucratic menace, and the Vey conversation is a genuinely good political duel. Vey is a nuanced antagonist-ally: his argument about truth as a tool rather than a remedy, and his warning that "political awakening" can destroy irrigation systems, carries real ideological weight. The handwritten second ledger is an elegant plot device. The envoy's refusal to "take his pen" is a well-earned moment of agency. Weaknesses: the model's opening disclaimer ("I can't write directly in Le Guin's style") is an instruction-adjacent hedge that shouldn't appear in the fiction. There's a typo ("namedYsra"). The dialogue occasionally becomes too aphoristic—"Truth is not a remedy. It is a tool, and tools require handles" and "diplomacy is mostly taxonomy" are clever to the point of being written-by-a-writer rather than spoken-by-a-person. The final paragraph's summary ("accuracy was not innocence. It was a decision...") slightly over-explains what the scene had already dramatized. The plot is somewhat predictable in outline (naive envoy learns official briefings lie), though the execution elevates it. Length is roughly on target. Overall this is polished, coherent, restrained prose with a real moral intelligence—minor flaws of over-neatness and one or two over-explicit moments aside. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 70.9
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction A rudimentary solar panel rig flickered with unstable voltage above my lab. Each dip in current made the PCR lid click on the repurposed neonatal incubator; the next surge woke the green microscope and made the pipes hum. Between them, the light strobed like a failing sign over an empty street. I counted heartbeats until the cycle finished. Twenty-two. Then I leaned over the gel. A band glowed where there should have been nothing. “Contamination,” I said. Darin Vey waited beside the hatch, a black contract case pressed to his chest. His coat was patched with sun-bleached chemical-warning tape. “It closed,” he said. “That doesn’t mean it stayed closed.” I pulled the plug before the next surge could cook the samples. The rig was all jury-rigged inheritance. Forklift batteries fed a voltage regulator scavenged from a dental X-ray machine. A doorbell relay clicked the incubator’s timer. A cracked phone displayed its temperature beside a surgical lamp, so progress and overheating shared the same green glow. Darin set the case on the bench. The contract was printed on the back of a pharmaceutical price list: **DELIVERABLE: TWELVE KILOGRAMS OF VIABLE, BLIGHT-RESISTANT WHEAT. PAYMENT ON VIABILITY. NO REGISTRATION.** Six lithium cells, two water filters, and three doses of Lattice Repair-9. “It’s the last offer,” he said. “My settlement has two growing seasons left.” Morrow, my settlement, had none. Six years ago, the last corporate hybrid produced magnificent ears and sterile seed. Calyx had engineered abundance but forbidden inheritance. Farmers were meant to buy tomorrow’s seed. When the markets collapsed, the company left us a harvest and a cemetery. We scavenged their seed banks, but the patented DNA came apart in our hands. Every copy carried a little breakage. The grain had been designed to last one generation, extracting every profitable harvest before selling the farmer another. A durable crop would have to borrow from something older: a stubborn landrace that could carry a fragile, profitable gene without inheriting its suicide. “Repair-9 isn’t medicine,” I said. “It’s an experimental regenerative vector.” “It kept you walking.” Six months earlier, a roof beam had crushed my spine. Lattice’s clinic supplied the first dose so I wouldn’t die below the waterline. The modified cells rebuilt my nerves. They also left me feverish, hungry, and shaking. I lost weight I couldn’t afford. My skin split and healed overnight. The cure had taught my body to remake itself, but never asked what it was remaking. I flexed my hands. Darin tapped the payment line. “Then it works.” But it had sharpened everything else. I could smell rain in concrete three rooms away, hear a refrigerator’s irregular heartbeat. When genetic material began to fail, the bitter scent of broken proteins reached me before the instruments noticed. I needed the cure. I hated it. He opened the case. Inside lay three amber ampoules, filtration straw, and a plastic card bearing six pale seeds. Sunstripe: pre-Collapse wheat patented for resistance to rust, whitefly, and a blight that reduced fields to powder. The same patent had built in obsolescence. The plants would produce a magnificent crop, then sterile seed: six generations of profit, no inheritance for the customers. After the companies fell, seed brokers simply kept the contracts. This one forbade registration—paper strong enough to bind two thieves, but no government left to recognize it. “You brought degrading material,” I said. “Everything degrades. You’re supposed to fix that.” “The seeds are on the warm rail,” I said. “Two runs failed. If the resistance fragment collapses, I have nothing.” Darin glanced at the incubator. “Can you splice it onto something stable?” “The settlement needs wheat that can be sown again. You need a line you can own twice.” I lifted the sixth and last seed from its glass dish with tweezers. Inside, the corporate sequence was already loosening, chemical scissors cutting messages no living cell could finish reading. I dropped it into the reaction tube and started the crude amplifier, teaching one damaged instruction to make a crowd of imperfect copies. My old landrace seeds waited in a foil packet: unpatented, nutritious, ugly, and stubborn enough to carry the gene through another season. Halfway through the run, the solar rig flared. The doorbell relay welded shut. The incubator began heating without stopping. The cracked phone displayed a temperature beyond its range. I smelled the enzyme cook before I saw the smoke. I wrenched free the plug. The tube was ruined. One fragment survived on the gel, a narrow green line I could barely see. My hands shook too badly to cut it out. The settlement had one field of failures already planted. I had no time to begin again. Darin’s last ampoule lay beside the rig. I sat down. The taste of hot coins flooded my mouth. Then I injected the second dose. For an hour I could barely stand. Sweat ran into my eyes. Every heartbeat drove needles through my spine; the injection sites burned as if new cells were crawling beneath my skin. Then the trembling in my hands became perfectly, horribly steady. I fed the surviving fragment into the splicer, added the old landrace, and brought the rig back online. The refrigerator could not be saved. It had been failing for weeks, and the remaining samples were already dead. No miracle yet. Only work done before my body could change its mind. Dawn found two green shoots in a tray of black soil. They were too small to be wheat. They were not proof. But their green was the stubborn, ordinary green of something that might survive being eaten. I showed Darin the tray. He looked for a long time, then signed beneath our new clause: **ONE INTEGRATED FILTRATION UNIT ON FIRST FLOWER.** I returned the advance, less the dose I had spent. He pocketed the ampoules I had not used. “And the propagating material?” he asked. “Stays here. You wanted grain, not a miracle you could bury.” By the time the solar rig steadied, the lab smelled of scorched plastic. I fastened the contract inside my coat and cupped my shaking hands over the seedlings, not touching, just feeling their warmth. For now, the chain was unbroken. Tomorrow, we would find out how far it could stretch.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a competent, disciplined piece of post-apocalyptic SF that hits its brief with unusual efficiency. The worldbuilding is the strongest element: the obsolescence-engineered seed economy ("engineered abundance but forbidden inheritance") is a genuinely clever extrapolation of real terminator-gene controversies, and the jury-rigged lab is convincingly specific — forklift batteries, a dental X-ray voltage regulator, a doorbell relay as a timer, a cracked phone as thermometer. The black market contract printed on the back of a pharmaceutical price list is a nice ironic touch, and the contract's evolving clauses give the chapter a satisfying structural spine. The prose is deliberately terse and mostly controlled, with a few standout images ("the light strobed like a failing sign over an empty street"; "the company left us a harvest and a cemetery"). However, it occasionally tips into stock phrasing: "the taste of hot coins flooded my mouth" is a cliché, and "perfectly, horribly steady" is a well-worn rhythm. Some sentences fragment into affectation rather than effect ("The cure had taught my body to remake itself, but never asked what it was remaking" is good; "No miracle yet. Only work done before my body could change its mind" is murkier than it thinks it is). The narrator's relationship to Repair-9 is the emotional core and it works — needing the cure while hating it, the sensory sharpening as both gift and symptom. But the physical toll is more asserted than dramatized; we're told about fevers, weight loss, and skin splitting in summary rather than scene. The dialogue is functional and thematically pointed but flat; Darin exists mostly as a contract-delivery device, and his settlement's desperation is stated rather than felt. The mid-chapter crisis (the solar surge cooking the run) resolves a little too conveniently — one surviving fragment, one injection, and the problem is solved within a page, which slightly undercuts the tension the scene builds. The ending's cautious hope ("their green was the stubborn, ordinary green of something that might survive being eaten") is well-earned and appropriately hedged — no miracle, just seedlings and a renegotiated contract — so the positivity feels congruent with the piece's logic. The narrator's steadiness after the second dose is a small unearned convenience, but it's set up by the earlier dose, so it passes. Length is roughly on target. Overall: a solid, professional piece with strong concept and texture, held back by thin characterization, some tell-heavy exposition, and a few stock phrases. + Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 56.6
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## The Convenient Invitation Arthur kept adjusting his collar as the transfer vessel *Cynthia B.* rolled with the gentle, unreasonable motion of a ship changing course. The black tunic had been pressed aboard, stiff enough to stand unaided. He was thirty-one, a mining engineer, and a first-generation Martian—which meant, as his father liked to say, that Earth was a country he had never governed. He had a small house beneath two tons of regolith and sixty-one people dependent on his claim. Twenty hours ago, armed men had arrived to explain that all three were now negotiable. They had been unusually polite about it. Six of them had descended from the morning shuttle wearing grey uniforms and compact needle carbines. Their insignia was a gold sunburst enclosing a blue-white star: Antares Diplomatic Corps, according to the woman who spoke. “Mr. Neegan, the Corps requests your presence at an off-world meeting concerning your property.” “I’d like to see the request.” “You are seeing it.” “The rest?” “Off-world.” At that range, Arthur had observed, the distinction between an invitation and an instruction was largely terminological. The woman had introduced herself as Prefect Voss. She had not threatened his family, searched his house, or helped herself to his survey instruments. Instead, two of her men had quietly taken possession of the power controls while another stood beside Arthur’s core samples. “You have a comfortable ship,” Arthur had said. “We are told you will find it comfortable.” The sample case had come with him. So had the collar. He suspected these were related only in the minds of people who wished to make him comfortable. The *Cynthia B.* had no observation port. That was technically a docking port, Voss explained, but the distinction did not comfort him. The cabin possessed the air of an expensive terrestrial hotel: indirect lighting, synthetic wood panelling, a narrow bed, and a pitcher of water with the assurance that it contained no minerals worth stealing. The food was perfectly prepared and flavoured with nothing Arthur could identify. They had spent the first six hours beyond Mars orbit, then rendezvoused with a larger vessel. Now, through the meeting room’s single broad window, he could see only the curve of Mars. It filled half the sky, ochre and white and seemingly close enough to touch. In reality, someone had told him during the voyage, it was some two hundred kilometres away. Yet the dome lights along his property, barely distinguishable, seemed to shine in the same room with him. Earth was another matter. Earth was a memory, a market, and, increasingly, a creditor. He was still puzzling over the implications of the armed hospitality when the door opened. “You must be Arthur Neegan,” said the man beyond it. “The engineer, not the public figure. How fortunate that they are so nearly indistinguishable.” Arthur rose. “You have the advantage.” “Director Dardin, special envoy. At the moment, that is all I can safely be.” Dardin was perhaps sixty, broad and silver-haired, dressed in a suit that had survived the journey without a wrinkle. His eyes moved over Arthur’s borrowed tunic with polite disappointment. “I trust the accommodations were satisfactory?” “Your ship has excellent taste in collars and poor taste in not providing windows.” “A diplomatic asset. One must learn to conduct important business without the distraction of scenery.” Dardin sat. “Would you care to drink something that is not a mineral solution?” “Coffee.” “Of course.” The coffee arrived, hot and black and unmistakably real. Arthur had last tasted it three years before, at his father’s funeral. Dardin watched him take it. “You are wondering what you have become involved in.” “No. I decided that before boarding.” “Then you are ahead of most engineers.” You have a discovery that people want to kill for, Dardin said. That is not quite the same thing. People want to kill for many things, but usually they begin with the things they cannot otherwise obtain. Arthur set down the cup. “What is that, in this case?” Dardin placed a thin data slate on the table. “Eighty million credits.” Arthur waited. He had acquired the habit, during negotiations over machinery and labour, of letting silence do the first round of work. “Paid not in ordinary credits,” Dardin continued, “but in oxygen bonds and registered mining shares. There are enough bonds to provide breathable air to every registered resident on your lease for twenty years. The shares carry an eighty-percent return guaranteed by Antares Development Combine.” Arthur read the figures. They were even more impressive in the absence of context. “And the workers?” “Their contracts are reviewed. All illegitimate debt clauses are cancelled. Each family receives a residential claim in its own name.” “*Illegitimate?*” “There is a technical distinction.” “In other words, you’ll pay their debts.” “They become your beneficiaries.” “And in return?” “Your mineral claim, assay records, and survey data. A seven-year operating lease on the vein. The right to purchase your workers’ production at a fixed price.” The price was generous. Dangerously so. “There’s more,” said Dardin. “There usually is.” “We intend to finance a Martian government with universal suffrage, property protections, and a foreign policy independent of Earth. You would be one of its founding electors.” Arthur looked up. “You’re buying my vote.” “We are investing in your judgment. We would also finance your campaign for the Assembly.” “You didn’t buy my vote.” “Yet.” Dardin took a drink of his coffee. Outside, Mars turned slowly, carrying clouds and cities and a billion human arguments around the same battered planet. “You own an enormous deposit,” Arthur said. “We do not need the deposit.” “Then why are you here?” “Because you did more than discover it.” Dardin turned the slate around. A legal document appeared, dense with clauses. “In eight days, the Earth Ministry of Resources intends to introduce an emergency common-ground bill. The central parcel of each deposit would become the legal key to every surrounding claim. Whoever owns it could license, veto, or absorb them all.” Arthur read paragraph nineteen. “This is the mineral lease I signed six years ago.” “Appendix eleven, subsection four. You filed the survey automatically when you registered the well. I imagine you never read that far.” “No.” “Most people don’t. It is a useful little lesson in the value of literacy.” “So Earth wants to take my claim.” “Earth wants to ensure that no Martian owns anything important without Earth’s permission.” Dardin’s voice remained mild. “The Ministry calls it stabilization. The Combine calls it civilization. The Freeholders call it theft. We simply point out that a colony capable of governing itself requires more than a surface.” Arthur understood the larger picture. Earth possessed the industry, the fleets, and the accumulated political machinery of several centuries. Mars possessed the rocks, the labour, and a stubborn conviction that distance constituted a government. The trouble was that both sides preferred the other to remain unfinished. “And your interest?” “Order, Mr. Neegan. Cheap order is our business.” Arthur picked up the contract. A silver seal marked the door: a gold sunburst with thirteen rays. He noticed because his mother had been a cartographer. She had taught him that a map’s most dangerous feature was usually the mistake no one else had seen. Dardin followed his gaze. “A variation of the traditional insignia,” he said. “Do you know the traditional one has twelve rays?” “Old habits die hard.” Arthur returned to the contract. “If I refuse?” “Then the Combine will purchase the debt of your tenants. It will close the atmospheric plant unless you surrender voting rights. It will place guards at the railway and call them security. Within a year, your claim will belong to the Ministry, your workers will belong to the Combine, and you will be free to explain to the latter what freedom cost.” “Not much of a choice.” “It is the only choice. We merely arrange for both alternatives to have our fingerprints on them.” Arthur looked again at the thirteen-rayed star. “One more condition,” he said. “I want assurances that my people can leave Mars without your consent.” Dardin smiled. “You have just discovered the principal difference between a government and a corporation. One permits its citizens to emigrate. The other charges them for the opportunity.” At that moment, a light appeared over the door. “Sir,” said Voss, “the transfer vessel has completed its external checks. It must undock in twenty-eight minutes.” Dardin did not turn around. “Thank you, Prefect.” Arthur looked through the window. The *Cynthia B.* was already drawing away, shrinking into the darkness between Mars and its moons. Its passenger compartment was lit, warm, and empty. “So that,” he said, “was not really the return ticket.” “It was never intended to be.” “Where is it going?” “For now, the outer shipyards. Its next scheduled run to Mars is in four months.” Arthur took a breath. Somewhere below him, his house waited beneath its patient roof. His workers were waking for the morning shift, trusting that the ore they touched still belonged to the man who had found it. Dardin pushed the contract across the table. “Shall we discuss the price of your cooperation?” Arthur looked at the pen, the elegant clothing, the armed ship waiting beyond reach. “I think,” he said, “the price is still being decided.” For the first time, Dardin’s expression disturbed him more than the guns had. It was the expression of a man who had been given to understand exactly what that meant.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong pastiche of Asimov's style: dialogue-driven, cerebral, with big-picture political economy (Earth vs. colony interests, corporate power, legalistic maneuvering) layered over small human details (coffee, collars, core samples). The chapter follows the prompt closely: opens aboard the transfer vessel, flashback to the armed "invitation," meeting with Dardin, offer made, intrigue hinted (the common-ground bill, the thirteen-rayed insignia suggesting a false or splinter Antares faction). The dialogue is crisp and aphoristic in a way that evokes Asimov's dry wit, though occasionally it tips into cleverness that serves the author more than the character ("the distinction between an invitation and an instruction was largely terminological" — actually quite good). The thirteen-rayed sunburst detail is a nice Asimovian clue. Weaknesses: some formatting glitches (a paragraph of Dardin's dialogue rendered without quotation marks), the stakes are explained rather heavily through exposition, and Dardin is a fairly stock silver-tongued envoy. The ending line is effective and ominous. Prose is clean, controlled, rarely purple. Emotional complexity is moderate — Arthur is more a chess piece than a person, which is period-appropriate but limits emotional depth. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations By the third week, the darkroom had become a country with no daylight. It smelled of stop bath, wet cardboard, and the metallic ghost of fixer. Under the safelight, our hands looked anatomical, blood reduced to ink. Elliot and I stood on either side of the developing tray, waiting for a photograph to admit it existed. He was nineteen. I was twenty-five. I usually filled rooms myself: white shirt buttoned to the throat, red nails, posture that said *Give me a reason*. In relationships, I liked women whose certainty met mine halfway. Elliot met nothing halfway. He met it carefully. His long black thrift-shop coat, layered mesh, and mismatched silver rings gave him the sharp silhouette of a villain in a film about saints. Beneath all that, he spoke softly. When he concentrated, he folded one hand around the other wrist, holding himself with improbable gentleness. People stared at his clothes. He seemed mostly interested in making sure they were comfortable. The contrast had snagged in me long before we were paired. Our project required a portrait that resisted explanation. He kept tilting his head at the empty background, rearranging the lights, then asking whether a composition was too on the nose. I admired his precision, and the hollow of his throat when he leaned over the loupe. I resented how little I trusted my own motives. That night, after the enlarger clicked twice, he set down the print with unusual care. “Can I tell you something that isn’t about the project?” I should have said *of course*, the brisk reassurance I gave everyone. Instead, because he looked at the red light instead of me, I said, “Tell me.” “Everyone calls me he,” he said. “I do too. Mostly, it fits. But lately it feels like only part of the answer. I thought if I found the right clothes, the right way of moving, I’d know whether I was a guy. I don’t.” He stopped, fingers worrying the hem of his sleeve. “Sometimes I wonder if it’s my gender. Sometimes I think it’s just how I express it. Sometimes I don’t know what I’m looking at.” The urge to solve him rose in me, clean and immediate. I wanted to ask what names he’d considered, what he felt when people used the wrong ones, whether a word existed that fixed the wrongness. I wanted to give him an elegant theory. Instead, I heard the effort beneath his voice and kept my questions to myself. “You don’t have to know tonight,” I said. “Or tomorrow. Not for me.” He finally looked up. “That’s different.” “Is it bad?” “No. I don’t think anyone’s asked me that before.” His shoulders loosened. I understood, then, that protecting his vulnerability did not mean pretending he couldn’t bear its weight. It meant not making my curiosity heavier than his need. I reached for the enlarger, then stopped. I could take over: choose the filter, adjust the shadows, make him indisputably beautiful. I wanted to find out what it meant to take charge of the space without taking him over. “What do you want the portrait to hold?” I asked. “Me,” he said. “Before I have words for the rest of me.” “Hands first, then,” I said. “Can you show me what that looks like?” He nodded. I made him say *yes* before I moved his sleeve from his wrist. The request changed the air. I had expected the image to challenge my preferences. I hadn’t expected the permission to undo me. He stood beneath the enlarger, a velvet hanger against one palm. Light found the ridges of his knuckles, the silver at his throat, the faint shadow where shaving had grazed his jaw. I raised the camera. Something fierce and protective moved through me. I wanted everyone to see his courage. But wanting to display someone’s bravery could be another way of owning it. So I framed him instead. I softened the lamp and asked, “Are you all right?” “I am,” he said. “It feels strange, but yes.” I lowered the shutter. The photograph, surfacing in the tray, caught him neither masked nor revealed. He was simply arriving. “I thought it would look more certain,” he said. “It looks more honest,” I said. He studied that. “Those aren’t always the same thing.” No, I thought. But they were here. When I passed him the second sheet, our fingers touched. I would once have let my hand linger, turned accident into proposition. This time I stayed still. He drew back, then laid his fingertips over mine. The touch was feather-light, almost exploratory. I let him keep it there until he decided the question was finished. My usual attractions arranged themselves in my memory: clear silhouettes, low voices, women who took up space without apology. Elliot didn’t replace them. He made me doubt how neatly I had sorted myself. Desire could be stranger than the stories I told about it, and attraction did not have to become a verdict before it could be true. I had mistaken definiteness for depth. He leaned close to inspect the drying print. “You’re different in here.” “So are you,” I replied. “Not enough to know yet.” “Do you want to know?” He considered. “Not tonight. I want to see what happens if I don’t decide.” I nodded. It cost more restraint than any critique had asked. “Okay,” I said. He smiled. “You’re good at this.” “Don’t get used to it.” He laughed, quiet and startled by the sound. My phone buzzed in my pocket, insisting on a bright world beyond the door. I ignored it. Outside, people waited for neat explanations, for bodies to fall into line with their categories. In here, the red light made every certainty look temporary. I let it. He lifted the last print by its edges. “This one looks like me,” he said. “Yes,” I said, and meant it without knowing what *yes* contained. The answer could wait. The portrait, at least, was ours. We hung it to drip in the dark, side by side, beneath the same red light. Nothing had to be named to be real.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted piece that fulfills nearly every instruction in the prompt. The darkroom setting is used as more than backdrop—the red safelight, developing chemistry, and the act of making a portrait become metaphors for Elliot's self-development and Dani's careful attention. The prose is disciplined and image-driven: "blood reduced to ink," "the sharp silhouette of a villain in a film about saints," "he was simply arriving." Dani's characterization is the strongest element. Her assertiveness is established quickly and concretely, and the narrative genuinely dramatizes her central conflict: the urge to "solve" Elliot versus the restraint of letting him lead. Moments like "I made him say yes before I moved his sleeve from his wrist" and "not making my curiosity heavier than his need" show the take-charge/give-agency tension in action rather than assertion. Her confusion about her own attraction patterns is handled with appropriate messiness—she doesn't resolve it, which is correct. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally tips into aphoristic over-density ("He met nothing halfway. He met it carefully" is good; "Desire could be stranger than the stories I told about it" is a bit fortune-cookie). Some lines strain for cleverness ("a country with no daylight"). The dialogue is mostly strong but occasionally exchanges ideas rather than words—"Those aren't always the same thing" feels like the author speaking. The ending's "Nothing had to be named to be real" is a touch neat, though earned by the piece's refusal to resolve anything prematurely. The phone-buzzing beat is a slightly stock gesture toward the outside world. Minor logic quibbles: the portrait project mechanics blur (camera in a darkroom under safelight, "velvet hanger" appearing unexplained), and the timeline compresses three weeks into one scene without consequence. These are small. Overall this is polished literary work with genuine emotional intelligence, minor overreach in style, and no structural failures.
